Their rulers wail," declares the LORD, "and continually all the day my name is despised.<sup>6</sup>Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am."<sup>7</sup>How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, "Your God reigns."<sup>8</sup>The voice of your watchmen—they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion.<sup>9</sup>Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.<sup>11</sup>Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard.<sup>13</sup>Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted.<sup>14</sup>As many were astonished at you— his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the children of mankind—<sup>15</sup>so shall he sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him, for that which has not been told them they see, and that which they have not heard they understand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wake Up and Get Dressed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zion is ordered awake. Verses 1 and 2 tell her to put on strength and her festival clothes, shake off the dust, get up off the ground and untie her own neck. Verses 3 and 4 give the economics of it: she was sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money, which is the pattern from Egypt onward. Verses 5 and 6 state God's own motive — his name is being despised all day long among the nations — and promise that his people will know that name, ending on two of the shortest words God ever says about himself: here I am.
verseByVerse.theology: The imperatives rest on an indicative that has already happened: she is told to rise because she has been redeemed, not in order to be. That order is the whole logic of gospel commands, which never ask a person to produce a standing they do not have but to start living in one they have been given. And verse 3 grounds the freeness of grace in law rather than sentiment: the captor paid nothing, so he is owed nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 1 is the answer to a prayer prayed one chapter earlier. In 51:9 the people cry, 'Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD.' Here the same three words come back addressed to them: 'Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion.' The arm was never asleep. The exiles' problem was never that God needed rousing.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city; for there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean. Shake yourself from the dust and arise; be seated, O Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, O captive daughter of Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city."

Turn back one chapter before reading this one. In 51:9 the people pray: "Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD." They are asking God to wake up. They believe the problem is a sleeping God, and they say so in three words.

Here those same three words come back, aimed the other way. Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion. God does not argue with the prayer. He repeats it to the people who prayed it. The arm was never asleep; the city was.

"Put on your beautiful garments." She is not told to work, or to repent, or to prepare a defence. She is told to get dressed — and to get dressed for a festival, in the clothes you would put on for the best day of the year. The command is disorientating precisely because nothing in her circumstances has changed yet.

"Shake yourself from the dust and arise; be seated, O Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, O captive daughter of Zion."

Four movements, and they take her from the floor to a chair. Sitting in dust was what mourners and prisoners did; getting up and sitting down properly is what a person does who has stopped mourning. And loose the bonds from your neck — she is told to untie herself, which she could not have done a moment earlier and can do now, because verse 3 is about to say the price has been settled.

That is the order of every command God gives his people, and it never runs the other way. He does not say free yourself and then I will redeem you. He says: you have been redeemed, now take the rope off. The instruction is not the condition of the rescue; it is the first act of a rescued person.

Which is why a Christian who feels bound is usually not being asked to try harder at being free. He is being asked to believe an announcement that has already been made about him, and then to stand up.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money." For thus says the Lord GOD: "My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there, and the Assyrian oppressed them for nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus says the LORD: 'You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money.'"

Two halves of one transaction, and both of them are free. God got no price when Israel went into exile — nobody paid him for her, and the phrase in the previous chapter was blunter still: he sold her for her own iniquities. And Babylon will get no price when she comes out. No ransom is negotiated, no compensation paid, no settlement reached.

The reason is legal rather than sentimental. A captor with no claim is owed nothing. If Babylon had bought Israel fairly, a redemption price would be due; because she simply took what was not hers, God can walk in and take it back without a transaction. Grace is free at this end because the claim against it was never valid in the first place.

"My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there, and the Assyrian oppressed them for nothing."

Then the history, and it is given as a pattern rather than a list. Egypt at the beginning, Assyria in the middle, Babylon now. Three times the same shape: a people taken by someone with no right to them, and a God who comes and gets them out. The exiles are not living through something unprecedented. They are living through the third act of a play whose ending they already know.

And the word that keeps recurring is for nothing. Taken for nothing, oppressed for nothing, redeemed without money. Everything about this exchange is unpaid on one side and unearned on the other, which is a fair description of how anyone gets home.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore what have I here," declares the LORD, "seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Their rulers wail," declares the LORD, "and continually all the day my name is despised. Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"'Now therefore what have I here,' declares the LORD, 'seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Their rulers wail,' declares the LORD, 'and continually all the day my name is despised.'"

God gives his reason for acting, and it is not the one most readers would predict. Not first their suffering, though he has spoken of that at length. His name. All day long, in Babylon, people are drawing the obvious conclusion from a defeated people — that their God was too weak to hold his own city — and the conclusion is being said out loud where he can hear it.

That is a strange comfort, and a very solid one. If God rescued only when he was moved by pity, the rescue would rest on the strength of a feeling. Because his own reputation is staked on it, the rescue rests on something that cannot waver. Israel's safety is welded to God's honour, and he will not have his name despised.

"Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am."

The chapter has moved from the nations mocking the name to the people knowing it, and then it ends on two words. Hinneni. Here I am.

Those are the words a servant says when a master calls. They are what Abraham said on the mountain, what Moses said at the bush, what Isaiah himself said in chapter 6 when God asked whom he should send. And here it is God saying it — the master answering, present and available, to people who had spent seventy years convinced he was not listening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Beautiful Feet, and an Unhurried Exodus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A runner appears on the ridge above the city. Verse 7 calls his feet beautiful and compresses his message into four announcements ending in two words: your God reigns. Verse 8 has the watchmen singing because they can see the LORD returning at close range. Verses 9 and 10 order the rubble itself to sing and show God rolling up his sleeve in front of every nation on earth. Verses 11 and 12 send the people out — but unhurried, purified, carrying holy vessels, with God going in front of them and God bringing up the rear.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is the Old Testament's clearest statement of what a gospel announcement actually is, and Paul quotes it as the ground for sending preachers at all: how are they to hear without someone preaching (Rom. 10:14-15)? The content is reducible to a single claim about who is on the throne. And verse 10's bared arm sets up the question chapter 53 opens with — to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? The arm is bared before all the nations here, and in the next chapter nobody recognises it.
verseByVerse.examples: The contrast in verse 12 with the first exodus is deliberate and pastoral. Israel left Egypt in haste, with unleavened bread and sandals on, running. This departure is not a flight from anything: nobody is chasing them, so nobody needs to hurry. A rescue that has to be rushed is a rescue that might still fail, and this one is already secured at both ends of the column.

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, "Your God reigns." The voice of your watchmen—they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, 'Your God reigns.'"

Picture the scene, because Isaiah has built it carefully. A city under occupation, a battle fought somewhere out of sight, and everybody waiting to hear which way it went. The first anyone will know is a runner appearing on the skyline of the hills above the town. Long before his words can be heard, his feet can be seen — and the watchers are staring at the ridge.

That is why the beauty lands on the feet, which is not where beauty normally goes. They are the least lovely part of a man who has run twenty miles over rock. They are beautiful because of what is arriving with them.

The message comes in four announcements that build: good news, peace, good news of happiness, salvation. And then it is compressed into two words: your God reigns. That is the whole of it. Not that the situation has improved, not that the enemy has weakened, but that God is on the throne and the outcome follows from the fact.

Paul quotes this verse to answer a chain of questions about how anyone comes to faith. How are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? "As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!'" (Rom. 10:14-15). The runner on the ridge became, in Paul's hands, the argument for sending anybody anywhere.

"The voice of your watchmen — they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion."

The watchmen were posted to see trouble coming. What they see instead is God coming back, and they see it eye to eye — at close range, face on, with nothing between. Men whose entire job was vigilance stop watching and start singing.

verseByVerse.quote: Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem."

The instruction is given to rubble. Not to the returning exiles, not to the priests — to the waste places, the burnt districts nobody had rebuilt, the parts of the city that were only evidence of what had happened. They are told to sing.

And the tenses are the point. He has comforted. He has redeemed. Isaiah writes it as finished while the ruins are still ruins, which is what makes the command to sing possible at all. The rubble is not singing in hope of something. It is singing about something done.

"The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God."

Baring the arm is what a man does before hard work or a fight — the sleeve pushed back, the muscle out where everyone can see it. God does it publicly, in front of every nation, and the whole earth is going to watch the result.

Hold that image for one chapter. The very next thing said about the arm of the LORD is a question: "To whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?" (53:1), and the answer is almost nobody. God bares his arm in front of the world in 52:10, and in 53:2 what the world actually sees is a man with no form or majesty that anyone should look at him. The arm was bared exactly as promised. It simply did not look like an arm.

verseByVerse.quote: Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD. For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD."

The order to leave, doubled like the order to wake. And the instructions attached are priestly rather than practical — no packing list, no route, no rations. Touch nothing unclean. Purify yourselves. Carry the vessels properly.

The temple articles that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off are going home, and the people carrying them are being treated as though they were Levites. A column of freed slaves walking out of an occupied city is described as a religious procession, because that is what Isaiah understands it to be.

"For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard."

Now compare the first exodus, which every reader would have had in mind. That one was eaten standing up, with belts fastened and sandals on and staff in hand, in haste (Exod. 12:11) — and then pursued to the edge of the sea by chariots. It was an escape.

This is not. You shall not go out in haste. Nobody is chasing them, so nobody needs to run. And the reason is given at both ends of the column: God in front, God behind. There is no direction from which anything can arrive.

A rescue that has to be hurried is a rescue that could still fail. This one is secured front and rear before the first foot moves, which is why the people can walk out of Babylon at the pace of the slowest among them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–15 — Behold My Servant — the Song Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fourth and greatest Servant Song opens here, three verses before the chapter break. Verse 13 announces the outcome before the story: the servant will act wisely and be raised high — three verbs of exaltation stacked up, in the language used of God enthroned in chapter 6. Verse 14 immediately undercuts it with the reason people stared: his appearance was marred beyond human semblance. Verse 15 turns that staring into silence — he will sprinkle many nations, and kings will shut their mouths in front of him.
verseByVerse.theology: God gives away the ending first. Before a word about suffering, the servant is high and lifted up and exalted, which is where the poem starts and where it will finish (53:12); the horror in between is framed by a verdict already delivered. The phrase in verse 13 is the one used of the Lord on the throne at 6:1, and Isaiah applies it to a man whose face people could not look at. Verse 15's verb is the priestly one for the sprinkling of blood, which makes the servant priest as well as victim before the fourth song has properly begun.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul quotes verse 15 to explain why he would only preach where Christ had not been named: those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand (Rom. 15:20-21). The verse became a pioneer missionary's charter. And the astonishment of verse 14 and the shut mouths of verse 15 are the same reaction at two stages — first at what was done to him, then at who he turned out to be.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted."

The greatest of the four Servant Songs begins here, three verses before the chapter break, and God begins it by giving away the ending.

Before a syllable about suffering — before the marred face in the next verse, before the sorrows and the piercing and the grave of the chapter that follows — the first thing said about the servant is that he comes out on top. He shall act wisely, which in Hebrew carries both the wisdom and the success it produces: he will do it well and it will work. And then three verbs piled up, each meaning to be raised: high, lifted up, exalted.

That framing changes how everything after it is read. The horror in chapter 53 is not an open question with an uncertain outcome. It is enclosed at both ends by a verdict already delivered — high and lifted up here, a portion with the many at 53:12 — and the reader goes into the darkest passage in the Old Testament already knowing how it finishes.

And the phrase itself has been used before, in this book, once. In chapter 6 Isaiah saw the Lord "sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up," with the seraphim covering their faces and the building shaking (6:1). Those are the words. Isaiah takes the vocabulary of God enthroned in the temple and lays it on a servant whose appearance, one verse later, will be beyond human semblance.

He does not explain it. He simply uses the throne language of the Holy One for a man, and lets the reader stand between the two sentences and work out what he is being told.

verseByVerse.quote: As many were astonished at you— his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the children of mankind— so shall he sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him, for that which has not been told them they see, and that which they have not heard they understand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As many were astonished at you — his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the children of mankind."

The exaltation of verse 13 is immediately undercut, and the word for it is strong. Marred is disfigurement, spoiling, the ruin of a thing's shape. Beyond human semblance means past the point where the eye registers a person. Not badly beaten — no longer recognisably one of us.

And the reaction Isaiah records is astonishment, the word for being appalled into stillness. People stopped and stared, the way traffic stops at an accident, at something they could not take in and could not look away from.

"So shall he sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him."

The verb is the priestly one. Sprinkling is what a priest does with blood — on the altar, on the mercy seat, on the people — to make what was unclean fit to approach God (Lev. 4; 16). Some translators render it "startle" instead, since the Hebrew is disputed, and the sense of shock would fit the verse; but the word as it stands is the one from the sacrificial system, and it means the disfigured man of verse 14 is the priest, not only the victim. He is doing something with what has been done to him.

Then the reversal, and it matches the astonishment exactly. In verse 14 people stare in horror. In verse 15 kings shut their mouths — the gesture of men who have run out of anything to say. The same figure produces both reactions, at different points in the story.

"For that which has not been told them they see, and that which they have not heard they understand." Paul made this his working rule. He would preach where Christ had not been named, "but as it is written, 'Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand'" (Rom. 15:20-21). The song that begins here was, from its first appearance, aimed at people who had no reason at all to be expecting it.

52.theology:
The imperative rests on the indicative. Zion is told to rise and dress because she has been redeemed, not in order to be. That order runs through the whole chapter — loose your own bonds (v. 2) comes after you shall be redeemed (v. 3) — and it is the structure of every command God gives his people. And the freeness is grounded in law rather than in sentiment: the captor paid nothing for her, so he is owed nothing for her.

God’s name as the ground of rescue. Verse 5 gives the motive for the exodus from Babylon and it is God’s own honour, publicly despised while his people sit in captivity. That is a more solid foundation than divine sympathy, because a reputation staked cannot waver as a feeling might. The chapter ends this movement on hinneni — here I am — the servant’s answer to a master, spoken by God to his people.

The song opens with the verdict. Before any suffering is mentioned, the servant is high and lifted up and exalted (v. 13), in the vocabulary used of God on the throne at 6:1. The atrocity of chapter 53 is therefore framed at both ends by an outcome already announced. Verse 15 adds the priestly note before the song has properly begun: the disfigured man sprinkles many nations, which is what a priest does with blood, so he is not only the victim of what happens to him.

53.subtitle: The Suffering Servant
53.intro:
Overview. Isaiah 53 is the summit of the book and the clearest sight of the cross anywhere in the Old Testament. It is the last of four Servant Songs, and it begins at 52:13, not at 53:1 — the poem runs in five strophes of three verses, opening with God’s verdict on his servant (52:13-15) before the world gives its own. The figure it describes suffers for sins that are not his: pierced for transgressions, crushed for iniquities, bearing the iniquity of us all, and then, impossibly, seeing offspring and length of days after being cut off out of the land of the living.

The New Testament writers return to this chapter constantly and apply it to one person. Matthew quotes v. 4 (8:17), Luke has Jesus quote v. 12 of himself (22:37), John quotes v. 1 to explain unbelief (12:38), Philip preaches Jesus from vv. 7-8 (Acts 8:32-35), Paul cites it twice (Rom. 10:16; 15:21), and Peter builds a whole paragraph out of vv. 5, 6, 9 and 12 (1 Pet. 2:22-25). The chapter is written in the past tense, as though the suffering were already finished and the speakers were looking back at it in astonishment — which is exactly the position of everyone who has since believed the report.

keyVerse.quote: “But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.”
keyVerse.note: This verse is the clearest statement of penal substitutionary atonement in the entire Bible. The prepositions carry the weight: for our transgressions, for our iniquities. The chastisement (divine judicial punishment) fell on him so that peace could come to us. This is not one theory of the atonement among others — it is the grammar Isaiah uses to describe what God planned.

53.theology:
Penal substitution. This is the Old Testament’s fullest account of what later theology calls penal substitution: real guilt, real punishment, borne by another. All the parts are here — the guilt of “all we” (v. 6), the categories of piercing for transgressions and crushing for iniquities (v. 5), and the result, peace and healing for those whose iniquity he carried. What settles it as substitution rather than mere sympathy is the grammar of v. 5: four possessives on our side, four wounds on his, and nothing shared.

The Father is the agent, not the spectator. Verse 6 says the LORD laid the iniquity on him and v. 10 says it was the LORD’s will to crush him. This forecloses the picture of a kind Son winning round a reluctant Father. Mercy is not extracted from justice in this chapter; justice is the instrument mercy uses. R. C. Sproul called Isaiah 53 the chapter that makes the cross comprehensible, and it is verse 10 that does the work.

Justification, and resurrection. Verse 11 holds both halves of justification in one line: he bears their iniquities, and he makes many to be accounted righteous — a courtroom verdict, declared, on a ground outside the person declared. And the promises made to a man already cut off out of the land of the living (vv. 8, 10) — offspring, length of days, satisfaction — require a resurrection that Isaiah states without explaining. On the extent of the “many,” godly readers differ and this chapter does not settle it; what it does settle is the efficacy. The servant does not make many righteous available. He makes many righteous.
53.reflection: The chapter opens with a question about believing: “Who has believed what he heard from us?” And it closes with intercession: the Servant makes intercession for the transgressors. You are among the transgressors for whom he intercedes. What difference does it make — practically, emotionally, theologically — to know that the risen Christ is right now interceding for you at the Father’s right hand (Rom. 8:34)?

and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not.<sup>4</sup>Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted.<sup>5</sup>But he was pierced for our transgressions; verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song's second strophe (52:13-15 is the first) turns from God's verdict on his servant to the world's. Verse 1 is a lament over unbelief: the news has been announced and not received. Verse 2 explains why — he came up like a shoot out of dry ground, with nothing about him to attract a second look. Verse 3 states the verdict the world reached: despised, rejected, a man of sorrows, a face people turned away from. The speakers are not enemies. They are the confessing community, looking back at what they once thought.
verseByVerse.theology: The offence of the incarnation is located here rather than at the cross. The Word became flesh in a form that gave the eye nothing to admire, so that faith could never rest on appearance. What verse 1 calls the arm of the LORD — the muscle that split the sea at 51:9 and was bared before the nations at 52:10 — is revealed in a man from whom people looked away. Revelation and concealment are the same act.
verseByVerse.examples: John quotes verse 1 at the close of Jesus' public ministry (John 12:38) to explain why the signs did not produce faith. The problem was never a shortage of evidence. Every generation repeats the sorting of verse 2, choosing by appearance and assuming that what is impressive is what is important.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song does not open with the servant. It opens with a complaint about how badly the news has gone down. "Who has believed what he has heard from us?" Somebody has been sent running with a report — the herald of 52:7, whose feet on the mountains are called beautiful — and the answer to his question is: almost nobody.

"And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?" Follow that phrase back through the book. The arm of the LORD is the muscle of God in action: the arm that cut Rahab in pieces and dried up the sea (51:9-10), the arm bared in the sight of all the nations (52:10). Every reader of Isaiah knows what the arm looks like when it is revealed. It looks like the Red Sea standing up in two walls.

Here it is revealed, and it looks like a man nobody wanted to look at. That is the whole difficulty of verse 1. The unbelief is not stubbornness in the face of an obvious miracle; it is the entirely natural failure to recognise omnipotence in that form.

Verse 2 says why. "He grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground." Before him — before God, who was watching the whole time, although nobody else was. A shoot out of dry ground is a plant with no reason to be there: no water, no shelter, no advantage. Nazareth, a carpenter's shop, thirty years of nothing that would appear in an account of the period.

Then the flat sentence: "he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him." This does not say he was ugly. It says there was nothing about him that would make you want him — and the four Gospels, which describe a great many faces, never once describe his. Here is a test that can be run on anybody. Make an honest list of what draws you to a person: how they look, what they have, who else admires them, what associating with them would do for you. That list, exactly as it stands, is the instrument by which a whole generation walked past God in the flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He was despised and rejected by men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief."

The two Hebrew words carry more weight than the English suggests. Mak'ovot means pains, the physical and mental kind together; choli means sickness. And acquainted with is yedua', known — he was known by grief the way a man is known by his trade. Grief was not an episode in his life. It was his address.

"And as one from whom men hide their faces." Isaiah does not describe hostility here. He describes a reflex. It is what happens in a hospital corridor when the door of the wrong room is open; what happens on a pavement when someone is weeping and everyone develops an interest in the middle distance. We look away from concentrated pain because we cannot hold it, and the looking away is not cruelty, which is exactly why it indicts us so thoroughly.

"And we esteemed him not." The verb is chashav, to reckon or account — the book-keeping word. We did the sum on him and wrote nothing in the column. Hold onto it, because Isaiah is about to use it again in the very next verse and reveal that our arithmetic was inverted.

John says it in four words at the head of his Gospel: "his own people did not receive him" (John 1:11). The one through whom the world was made stood in it and was passed over. Every eye that turned away was an eye he had designed. He went on holding together the atoms of the men who despised him, and did not stop.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The centre of the poem and, on any Christian reading, the centre of the Old Testament. Verse 4 turns the confession round: the griefs he was known by were ours, and we had read his suffering as God's verdict on him. Verse 5 states the exchange in four clauses, each with a possessive: our transgressions, our iniquities, our peace, our healing — and the piercing and crushing fall on him. Verse 6 gives the reason and names the agent: every one of us turned aside, and the LORD laid the iniquity of us all on him.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the Old Testament's fullest statement of what later theology calls penal substitution: the guilt is real, the punishment is real, and it is borne by another at God's own initiative. Verse 6 forecloses the reading in which the Son wins a reluctant Father round. The LORD is the subject of the sentence. Mercy is not extracted from justice here; justice is the instrument mercy uses.
verseByVerse.examples: Matthew applies verse 4 to an evening of healings (Matt. 8:17) and Peter applies verse 5 to the cross (1 Pet. 2:24); both are right, because the sicknesses of the world and its sin are the same wound at different depths. Verse 6 remains the one sentence in Scripture that most people can say of themselves without argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows." The Hebrew opens with akhen, a word of correction: no — actually. Everything before this was the world's reading. This is the truth breaking in.

And look at which two words come back. Griefs and sorrows here are the same choli and mak'ovot that made him a man of sorrows in verse 3. The grief he was known by was never his own. He was carrying it. Matthew saw that clearly enough to quote this line over an evening of healings in Capernaum (Matt. 8:17) — the bearing began long before Calvary, in every case he touched.

"Yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted." There is the reckoning verb again, and here is the exact shape of the mistake. The crowd at the cross was not wrong to think that God was judging. They were wrong about who was being judged. They got the theology right and the direction backwards, which is a far more dangerous error than simple unbelief.

Then verse 5, four clauses, and the whole gospel is in their grammar. "He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace; and with his wounds we are healed." Four times the possession is ours and four times the wound is his. Nothing in the sentence is shared. It is not that he suffered alongside us; the transaction moves in one direction only.

Slow down on the nouns. Pierced and crushed are violent, final words — not wounded, not bruised. The chastisement is musar, the discipline a father administers; it fell on him and the peace arrived at us, which is not a mood but a treaty: the war is over because the terms were met somewhere else. And wounds is chaburah, the raised welt a blow leaves on skin. By his stripe we are healed.

He was pierced, and he did not put out his hand to stop it. He was crushed, and the crushing was not a defeat but the price He had come to pay. There is no other place in Scripture where the cost of mercy is set out at this range and in this detail, and the one who paid it is worthy of every word.

verseByVerse.quote: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all."

Notice how the verse is built. It begins with all and it ends with all, and between the two stands each individual with his own private direction. The condition is universal and the wandering is personal. Nobody strays in a crowd; each of us has a particular way of our own that we turned into.

And the picture is sheep, not wolves. Isaiah could have said we were rebels, and elsewhere in the book he does. Here he chooses the animal famous for drifting off while eating, one mouthful at a time, until the flock is a field away. That is how most people are actually lost — not by deciding against God on a particular afternoon, but by grazing steadily in a direction nobody chose.

Then the second half, and the agent is named: the LORD has laid it on him. The verb is hiphgia', to make something fall upon, to cause it to meet him. God did not permit this or allow it to happen; he laid it. And remember the word, because it is the same root that closes the chapter in verse 12, where the servant makes intercession — he who had our sin made to meet him now makes our case meet God.

Here is the test. Most people will grant the first half of the verse without much argument; it is not hard to admit you have gone your own way. The second half is where faith actually happens, because it asks you to believe that the iniquity you know to be yours is no longer where you left it. Ask which half you would find harder to say out loud, and you will know whether verse 6 has done its work.

"You were straying like sheep," Peter writes to people who had read this verse all their lives, "but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls" (1 Pet. 2:25). The one on whom the iniquity was laid is the Shepherd it was laid for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — Silent, Cut Off, and Buried
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third strophe follows the servant through trial, execution and burial. Verse 7 is the silence — oppressed and afflicted, he did not open his mouth, like a lamb led to slaughter. Verse 8 is the sentence and its result: taken away by oppression and judgment, cut off out of the land of the living, and struck for the transgression of God's people. Verse 9 is the grave, assigned with the wicked and given by a rich man, over a man who had done no violence and spoken no lie.
verseByVerse.theology: The sinlessness clause in verse 9 is load-bearing. A substitute with sin of his own has a debt of his own and can pay nobody else's. Isaiah states the qualification in the two areas where every other human being fails — what he did and what he said — and Peter quotes it exactly at 1 Peter 2:22.
verseByVerse.examples: Philip found the Ethiopian official reading verses 7 and 8 aloud and asking the only question that matters about them: about whom does the prophet say this? Beginning with that passage, Philip told him the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:32-35). It is the earliest recorded Christian exposition of this chapter, and the sermon reached the water.

verseByVerse.quote: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth." Isaiah says it twice in one verse — the second time after the images of the lamb and the sheep — and the repetition is the point. This is not a man too broken to speak. It is a man declining to.

Read it against the trials. He is silent before the high priest until put on oath (Matt. 26:62-63); he gives Pilate no answer, "not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed" (Matt. 27:14); and before Herod, who questioned him at some length hoping for a miracle, he says nothing at all (Luke 23:9). Any one of those silences could have been broken with a sentence that would have ended the proceedings. The chapter before this one has the same servant saying "I gave my back to those who strike" and setting his face like a flint (50:6-7). The silence is not passivity. It is the same resolve, holding still.

"Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter." This is the sentence an Ethiopian official was reading aloud in a chariot on the Gaza road when Philip drew alongside, and his question — about whom does the prophet say this, himself or someone else? — is the right question and the only one. Philip began with that passage and told him the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:32-35).

Verse 8 is famously difficult Hebrew, and honesty requires saying so; but its main clauses are not in doubt. "By oppression and judgment he was taken away" — the machinery of law and power, working properly, removes him. "Who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living?" To be cut off with no descendant was the bleakest thing that could be said of a man in Israel, a name ending in the middle of a sentence. Keep it in view for two verses; Isaiah is going to promise this childless dead man a family.

And then the possessive changes hands. He was "stricken for the transgression of my people." The confessing crowd has been saying our since verse 4. Now God speaks, and calls them his.

verseByVerse.quote: And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death."

Two burials are named in one line, and they do not belong together. Executed criminals were disposed of, not buried — thrown where the other bodies went, which is the fate the sentence assigns him. A rich man's tomb is the opposite: a cut chamber, a rolling stone, spices, honour. Isaiah writes both, and the collision sat unexplained for seven hundred years until a wealthy member of the council went to Pilate and asked for the body, and laid it in his own new tomb (Matt. 27:57-60).

The burial is not a footnote to the death. It is the seal on it: a body that is wrapped and carried and shut behind a stone is a body everyone agrees is dead. And it is the first movement upward in the whole poem. The descent has been unbroken since verse 2 — unwanted, despised, pierced, crushed, silenced, cut off — and here, at the very bottom, something is done for him rather than to him.

Then the reason, and it is a legal one: "although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth." Isaiah tests him in the two places where every human life fails — what a man does with his hands and what he does with his tongue — and returns nothing on either. Peter, writing to slaves being punished unjustly, quotes exactly this clause of him (1 Pet. 2:22).

That clause is doing more than praising him. A substitute with sin of his own has a debt of his own, and a debtor cannot stand surety. The innocence in verse 9 is what makes the exchange in verse 5 lawful rather than merely moving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — He Shall See and Be Satisfied
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final strophe turns without warning. Verse 10 says the crushing was the will of the LORD and calls the servant's life a guilt offering — and then promises him offspring and long life, which a dead man cannot have. Verse 11 has him looking at the outcome and being satisfied, and accounting many righteous by bearing their iniquities. Verse 12 gives him the victor's portion, names him among the transgressors, and leaves him alive and interceding.
verseByVerse.theology: Justification is stated here in its two halves, which the New Testament will keep together: he bears their iniquities, and he makes many to be accounted righteous. The verb in verse 11 is a courtroom word — to declare in the right, not to make gradually better. And the future tenses in a poem about a grave are the Old Testament's most explicit demand for resurrection: a soul poured out to death is promised offspring, length of days and satisfaction.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus quoted verse 12 of himself on the last night, saying that this Scripture must be fulfilled in him (Luke 22:37). The intercession of the final clause has not stopped: Romans 8:34 and Hebrews 7:25 both describe the risen Christ praying for his people now, which is this verse in the present tense.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief."

This is the hardest sentence in the Old Testament, and softening it would be a kindness to nobody. The verb behind the will of is chafets — to delight in, to take pleasure in. It was the LORD's good pleasure to crush him. Whatever else is said about the cross, it cannot be said that the Father was a bystander to it. Nor does this mean he watched his Son's agony with enjoyment; chafets is the settled pleasure of a purpose achieved, and the purpose being achieved was the rescue of the people in verse 6. Read the two together and the sentence becomes bearable: what God delighted in was not the pain but what the pain was buying.

"When his soul makes an offering for guilt." The word is asham, and it is a specific sacrifice, not a general one — the guilt offering of Leviticus 5:14-6:7, the only one that came with a repayment attached. Ordinary sin offerings dealt with defilement; the asham dealt with debt, and the worshipper brought the ram and the restitution plus a fifth. Isaiah is not saying the servant makes God feel differently about us. He is saying the servant pays back what was taken.

And then the impossible clauses, in the future tense, in the middle of a funeral: "he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days." Two verses ago this man was cut off out of the land of the living with no future at all. Now he is promised children and length of days. There is only one way for both sentences to be true about one person, and Isaiah states it seven centuries early without a word of explanation.

"Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied." Satisfied is a strong word, and it is the answer to a question worth asking honestly: was it worth it to him? The text says he looks at what the anguish bought and is content — which is what Hebrews means by "for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross" (Heb. 12:2). If you have ever wondered whether you personally are worth that transaction, the answer is not yours to calculate. He has done the sum, and he is satisfied.

"By his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities." Both halves of justification stand in one line. Accounted righteous is hitsdiq, a courtroom verb — to declare in the right, not to make gradually better — and the ground of the verdict is the clause beside it: he bears their iniquities. Our sin was reckoned to him in verse 6; his standing is reckoned to us here. Godly readers differ over how wide many reaches, and Isaiah does not settle that debate; what he settles is the efficacy. The servant does not make many righteous available. He makes many righteous.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong."

The imagery turns military at the last moment: the commander's share, the spoil parted out after the battle. And it begins with therefore. The exaltation is not compensation offered to console him for a bad afternoon; it is the wage of an achievement, grounded in the four clauses that follow — because he poured out his soul to death, was numbered with the transgressors, bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.

"Numbered with the transgressors." Jesus quoted this clause of himself, by name, on the last night of his life: "For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me" (Luke 22:37). Within hours he was crucified between two criminals, filed with them in the record — and one of them, in the last minutes available to him, asked to be remembered and was promised paradise. Even the fulfilment of the clause acquired a trophy.

Then the last verb in the poem, and it is in the present tense: he makes intercession for the transgressors. Not made. The root is paga', the same root as verse 6, where the LORD caused our iniquity to meet him. The traffic has reversed. What met him at the cross was our guilt; what he now makes meet God is our case. Romans 8:34 and Hebrews 7:25 are both this clause written out in the present tense — he always lives to make intercession for them.

So the poem that opened with a report nobody believed closes with the man in the report praying for the people who did not believe it. He is not pleading; he is entitled. The wounds are the argument, the verdict is already in, and the intercession has not paused for two thousand years — not this morning, not while this was being read. He was despised and we esteemed him not, and he is at this moment naming us before the throne of God.

6.subtitle: Holy, Holy, Holy — Isaiah's Vision and Call
6.intro:
Overview. Isaiah’s call comes in chapter 6 rather than chapter 1, and the placement is deliberate: only after five chapters setting out what God requires does the prophet see who God is. He is shown the Lord enthroned in the temple, attended by seraphim whose threefold cry — Holy, holy, holy — is the only attribute of God that Scripture ever raises to that degree. The vision ruins him. He confesses unclean lips, is cleansed by a coal carried from the altar, overhears God asking whom he shall send, and volunteers.

Then the commission turns strange. He is sent to preach a message that will harden rather than heal, until the cities are empty and the people carried away. The chapter’s last four words are its hope: a felled tree leaves a stump, and the holy seed is that stump — a line that runs forward to the shoot from Jesse’s stump in chapter 11 and the root out of dry ground in chapter 53. Two details of the setting repay attention: Uzziah died a leper for forcing his way into the holy place (2 Chr. 26:16-21), and John says the glory Isaiah saw here was Christ’s (John 12:41).

keyVerse.quote: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.”
keyVerse.note: The trisagion is the heart of Isaiah's vision and arguably the heart of the entire book. Every chapter of Isaiah flows from this reality: God is holy, and the earth belongs to him. Judgment is what holiness does when it encounters persistent unrepentance. Comfort is what holiness does when it encounters the broken and contrite. The missionary call of verse 8 is also a response to this: if the whole earth is full of his glory, the whole earth needs to hear about it.

6.theology:
Holiness. This is the Old Testament’s defining text on holiness, and it presents it as more than moral purity. God is in a category with nobody else in it — uncreated where all else is made — which is why sinless creatures still cover their faces. The veiling in verse 2 is creatureliness, not shame. Hebrew raises a word to its highest degree by doubling it; only here is anything tripled.

Atonement and access. Verses 5-7 run in the gospel’s own order and it is never reversed: the sight of holiness produces the knowledge of guilt, and the confession of guilt is met by an act of atonement that comes from the altar, where something has died. Isaiah contributes nothing and is asked for nothing. Set the chapter’s two touches side by side — the LORD touched Uzziah and he was a leper (2 Kings 15:5); the seraph touched Isaiah and his guilt was gone — and the difference is not the men but the altar the fire came through.

Judicial hardening, and its limit. In verses 9-10 God confirms in blindness those who have already refused to see, and the New Testament reaches for the passage in all four Gospels and Acts whenever unbelief persists in the face of evidence. Two things stand together: God hardens (Isaiah 6:10) and they harden themselves (Matt. 13:15). Neither cancels the other. And verse 13 sets the limit — the hardening is real and it is not the last word, because the stump left in the ash is holy seed.
6.reflection: Isaiah's “Here am I! Send me” is often quoted as a model of eagerness for service — but it only makes sense after what precedes it. He is not a volunteer who has assessed the risks and decided to help. He is a ruined man who has been remade by the coal from the altar, and his readiness is the overflow of that experience. True willingness for costly service is always downstream of being undone and restored.
6.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple.<sup>2</sup>Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew.<sup>3</sup>And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!"<sup>4</sup>And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.<sup>5</sup>And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!"<sup>6</sup>Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar.<sup>7</sup>And he touched my mouth and said: "Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for."<sup>8</sup>And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then I said, "Here I am! Send me."<sup>9</sup>And he said, "Go, and say to this people: "'Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive.'<sup>10</sup>Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed."<sup>11</sup>Then I said, "How long, O Lord?" And he said: "Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without people, and the land is a desolate waste,<sup>12</sup>and the LORD removes people far away, and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land.<sup>13</sup>And though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again, like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled." The holy seed is its stump.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Throne That Was Never Vacant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah dates his vision to the year King Uzziah died, and the dating is the point: an earthly throne falls empty and the prophet is shown the one that never does. Verse 1 has the Lord seated, high and lifted up, the hem of his robe alone filling the temple. Verse 2 introduces the seraphim, the burning ones, who use four of their six wings to cover themselves. Verse 3 is their cry, the only attribute of God that Scripture ever states three times over. Verse 4 has the building itself reacting — foundations shaking at a created voice, and the house filling with smoke.
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness in this chapter is not first a moral quality but an ontological one — a matter of what God is, not merely of how he behaves. He is in a category by himself, uncreated where everything else is made. That is why the seraphim, who have no sin to hide, still cover themselves: the veiling is not shame but creatureliness. The phrase Isaiah uses of the throne in verse 1, high and lifted up, is the phrase he will use of the servant at 52:13, which is the whole christology of the book in two words.
verseByVerse.examples: The trisagion of verse 3 became the church's oldest and most widely used ascription, sung in the liturgies of East and West and heard again around the throne in Revelation 4:8. Every congregation that says or sings Holy, holy, holy is quoting the seraphim, and doing at a distance what verse 4 shows the building doing at close range.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple."

Isaiah dates the vision, and the date is not decoration. Uzziah had reigned fifty-two years — long enough that nobody under sixty could remember another king — and the nation had been prosperous and secure for the whole of it. In roughly 740 BC that ended, and the throne in Jerusalem went empty. This is what Isaiah sees in the year the throne went empty: another throne, occupied.

And there is more in the name than the date. Uzziah did not die well. When he was strong he grew proud, walked into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense — work that belonged to the priests and not to him — and when eighty priests stood in his way and told him to leave, he raged at them with the censer in his hand. Leprosy broke out on his forehead while he stood there. He lived in a separate house, excluded from the house of the LORD, until the day he died (2 Chr. 26:16-21).

So the chapter opens on the year a king died for pushing into the holy place, and then takes a man very much further in, into the throne room itself. Hold that, because in six verses it will matter enormously.

"High and lifted up" — ram v'nissa. Remember the phrase. Isaiah uses it again of God at 57:15, of the One who is high and lifted up and inhabits eternity. He uses it of a human being exactly once: at 52:13, of a servant whose appearance was so marred as to be beyond human semblance. The same two words describe the enthroned Lord of this chapter and the disfigured man of that one, and the book never explains the overlap. It simply lays the two pictures down and lets a reader who has both of them work out who he has been looking at.

Only the hem is mentioned. "The train of his robe filled the temple" — not the Lord, not his glory, the trailing edge of his clothing, and it takes up the whole building. Isaiah is describing what he could take in, and he could take in the hem.

"Above him stood the seraphim." The name means burning ones, from the verb to burn. Each has six wings, and the arithmetic is the striking part: two for the face, two for the feet, and two for flying. Four of the six are for covering. These are creatures with no sin to conceal, standing closest to the throne, and two thirds of their equipment is given to not looking and not being seen.

verseByVerse.quote: And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!" And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And one called to another and said: 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!'"

Hebrew has no word for most and no ending for -est. It raises a word to its highest degree by saying it twice, and a handful of places in the Old Testament do that. Only here is anything said three times. Not powerful, powerful, powerful. Not faithful, faithful, faithful — and God is both. Of everything that could be said about him, the burning ones say holy, and they say it to the top of the language.

Holiness in this chapter is not chiefly moral, though it includes the moral. It is the fact that God is in a category with nobody else in it. Everything the reader has ever encountered was made; he was not. All comparison fails at the first step. That is why creatures without sin still cover their faces — the veiling is not guilt, it is creatureliness meeting the uncreated.

And then the second line swings the door outward: "the whole earth is full of his glory." Not the temple. The whole earth. What Isaiah is watching in a room is the actual condition of the fields outside it, of Assyria, of the sea. The glory is not concentrated here and absent there; it is everywhere, and this vision is simply the moment the curtain came off.

"And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke." Note carefully whose voice does it. God has not spoken yet. A created being says a sentence, and the stonework moves. Then smoke — the same veiling cloud that covered Sinai and filled the tabernacle, God concealing himself at the very moment of disclosure, because unveiled glory would not leave a man alive to write the chapter.

Six wings, and four of them for covering. A voice that shakes foundations, and it is not his. A hem that fills a temple. He is not like anything. There is no second of him, no rival, no category, nothing to set beside him for scale, and the burning ones have looked at this for as long as they have existed and have never once grown used to it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 5 pronounced six woes on other people. In verse 5 Isaiah pronounces the seventh on himself, and it is not a confession of inadequacy but of ruin: I am lost. He names the failure precisely — unclean lips, the exact instrument of his calling — and refuses to separate himself from his nation, which shares the same defilement. Verses 6 and 7 are the answer, and it comes from the altar: a burning coal carried in tongs, laid on the offending mouth, with the verdict spoken over it — guilt taken away, sin atoned for.
verseByVerse.theology: The order is the gospel's order and it is never reversed. The vision of holiness produces the knowledge of guilt; the confession of guilt is met by an act of atonement; and the atonement comes from the altar, the place where something has died. Isaiah does nothing to prepare himself and is asked for nothing. Access to God is always the result of a sacrifice applied, never of a moral improvement achieved.
verseByVerse.examples: A cleansing that comes from an altar rather than from effort is precisely what makes assurance possible. Anyone who has tried to feel forgiven by resolving to do better knows the difference. The coal in verse 6 touches the one part of Isaiah he had just named as unclean, and the word in verse 7 is spoken over him before he has done anything at all with his cleaned mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And I said: 'Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!'"

Count the woes. Chapter 5 has six of them, and Isaiah has been handing them out: woe to those who join house to house, who rise early for strong drink, who call evil good, who are wise in their own eyes. He was right every time. Here is the seventh woe in the sequence, and it is his own, and it is the first one he has pronounced from the inside.

"I am lost" is nidmeti — undone, ruined, brought to silence. He does not say he feels unworthy, or that he is not quite ready, or that he needs more time. Those are the things a man says when he is comparing himself with other men. Isaiah has stopped comparing.

And the diagnosis is exact. Not unclean generally — unclean lips. He has just heard lips that exist to say holy and do nothing else, and the contrast has found him at the precise point of his own calling. A prophet is a mouth. The one faculty his entire life depends on is the one he now knows is filthy.

Then the part that is easy to skim: "and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips." He does not use his vision to climb out of his nation. He is not standing at the throne saying, at last, someone who understands. He is one of them and says so.

Here is a test, and it is uncomfortable. Most of us assess ourselves against the people nearest us, which is why we come out around average and can live with it. Try the other measurement. Not against your neighbour, your colleague or the man in the news, but against the one the seraphim cannot look at. Everyone who has ever done that honestly has arrived at the same word Isaiah used, and nobody has ever arrived at it by trying harder.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. And he touched my mouth and said: "Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar."

The response to verse 5 is immediate — then, with nothing in between. Isaiah is not left in his ruin to see what he will do about it. But look where the remedy comes from. Not from the throne and not from the seraph's own resources: from the altar, the one piece of furniture in the building where something has died. The coal is hot because of a sacrifice.

And it is carried with tongs. The being whose whole nature is fire does not handle this thing with bare hands. Whatever is on that altar is holier than the seraphim are.

"And he touched my mouth." Now go back to verse 1. The last man in this book to have holiness brought into contact with him was Uzziah, of whom Scripture says that the LORD touched the king, and he was a leper to the day of his death (2 Kings 15:5). The root is the same one used here. Uzziah was touched and it destroyed him; Isaiah is touched, in a far holier place, and it cleans him. The difference is not the men — one was a king and the other admits he is undone — and it is not the degree of exposure, since Isaiah's is greater. The difference is the altar. What came at Uzziah came unmediated. What comes at Isaiah has been through the fire of a sacrifice first.

"Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for." Two nouns and two verbs, and no conditions attached to any of them. Guilt is the liability, and it is taken away, carried off. Sin is the offence, and it is atoned for — the word is kuppar, covered, the verb that will name the Day of Atonement. Notice the tense as well. Not shall be, not may be if he perseveres. It is announced as done, over the man, while he is still standing there with the smoke in the room.

The coal came from the altar and the altar had a victim on it. Every believer since has been cleansed the same way and by the same logic, at an altar outside a city wall, where the fire fell on someone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Send Me, and the Message That Hardens
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verse 8 is the most quoted volunteering in Scripture, and it is only intelligible after verse 7. Isaiah overhears the divine council rather than being addressed by it, and answers anyway. Verses 9 and 10 give him the strangest commission in prophecy: preach so that they hear without understanding, until the seeing and hearing that would heal them is withheld. Verse 11 is his one question — how long? — and verse 12 is the bleak answer: until the cities are empty and the people removed. Verse 13 grants a tenth, burns even that, and then, in its last four words, plants the whole hope of the book in a charred stump.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 9-10 are the classic Old Testament statement of judicial hardening: God confirming in blindness those who have already refused to see. The word that should have saved becomes the instrument of judgment, not because God is arbitrary but because a rejected offer of grace does not stay indefinitely on the table. Held against verse 13, the doctrine finds its limit — the hardening is real and it is not the last word. The tree comes down; the stump is holy seed.
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah 6:9-10 is quoted or applied in all four Gospels and in Acts (Matt. 13:14-15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; John 12:40; Acts 28:26-27), always to explain why people who had the evidence did not believe. John adds the line that identifies the figure on the throne: Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him (John 12:41). The stump of verse 13 becomes the shoot from the stump of Jesse at 11:1 and the root out of dry ground at 53:2.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then I said, "Here I am! Send me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' Then I said, 'Here I am! Send me.'"

Isaiah is not addressed. He overhears. The question goes out into the council and he is not named in it, which means his answer is a volunteer stepping into a conversation he was not part of — a man with the taste of a hot coal still in his mouth saying, before anyone asks him, that he will go.

"Who will go for us?" The plural sits there in the Hebrew, alongside the singular "shall I send", and the church has always read it as an opening rather than a proof: the one God, and something in him that can say us. Read it beside John 12:41, where John says that Isaiah saw his glory — Christ's — and spoke of him, and the shape of the sentence stops being strange.

Now the order, because everything depends on it. The commission comes in verse 8. The cleansing came in verse 7. Isaiah could not have said this one verse earlier; the man in verse 5 was undone and had nothing to offer anybody. What made him usable was not a recovery of confidence but a coal from an altar, and his readiness is the overflow of being forgiven rather than the price of it.

Turn that into a question. When you hang back from something God has plainly put in front of you, is it humility — or is it that you have not actually believed verse 7 about yourself? A great deal of Christian reluctance is undealt-with guilt wearing modesty's coat. The cure is not a firmer resolution. It is to hear the sentence spoken over the mouth that has just been cleaned, and then to answer.

Notice too what he volunteers for: nothing specified. He accepts before the job description arrives, and the job description, when it comes in the next verse, is the worst one in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Go, and say to this people: "'Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive.' Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Go, and say to this people: 'Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive.' Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed."

Every preacher's instinct is to soften this and it should be resisted. Isaiah is being sent to preach, and the stated effect of his preaching is that the people will be less able to repent afterwards than before. The final clause says the quiet part out loud: lest they turn and be healed. Healing is being withheld.

Two things have to be held together, and Scripture holds both without embarrassment. The first is that this is judicial, not arbitrary. Chapters 1 to 5 have already shown a people who had every advantage — a vineyard dug, cleared, planted and fenced by God himself (5:1-7) — and who produced wild grapes. The hardening in chapter 6 is not God deciding at random to blind an innocent nation. It is God confirming a verdict the nation has spent five chapters pronouncing on itself. There is a point at which a refused offer is withdrawn, and Isaiah is sent to be the instrument of the withdrawal.

The second is that human responsibility is never dissolved by it. Watch what happens when Matthew quotes this passage. Isaiah has God commanding, "Make the heart of this people dull." Matthew's citation runs, "For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed" (Matt. 13:15). Same verse, and the closing is now something they did to themselves. Both are true and the Bible never resolves the tension into a formula. God hardens; they harden themselves; and no one at the last day will be able to say he wanted to see and was prevented.

This passage is quoted or applied in all four Gospels and in Acts (Matt. 13:14-15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; John 12:40; Acts 28:26-27), and always for the same purpose — to explain why people standing in front of overwhelming evidence did not believe it. It is the answer the New Testament reaches for when the problem is not a shortage of light.

And there is a mercy hidden in the commission that is easy to miss. Isaiah is not told his ministry will be pointless. He is told it will not produce national repentance. He is sent anyway, and he goes, and he keeps going for something like fifty years — writing, as it turns out, the book an Ethiopian official would be reading aloud in a chariot seven centuries later when Philip climbed up beside him and preached Jesus from it (Acts 8:30-35). Faithfulness was never measured by the response in the room.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "How long, O Lord?" And he said: "Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without people, and the land is a desolate waste, and the LORD removes people far away, and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then I said, 'How long, O Lord?'"

It is the only question Isaiah asks in the whole chapter, and it tells you what kind of man received this commission. He does not object and he does not bargain. But he does not accept it comfortably either. The bearer of the hardening word finds it unbearable and says so, which is the mark of a true prophet as against a man who enjoys announcing judgment. Jeremiah asks it, and the psalms ask it constantly, and the martyrs under the altar are still asking it in Revelation 6:10.

"And he said: 'Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without people, and the land is a desolate waste, and the LORD removes people far away, and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land.'"

The answer is worse than the question. Not until they listen. Not for a generation. Until the cities are empty. The picture is specific and domestic — houses with nobody in them, doors standing open, fields going back to scrub — and it is exactly what the Babylonian deportations produced a century and a half later.

What God does not do here is negotiate. He tells his prophet the truth about how long, and the truth is terrible, and Isaiah is left holding it for the rest of his life. There is a kind of comfort in that which is rarely noticed: God does not manage his servants with optimistic estimates. He tells them what it will actually cost and then sends them.

verseByVerse.quote: And though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again, like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled." The holy seed is its stump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again, like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled." The holy seed is its stump.

The chapter has one more turn of the screw before it relents. Suppose a tenth survives the desolation of verse 12 — the remnant everyone hopes for. That tenth will be burned too. This is decimation applied to a decimation, and it is not rhetorical: the exile came in waves, and each wave took the survivors of the last.

Then the image changes, and everything changes with it. "Like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled." Anyone who has taken down a large tree knows the picture. The trunk is gone, the branches are gone, the shade and the fruit and the shape of it are gone, and what is left in the ground is an ugly disc of cut wood that looks exactly like the end of the matter. It is not the end of the matter. A stump is a live root system with its top taken off.

And then the last four words of the chapter, which arrive with no explanation whatever: "The holy seed is its stump."

Follow that seed forward, because Isaiah does. In chapter 11 the stump is named — "there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit" (11:1) — the felled royal line putting out a green shoot. In chapter 53 the shoot is a person, growing up before God "like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground" (53:2), with nothing about him to attract a second look. The stump in the ash of chapter 6 is the same wood as the man on the cross.

Which means the chapter that begins with a dead king and ends with a burnt field is, in its last clause, about Jesus of Nazareth. Everything visible has been taken away and the promise is still in the ground. God had said he would judge, and he judged, and there was never a moment when the fire was outside his hand or the seed outside his keeping. The tree came down. The stump was holy. And out of that stump, in the fullness of time, came the one whose glory Isaiah had seen from the beginning.

7.subtitle: The Sign of Immanuel
7.intro:
Overview. About 734 BC, Syria and the northern kingdom march on Jerusalem to depose Ahaz and put a puppet on David’s throne, and the house of David shakes like a forest in a wind. Isaiah is sent to meet the king at the city’s water supply — where Ahaz is planning for a siege — with a son whose name means a remnant shall return, and with God’s estimate of the crisis: two smouldering stumps of firebrands, sticks with the flame already gone. The condition attached is a Hebrew pun that carries the whole chapter — if you will not believe, you will not be established. Faith and stability are the same word.

God then offers Ahaz any sign he likes, from the depths of Sheol to the height of heaven, and Ahaz refuses in the language of piety, quoting Scripture to avoid it, because he has already bought Assyrian protection with temple silver. The sign is given anyway, over his head, to the dynasty: a son called Immanuel, God with us.
