The rest of the chapter shows what the Assyrian arrangement actually buys — a hired razor that shaves the country bare, one cow and two sheep where a farm used to be, and the vineyards of chapter 5 gone back to briers and thorns.

keyVerse.quote: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.”
keyVerse.note: The sign is given not to Ahaz but despite Ahaz — it is addressed to “the house of David” (v. 13), the dynasty that will eventually produce the one the sign points to. Matthew's use of this verse is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of what the near event was designed to foreshadow: a birth that is genuinely miraculous, a child who is genuinely God-with-us, in a way that no ordinary birth in Isaiah's day could be.

7.theology:
Faith is not an addition to security; it is the floor. The wordplay in verse 9 — im lo ta’aminu ki lo te’amenu, both verbs from the root behind amen — says that believing and being established are one thing. Ahaz is not asked to feel calmer about Syria but told where the ground is, and warned that he is standing somewhere else. What he chooses instead is instructive: the threat he would not trust God about was nearly spent, and the empire he hired to avoid it destroyed him.

The sign, near and far. Verse 16 fixes a timetable that requires something in Ahaz’s own lifetime, and Matthew says a birth in Bethlehem seven centuries later fulfilled the same words (Matt. 1:22-23). Both are true: the near event is the shadow and Christ is the object that cast it. On almah, the honest position is that the word means a young woman of marriageable age rather than being a technical term for virgin — but it never once describes a married woman in the Old Testament, the pre-Christian Jewish translators rendered it parthenos, and a sign promised to reach from Sheol to heaven is not an ordinary birth.

Immanuel. The answer given to a terrified dynasty is not a battle plan but a name, and the name is a preposition: God with us. It has never meant God instead of trouble — the same child eats the subsistence food of a ruined country — but God present inside it. Matthew opens his Gospel with this verse and ends it with the risen Christ saying I am with you always, to the end of the age.
7.reflection: Ahaz's refusal of a sign is a portrait of a peculiarly religious form of unbelief: using the language of reverence to avoid the demand of trust. It is possible to be scrupulously religious while refusing to actually rely on God. The question Isaiah's chapter asks is the same one it asked Ahaz: where is your security actually resting — on the word of God, or on the alliance you have quietly arranged?
7.text: <sup>1</sup>In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but could not yet mount an attack against it.<sup>2</sup>When the house of David was told, "Syria is in league with Ephraim," the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to Isaiah, "Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field.<sup>4</sup>And say to him, 'Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria and the son of Remaliah.<sup>5</sup>Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you, saying,<sup>6</sup>"Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us conquer it for ourselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it,"<sup>7</sup>thus says the Lord GOD: "'It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass.<sup>8</sup>For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered from being a people.<sup>9</sup>And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.'"<sup>10</sup>Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz:<sup>11</sup>"Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven."<sup>12</sup>But Ahaz said, "I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test."<sup>13</sup>And he said, "Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?<sup>14</sup>Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.<sup>15</sup>He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good.<sup>16</sup>For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted.<sup>17</sup>The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father's house such days as have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah—the king of Assyria!"<sup>18</sup>In that day the LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.<sup>19</sup>And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thornbushes, and on all the pastures.<sup>20</sup>In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River —with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also.<sup>21</sup>In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep,<sup>22</sup>and because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey.<sup>23</sup>In that day every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns.<sup>24</sup>With bow and arrows a man will come there, for all the land will be briers and thorns.<sup>25</sup>And as for all the hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns, but they will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens in a war scare. Verses 1 and 2 have Syria and northern Israel marching on Jerusalem, and the house of David shaking like trees in a wind. Verses 3 and 4 send Isaiah out to meet the king at the city's water supply, with a son whose name is a sermon, and with four imperatives: be careful, be quiet, do not fear, do not let your heart be faint. Verses 5 and 6 name the plot — depose the Davidic king and install a puppet. Verses 7 to 9 answer it with a flat verdict, a series of deflating reductions, and a condition that decides everything.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is the hinge of the chapter and the wordplay is the theology: im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu — if you will not believe, you will not be established. Both verbs are the root aman, the root behind amen. Faith and stability are the same word in Hebrew, which means trust is not a religious extra added to a security policy; it IS the security. Ahaz is not being asked to feel differently about the coalition. He is being told where the ground is.
verseByVerse.examples: God's assessment in verse 4 is deliberately deflating: the two kings terrifying Judah are smouldering stumps of firebrands — sticks pulled from a fire that are producing smoke and no longer flame. Both were dead within a few years. The habit of borrowing God's estimate of a threat, rather than the one arriving through the news, is most of what verse 4 is asking for.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but could not yet mount an attack against it. When the house of David was told, "Syria is in league with Ephraim," the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but could not yet mount an attack against it."

The politics can be given in a sentence. Assyria is expanding westward and swallowing small states. Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel have formed a coalition to resist it, and they want Judah in the alliance. Judah has declined. So the two of them march on Jerusalem to remove Ahaz and put in a king who will join. It is about 734 BC.

Note the clause at the end of verse 1 before anything else happens: but could not yet mount an attack against it. Isaiah tells you the outcome before he tells you the fear. The siege never comes off. God's restraint is already in place, holding the thing at arm's length, before a word of prophecy has been spoken.

"When the house of David was told, 'Syria is in league with Ephraim,' the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind."

And here is the fear, in one of the best images in the book. Not a tree in a wind — a whole forest, every trunk moving at once, the sound of it. That is what the news does to Jerusalem: the king and the population shaking together, in the same rhythm, because somebody has come in with a report.

Two details are doing quiet work. Isaiah does not say Ahaz was told; he says the house of David was told. The dynasty is named, because the promise God made to David is what is actually under threat here, and the chapter will not let that out of sight. And the trembling is shared — the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people. A frightened leader does not keep it to himself. Fear is the most contagious thing a man in authority carries, and it moves outward from him at the speed of conversation.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Isaiah, "Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field. And say to him, 'Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria and the son of Remaliah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the LORD said to Isaiah, 'Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field.'"

Notice where God sends him, because Isaiah records the address with unusual care. The upper pool is Jerusalem's water supply, and the conduit is the channel running from it. Ahaz is out there for one reason: a city under siege dies of thirst before it dies of anything else, and he has gone to see whether the water can be secured. He is doing contingency planning, and God meets him mid-calculation.

Now hold that spot in mind, because Isaiah will bring you back to it. Thirty chapters later, the Assyrian field commander comes up to taunt King Hezekiah, and he stands "by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field" (36:2). The same words. The same patch of ground.

Two kings of Judah, at one spot, facing an army each. Ahaz is offered a sign and turns it down, then buys Assyrian protection with temple silver. Hezekiah takes the enemy's letter, carries it into the house of the LORD, and spreads it out before God. One kingdom is ruined and one is delivered, and the book quietly puts both decisions at the same address.

"You and Shear-jashub your son." The boy comes because his name is the message: a remnant shall return. It cuts both ways, which is the point — only a remnant, but a remnant. Isaiah has to stand in front of a terrified king holding the hand of a child whose name says the nation will be cut down and will not be finished.

"Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands."

Four commands, and then God's estimate of the crisis. Not two kings, not two armies — two smouldering stumps of firebrands: sticks that have been pulled out of a fire and are giving off smoke because the flame has gone. They look alarming from a distance. There is no heat left in either. Within a few years both men were dead and both kingdoms finished, exactly as described.

verseByVerse.quote: Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you, saying, "Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us conquer it for ourselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you, saying, 'Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us conquer it for ourselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it.'"

God quotes the enemy's war council back to Ahaz. Whatever was said in a room in Damascus, God heard it and can repeat it — which is itself part of the comfort, and is easy to skim past. Nothing was said about Judah in private that God was not present for.

And look at their first objective: let us go up against Judah and terrify it. Before conquest, terror. They intend to win the war in the population's stomach before they win it on the ground, which is why verse 2 matters so much. When the forest shook, the campaign was already partly successful, and not a single soldier had arrived.

The real target is in the last clause. Set up the son of Tabeel as king. We do not know who he was, and the vagueness is the insult — some nobody, named only as somebody's son, to be installed on the throne of David.

That is what makes this a theological crisis and not merely a military one. God had promised David a house and a throne and a kingdom for ever (2 Sam. 7:16). Put a non-Davidic man on that throne and the promise is broken in public. So the coalition is not simply attacking a small state. Whether they know it or not, they are attacking a sentence God said, and everything in the chapter follows from the fact that the sentence cannot fall.

verseByVerse.quote: thus says the Lord GOD: "'It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass. For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered from being a people. And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the Lord GOD: 'It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass.'"

The reply comes before the argument. Not it will be difficult for them, not I will help you resist it. It will not happen. The verdict is delivered flat, and everything after it is explanation.

"For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin... And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah."

Then the deflation, and it works by reduction. What is Syria? A city. What is the city? A man. What is Israel? A city. What is that city? A man — and not even named, just the son of Remaliah, which in that culture is how you refer to somebody you do not think worth naming.

The whole terror of verse 2 is being taken apart into its actual components, and the components are two mortal men in two walled towns. Fear inflates; God is doing the arithmetic that deflates. What exactly is this thing, and what is it made of, and who is actually behind it? Most fears do not survive being itemised, and the ones that do are the ones worth taking to God rather than to a policy.

"If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all."

In Hebrew this is a pun that carries the theology of the chapter: im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu. Both verbs come from aman — to be firm, solid, reliable — which is also the root of the word every congregation says at the end of a prayer. Amen.

So the sentence could be rendered: if you will not hold on, you will not be held up. If you do not rely, you will not be reliable. Faith and stability are the same word, which means trust is not a spiritual extra bolted onto a sound defence policy. It is the ground. Ahaz is not being asked to feel calmer about Syria. He is being told where the floor is, and warned that he is standing somewhere else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The Sign He Would Not Ask For
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God offers Ahaz a blank cheque: ask for any sign at all, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven (vv. 10-11). Ahaz refuses in the language of piety, quoting Scripture to avoid obeying it (v. 12), and Isaiah's patience gives way (v. 13). The sign is given anyway, over the king's head, to the house of David: a son named Immanuel (v. 14). Verses 15 and 16 attach a timetable — before the child can tell right from wrong, the two kings will be gone — and verse 17 delivers the sting: what comes next is the king of Assyria.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the chapter where a promise is given to a man who has already refused it, and it is the clearest case in Scripture of a prophecy with a near horizon and a far one. Something had to happen in Ahaz's lifetime for the timetable in verse 16 to mean anything; and Matthew, writing about a birth seven centuries later, says all this took place to fulfil what the Lord had spoken by the prophet (Matt. 1:22-23). The near event is real and it is not the whole of what the sign was for.
verseByVerse.examples: Ahaz's refusal in verse 12 is a recognisable and respectable form of unbelief: he quotes Deuteronomy 6:16 about not putting God to the test, and he is using it to avoid a decision he has already made privately. He had sent to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria for help and stripped the temple to pay for it (2 Kings 16:7-8). A sign from God would have complicated the arrangement.

verseByVerse.quote: Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz: "Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz: 'Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven.'"

Start with the first word. Again. Ahaz has already been given a word from God and has not responded to it, and God comes back. That single adverb says more about the divine character than the rest of the offer does.

And what an offer it is. Elsewhere in Scripture people ask for signs and are sometimes rebuked for it; here God volunteers one, unprompted, and lets the king write the terms himself. Ask a sign. Any sign. Name it.

"Let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven." The two limits are the bottom of the grave and the top of the sky, and between them is everything there is. God is not offering a modest confirmation. He is putting the whole range of the possible at the disposal of a frightened, faithless king and inviting him to choose.

Which settles one question permanently. Whatever Ahaz's problem turns out to be, it is not a shortage of evidence, and it never was. God has closed off that excuse before the refusal happens. Nobody reading this chapter can say the king was asked to trust in the dark; he was asked to name what would convince him, with a blank cheque in his hand.

Note too the possessive God uses: the LORD your God. After the trembling, after the Assyrian correspondence already under way, God is still claiming the relationship out loud. Hold that phrase for three verses.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ahaz said, "I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test." And he said, "Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But Ahaz said, 'I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test.'"

It is the most religious sentence in the chapter and it is a lie. Ahaz is quoting Scripture — Deuteronomy 6:16, you shall not put the LORD your God to the test — and quoting it accurately. He sounds like the only reverent man in the room.

The trouble is that God has just commanded him to ask. A text about not demanding proof from God cannot be used to refuse proof God has offered; that is not obedience to Deuteronomy, it is Deuteronomy conscripted as cover.

And we know what is being covered, because the history is on record. Ahaz had already sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria saying, "I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me" — and he had stripped the silver and gold out of the house of the LORD and the palace treasury to pay for it (2 Kings 16:7-8). The decision was made. A sign from God would only have complicated a deal already signed.

That is the form of unbelief this chapter exists to expose, and it is not the noisy kind. It is the man who will not ask God for anything because he has quietly arranged matters and does not want the arrangement disturbed. The refusal is dressed as humility. Underneath it is a man who has decided, and who would rather not be given a reason to undecide.

"Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?"

Isaiah's patience finally goes. But listen to the pronoun. Two verses ago God said the LORD your God. Isaiah now says my God. The prophet will not leave the possessive in the king's mouth after what has just come out of it.

And he addresses the house of David, not Ahaz. The individual has just disqualified himself from the conversation. What follows is spoken over his head, to a dynasty with a promise attached, and it is the greatest thing in the book.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

Therefore. Because you would not ask — not despite it. The refusal does not cancel the sign; it provokes it. A king declines a gift and God gives one anyway, and it turns out to be immeasurably larger than anything Ahaz would have thought to request from the depths or the heights.

And the Lord himself will give it. Ahaz was invited to choose and would not, so the choosing is taken out of his hands entirely.

Now the difficulty, which deserves a straight answer rather than a managed one. The Hebrew word is almah. It means a young woman of marriageable age, and it does not mean "virgin" the way a technical term would; there is another Hebrew word (betulah) that carries that sense more precisely. Jewish readers have long argued from this that Isaiah is describing an ordinary young woman in the eighth century BC, and Christian readers should feel the force of that rather than talk past it.

Three things stand on the other side. First, every occurrence of almah in the Old Testament is of an unmarried girl; the word never once describes a married woman, so "virgin" is a fair reading of it even if it is not the word's technical definition. Second, the Jewish scholars who translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek — two centuries before Christ, with no Christian argument to make — rendered it parthenos, which is unambiguous. And third, a sign in this passage was supposed to reach from Sheol to heaven. A young woman having a baby in the usual way is not a sign of that order; it is what happens every week.

So the shape of it is this. Something happened in Ahaz's own lifetime — verse 16 fixes a timetable that would be meaningless otherwise — and it was never the whole of what the sign was for. Matthew, writing about a birth in Bethlehem seven hundred years later, says plainly: all this took place to fulfil what the Lord had spoken by the prophet (Matt. 1:22-23). The near event was the shadow. He is naming the object that cast it.

And the name is the thing. Immanuel — God with us. Not God for us, or God above us, or God watching. With. To a king shaking like a forest, that is the whole answer, and it is not a strategy or a reassurance but a person. Matthew opens his Gospel with this verse and closes it, twenty-eight chapters later, with the last words Jesus says on earth: behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age. The name given to a frightened dynasty is the promise the risen Christ leaves with his church, and between those two sentences stands everything he did.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good. For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good. For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted."

The sign now acquires a clock. A small child takes a few years to reach the age of moral discrimination — to know that this is wrong and that is right. Before the boy gets there, the two kingdoms terrifying Ahaz will be empty ground.

It happened. Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC and Rezin was killed; Samaria fell in 722 and the northern kingdom ended. Neither man survived the decade. Ahaz was shaking like a forest at two states that had a handful of years left in them.

But look at what the child is eating, because it is not what it sounds like. Curds and honey reads like a delicacy and it is nothing of the kind. Verse 22 will explain: when the fields have been trampled and the vineyards are gone, what is left is whatever a surviving cow gives and whatever wild bees make. This is what you eat when the farm has stopped. It is the food of a land that has reverted.

So the sign is double-edged all the way through, and Isaiah does not soften it. The child's name is God-with-us. The child's diet is the diet of a ruined country. Both are part of the same sign, and anyone tempted to take the promise as a guarantee that nothing hard will happen has to reckon with the menu.

God with us has never meant God instead of trouble. It means God present in the middle of it, which is a smaller thing to say and a far larger thing to have.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father's house such days as have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah—the king of Assyria!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father's house such days as have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah — the king of Assyria!"

The sentence is built to detonate at the end. It rolls out across three targets — you, your people, your father's house — and reaches for the worst benchmark in the national memory: the day the kingdom split after Solomon, when ten tribes walked away and Israel stopped being one nation. Nothing that bad has happened since. Something that bad is coming.

And then, after all the build-up, the identification, held to the last two words: the king of Assyria.

That is the man Ahaz has just paid. He emptied the temple treasury to hire this protection, and Isaiah announces him as the disaster. The ally is the catastrophe. The solution is the judgment. The very thing bought at such cost to keep the trouble out is the door the trouble walks through.

This is what unbelief actually purchases, and Isaiah presents it as arithmetic rather than as bad luck. Ahaz was frightened of two smouldering stumps, and to avoid them he invited a fire. The threat he would not trust God about was small and nearly spent; the one he manufactured by not trusting was an empire.

It is a sober thing to sit with. The damage in most lives is rarely done by the thing that frightened us. It is done by what we reached for to avoid it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four oracles, each opening in that day, describe what Ahaz's Assyrian policy actually buys. Verses 18 and 19 have God whistling for Egypt's flies and Assyria's bees until they settle over every ravine and thornbush in the country. Verse 20 shaves the nation bare with a hired razor. Verses 21 and 22 reduce a farm to one cow and two sheep. Verses 23 to 25 turn the vineyards into briers and thorns, and the terraced hills into rough grazing.
verseByVerse.theology: The irony is structural rather than incidental: Ahaz hired Assyria, and God says the razor is his. The power a frightened man buys to protect himself becomes the instrument of his ruin, and Isaiah does not present this as bad luck but as the ordinary shape of unbelief's arithmetic. Faith deferred costs more than the thing it was avoiding.
verseByVerse.examples: The vineyard that reverts to briers and thorns in verses 23 to 25 is the vineyard of chapter 5, where God dug, cleared, planted and fenced and got wild grapes. What was promised there as a threat arrives here as a landscape. And the curds and honey of verses 15 and 22 are not the milk and honey of the promised land — they are what is left to eat when the ploughed fields are gone.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thornbushes, and on all the pastures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria."

Four oracles now follow, each opening in that day, and together they describe the country Ahaz's decision produces.

The picture in the first one is a man whistling for a dog, and what comes when he whistles is Egypt and Assyria — the two superpowers between which Judah was pinned for its entire existence. God calls them the way you call an animal, and they come. That is the sovereignty this chapter has been quietly asserting from verse 1: not that God permits the great powers to move, but that they move when he makes a noise with his lips.

The insects are chosen with care. A fly out of the Nile delta, where the standing water breeds them in clouds. A bee out of Assyria, which stings. Neither can be fought. You cannot defend a border against flies, and there is no army formation that keeps out bees; they arrive in numbers, through every gap, and settle.

"And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thornbushes, and on all the pastures."

Then the settling, and Isaiah lists the terrain until there is none left over. Ravines, rock clefts, thornbushes, pasture — the wild places and the farmed places, the high ground and the low. The clefts of the rocks are exactly where a population hides when an army comes. The hiding places are occupied too.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River —with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River — with the king of Assyria — the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also."

One word carries this verse: hired. Ahaz hired Assyria; he sent the money and made the arrangement. Isaiah says the razor is hired all right — and God is holding the handle. The king thinks he is the customer. He is the barber's work.

What follows is not a metaphor a modern reader feels immediately, so it needs saying plainly. In that world a man's beard was his dignity. Shaving it off was one of the gravest humiliations available; when David's envoys had half their beards cut off, they were too ashamed to go home and were told to stay in Jericho until it grew back (2 Sam. 10:4-5). It was an assault on a man's standing, not on his appearance.

And this shaving is total — head, body, beard, everything swept away in one pass. The nation is left as exposed as a man stripped of every hair, standing in public with nothing left to be dignified with.

The horror of the image is that Judah paid for it. This is not an invader arriving uninvited; it is the consequence of a contract signed in a moment of panic by a man who had been offered a sign as deep as Sheol and would not take it.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep, and because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep, and because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey."

The camera comes down from empires to one farmer, and what he has left is a heifer and two sheep. That is the whole holding. Isaiah does not say he owns them; he says he keeps them alive, which is the language of a man getting animals through a bad season rather than of a man with a farm.

Then the strangest phrase in the chapter: because of the abundance of milk that they give. Abundance, from one cow. And it is not prosperity — it is arithmetic. There is milk to spare because there is almost nobody left to drink it. The surplus is a measure of the depopulation. A full jug in an empty village.

"Everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey." And there is the phrase from verse 15 again, now fully explained. The food of Immanuel's childhood is the food of the survivors: what an animal gives and what wild bees make, because nothing is being sown.

Note what has quietly happened to the promised land. It was to be a land flowing with milk and honey — the phrase of the exodus, a description of abundance. Here are milk and honey again, and they mean the opposite: not a land so rich that it runs, but a land so empty that there is nothing else to eat. The same two words, turned inside out.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns. With bow and arrows a man will come there, for all the land will be briers and thorns. And as for all the hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns, but they will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns."

The valuation is precise, and it is the point. A thousand vines at a shekel each was a serious vineyard — the kind of asset a family builds over generations, terraced, walled, pruned, and passed down. Vines take years before they yield anything at all. Nobody plants one for himself.

All of it goes back to briers and thorns. Not burned, not seized — simply abandoned, and what grows on abandoned ground.

"With bow and arrows a man will come there, for all the land will be briers and thorns." A man walks onto what used to be the vineyard carrying hunting weapons, because there is game in it now. That single detail tells you how far it has gone. Cultivated land has become the sort of country you go into armed.

"And as for all the hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns, but they will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread."

The terraced hillsides are the saddest item on the list. Every one of those terraces was built by hand, stone by stone, to hold soil on a slope — the accumulated labour of centuries of families who never saw the finished result. Now nobody will even walk up there, because of the thorns.

Read all this next to chapter 5, and it is the same vineyard. There God dug it, cleared its stones, planted the choicest vine, built a watchtower and cut out a winepress, and looked for grapes and got wild ones — and said he would remove its hedge and let it be overgrown with briers and thorns. Chapter 5 was the sentence. Chapter 7 is the photograph. And it began with a king who was offered a sign as deep as the grave and as high as heaven, and said he would rather not.

8.subtitle: Fear God Alone
8.intro: Overview. Chapter 8 continues directly from chapter 7, moving through the immediate fulfilment of the Immanuel sign in the birth of Isaiah's second son, to the announcement that Assyria will overwhelm the land like a flood, to a searching call to fear God rather than the conspiracies and crises that are making everyone else afraid. The chapter ends in darkness — those who have rejected the word of God have no light — but Isaiah and his children stand within that darkness as living signs of God's purposes.

sections.title: Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz and the Flood of Assyria
sections.commentary:
Isaiah's second son is given a name that means “quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil” — a prophecy in a name. Before the child is old enough to say “my father” or “my mother,” the wealth of Damascus and Samaria will be carried off by Assyria. The sign is specific and dated: this is not vague prophecy but a named child whose growth will mark the timeline of fulfilment.

The image of the waters of Shiloah (v. 6) — the gentle stream through Jerusalem — being rejected in favour of the mighty Euphrates is one of Isaiah's most powerful metaphors. Judah has despised the quiet provision of God and longed for the impressive power of Assyria. The consequence is that the great river will come — but it will not stop at the border. It will rise “up to the neck,” leaving only the head above water. The very power chosen as a solution becomes the flooding problem.

v. 10 — “Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us.” The chapter places Immanuel here as a battle cry — not just a name but a declaration that all the plotting of the nations runs up against the fact of God's presence. Every alliance that does not account for God is building on nothing.

sections.title: Fear the LORD of Hosts
sections.commentary:
The LORD speaks directly to Isaiah and calls him out of the prevailing culture of fear: “Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread.” The nation is in a panic over Syria and Ephraim. God's word to Isaiah is: their fear is misplaced. Calibrate your dread to the right object.

v. 13 — “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honour as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” Fear of God is not offered here as a competitor to wisdom or courage but as their source. The person who fears God properly will not be paralysed by the fear of circumstances, because they understand that the one who controls all circumstances is also the one who is for them. Peter quotes this verse in 1 Peter 3:14–15, applying it to Christians facing persecution.

The closing verses are stark. Those who do not speak according to the law and testimony — the word of God — have no light in them. In the darkness that follows the rejection of God's word, people will look to the dead and find no answer. Isaiah and his children stand as signs and portents — living testimonies that God has spoken, even when the word is not welcomed.

keyVerse.quote: “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honour as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.”
keyVerse.note: This verse reorients what fear is for. Fear is not to be eliminated but redirected. The person who fears the right thing — the LORD of hosts — will be freed from the paralysing fear of everything else. Peter's use of this text in 1 Peter 3 makes the application explicit: in a hostile world, the answer to anxiety about circumstances is not stoic courage but a heart that is occupied with the holiness of God.

8.reflection: The chapter diagnoses a failure that is both common and hard to see in oneself: calibrating one's fear to the wrong object. The people of Judah were afraid of the right threats by the wrong standard — afraid of Syria when they should have been afraid of the God who governs Syria. The question the chapter asks directly: what is it in your own situation that is producing your deepest anxiety, and is that fear proportioned to the reality of who God is?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to me, "Take a large tablet and write on it in common characters, 'Belonging to Maher-shalal-hash-baz.'<sup>2</sup>And I will get reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah, to attest for me."<sup>3</sup>And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. Then the LORD said to me, "Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz;<sup>4</sup>for before the boy knows how to cry 'My father' or 'My mother,' the wealth of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria."<sup>5</sup>The LORD spoke to me again:<sup>6</sup>"Because this people has refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently, and rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah,<sup>7</sup>therefore, behold, the Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria and all his glory. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.<sup>14</sup>And he will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling to both houses of Israel, a trap and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>And many shall stumble on it. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Sign of Maher-shalal-hash-baz and the Darkness Before Dawn
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 8 continues the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. God commands Isaiah to inscribe a name—Maher-shalal-hash-baz ('swift is the plunder, speedy is the prey')—as a prophetic witness. Isaiah's son by the prophetess bears this name as a living sign. The chapter then turns to the choice facing Israel: the gentle waters of Shiloah (trust in God) or the overwhelming flood of Assyria (the consequence of faithlessness). The chapter ends with instructions to the prophet's disciples: bind the testimony, wait for God, and refuse the spirit of divination.
verseByVerse.examples: The pattern of the faithful remnant preserving God's word in a hostile culture is the permanent pattern of the church in any age of apostasy. Isaiah's instructions to 'bind the testimony, seal the teaching among my disciples' (v. 16) describe the ministry of every faithful pastor, parent, and teacher who preserves the word for the next generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, “Take a large tablet and write on it in common characters, 'Belonging to Maher-shalal-hash-baz.' And I will get reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah, to attest for me.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Take a large tablet and write on it in common characters'—the prophecy is inscribed publicly, in ordinary script that anyone can read. The word must be datable and verifiable. 'Maher-shalal-hash-baz'—the name means swift is the plunder, speedy is the prey: a prophecy of military conquest compressed into a name. The name-as-prophecy is characteristic of Isaiah's sign-children. 'I will get reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah'—two named witnesses provide legal verification; when the prophecy is fulfilled, the witnesses can confirm it was given beforehand. Oswalt: the prophetic word is not private oracle but public record—God's word is given in history and verified by history.

verseByVerse.quote: And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. Then the LORD said to me, “Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz; for before the boy knows how to cry 'My father' or 'My mother,' the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son'—Isaiah's wife is called the prophetess, either because she is a prophet herself or as the wife of a prophet. The son born is the living enactment of the written tablet: name becomes flesh. 'Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz'—the name confirmed at birth. 'Before the boy knows how to cry “My father” or “My mother”'—within two years at most: the earliest words a child learns. 'The riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria'—Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC; the timeline is precise. Motyer: the sign-child makes the prophetic word embodied and time-stamped—it cannot be claimed later as coincidence.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to me again: “Because this people has refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently, and rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The waters of Shiloah that flow gently'—Shiloah (later Siloam) was Jerusalem's primary water source: a small, gentle stream running from the Gihon spring. Its gentleness is the gentleness of trust in God—quiet, unpretentious, life-giving. 'This people has refused the waters of Shiloah'—the covenant community has rejected the quiet provision of God. 'And rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah'—instead of rejoicing in God's protection, they rejoice in the foreign alliance. Childs: the people's rejoicing in Rezin and Pekah probably refers to the northern tribes who welcomed the Syro-Ephraimite coalition as liberation from the Davidic house. The rejected water is God's gentle rule; the preferred alternative is foreign military power.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore, behold, the Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria and all his glory. And it will rise over all its channels and go over all its banks, and it will sweep into Judah, it will overflow and pass on, reaching even to the neck, and its outspread wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Immanuel.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, mighty and many'—the River is the Euphrates: the Nile of Mesopotamia, a massive flood-force. What was refused (Shiloah's gentle stream) is replaced by what is terrifying (the Euphrates in flood). 'It will sweep into Judah, it will overflow and pass on, reaching even to the neck'—the flood reaches up to the neck: threatening drowning but not yet drowning. The land survives—barely. 'O Immanuel'—the address to Immanuel stops the flood imagery cold. The land is his land: 'your land.' Because it is Immanuel's land, the flood cannot finally overwhelm it. Motyer: the address to Immanuel is the theological key to the entire passage—the limit on Assyria's devastation is God-with-us.

verseByVerse.quote: Be broken, you peoples, and be shattered; give ear, all you far countries; strap on your armor and be shattered; strap on your armor and be shattered. Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Be broken, you peoples, and be shattered'—the defiant summons to the nations: try your worst; you will be shattered. The triple repetition of breaking (hattu, hatu, hatu) is a taunt: all the nations' preparations will end in the same result. 'Strap on your armor and be shattered'—the armor is real; the shattering is certain. Military preparation cannot overcome divine opposition. 'Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand'—the plans of the nations are dissolved by God's will. 'For God is with us'—the translation of Immanuel closes the taunt: the reason no coalition can succeed is the presence of God with his people. Oswalt: the battle cry of the remnant is not their strength but God's name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD spoke thus to me with his strong hand upon me, and warned me not to walk in the way of this people, saying: “Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD spoke thus to me with his strong hand upon me'—the intensity of prophetic reception: the hand of the LORD is the overwhelming pressure of divine communication (cf. Ezek. 1:3; 3:22). 'Warned me not to walk in the way of this people'—the prophet is called out of his culture's anxieties. The people's responses—conspiracy-fear, dread—are not Isaiah's responses. 'Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy'—the political paranoia of the court: every alliance is seen as conspiracy, every foreign contact as treason. Isaiah is to refuse this framework. Childs: the prophet must resist the pressure of public opinion, which tends to see every crisis through the lens of the prevailing fear.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling to both houses of Israel, a trap and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread'—the reorientation of fear: not the Syro-Ephraimite coalition, not Assyria, but the LORD. To fear God is to cease fearing everything else—not because everything else is harmless but because the LORD transcends every earthly threat. 'He will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling'—the same God is both refuge (sanctuary) and danger (stumbling stone), depending on where one stands relative to faith. For those who trust, he is the sanctuary; for those who refuse, he is the stone they trip over. Motyer: this verse is quoted in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8 as fulfilled in Christ—he is both cornerstone and stumbling stone.

verseByVerse.quote: And many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken; they shall be snared and taken.“ Bind up the testimony; seal the teaching among my disciples. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken; they shall be snared and taken'—the consequence of rejecting God as sanctuary: he becomes the trap. The nation that refuses its refuge finds its very refusal has set the snare. 'Bind up the testimony; seal the teaching among my disciples'—the command to preserve the prophetic word within the faithful remnant. When the nation rejects the word, it is entrusted to disciples who will guard and transmit it. Young: this is the origin of the prophetic scroll tradition—the word that the nation rejects is preserved by those who receive it. It anticipates the entire canonical function of the written prophetic word across generations.

verseByVerse.quote: I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob, and I will hope in him. Behold, I and the children whom the LORD has given me are signs and portents in Israel from the LORD of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob'—the prophet's personal confession of faith in a time of divine hiddenness. God's face is hidden from the nation; Isaiah waits anyway. This is the faith of the remnant: trusting God when evidence of his presence is withheld. 'I will hope in him'—hope directed not at circumstances but at God himself. 'I and the children whom the LORD has given me are signs and portents in Israel'—Isaiah's family is itself a prophetic text: Shear-jashub (a remnant shall return), Maher-shalal-hash-baz (swift is the plunder), and Immanuel (through the mother). Their names map the entire theological landscape of the crisis. Motyer: the prophet's household is a miniature of the faithful remnant within apostate Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they say to you, “Inquire of the mediums and the necromancers who chirp and mutter,” should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living? To the teaching and to the testimony! If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Inquire of the mediums and the necromancers who chirp and mutter'—the alternative to prophetic faith: consulting the dead through spirit mediums. The description chirp and mutter captures the technique of spirit-communication, which produced animal-like sounds. 'Should not a people inquire of their God?'—the rhetorical reversal: why would the living God's people consult the dead? 'Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living?'—the absurdity of necromancy exposed: the dead have no access to life's answers. 'To the teaching and to the testimony!'—the twofold foundation: Torah (teaching) and the prophetic word (testimony) are the only reliable guides. 'If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn'—no light whatsoever. Webb: the criterion for all wisdom is the written word of God.

verseByVerse.quote: They will pass through the land, greatly distressed and hungry. And when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish. And they will be thrust into thick darkness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They will pass through the land, greatly distressed and hungry'—the consequences of rejecting the word: not illumination but starvation. The people who refused God's light now wander in famine. 'When they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God'—hunger produces rage; rage produces blasphemy. The people curse the only one who could have helped them. 'And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish'—in every direction they look—upward (v. 21) and earthward—there is only darkness. 'And they will be thrust into thick darkness'—the final word of the chapter is darkness. It is the darkness before the great light of ch. 9:2. Childs: the structure is deliberate: the book descends into darkness so that the light can be appreciated as what it truly is.

9.subtitle: A Great Light — The Child Born to Us
9.intro:
Overview. Chapter 8 ended in the gloom of anguish; chapter 9 opens with the word but. The light comes first to Zebulun and Naphtali — the northern territories Assyria stripped first, the mixed border region a Jerusalem man would name with a slight tone in his voice — and Matthew quotes those verses to explain why Jesus based his ministry in Capernaum rather than the capital (Matt. 4:13-16). The joy is harvest-joy and victory-joy; the yoke breaks as on the day of Midian, when Gideon won with three hundred men; and the soldiers’ boots go on a bonfire.

Then the reason for all of it: to us a child is born, to us a son is given — born, which is how a human being arrives, and given, which is not — with the government on his shoulder, four throne-names, and a kingdom that has no end and never peaks. From verse 8 the chapter turns and does not turn back. A word falls on the northern kingdom; the people answer a collapse by rebuilding in better materials without once asking why it fell; and three times the same refrain closes a section — for all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.

keyVerse.quote: “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.”
keyVerse.note: The name Mighty God (El Gibbor) is the same phrase used of God himself in Isaiah 10:21. Isaiah is not hedging when he calls this coming child God; he is asserting it. The full weight of orthodox Christology — the genuine divinity of the Son — has its Old Testament foundation here. Matthew, Luke, and John each draw on Isaiah 9 in their portraits of Jesus.

9.theology:
The four names. This is the most compressed christology in the Old Testament, and the second name is the load-bearing one. El Gibbor, Mighty God, has sometimes been softened to “divine hero” — but Isaiah uses the identical phrase of God himself fifteen verses later at 10:21. If it means God there it means God here. Everlasting Father is not a confusion of the persons of the Trinity, which Isaiah is not yet thinking in: it is permanence and relationship, a king who fathers his people and does not die and leave them to a successor. And born beside given puts the two natures of Christ in one line, seven centuries early, without explanation.

The outstretched hand. The refrain at vv. 12, 17 and 21 is usually read as pure menace, and it is more than that. A hand stretched out is the posture of striking and the posture of reaching, and verse 13 says which one is being frustrated: the people did not turn to him who struck them. The judgment continues because it has not yet done what judgment in Scripture is nearly always sent to do.

Sin as a fire that feeds itself. In vv. 18-21 the subject of the burning is wickedness, not God — and in the same breath it is the wrath of the LORD. Both are true, because judgment here largely consists of God handing a people over to what they chose and declining to put it out. It ends with brothers devouring each other and finding their only remaining unity in a shared enemy. Isaiah placed the child and the four names before all of this, so the answer is already on the page when the reader reaches the worst of it.
9.reflection: Isaiah 9 was written to people living in the specific darkness of Assyrian occupation. The promise of a child born to them was addressed to their situation, not over it. Whatever darkness you are living in, the promise is the same: “the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.” The question is not whether the light has come — it has — but whether you are facing it.
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations.<sup>2</sup>The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone.<sup>3</sup>You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil.<sup>4</sup>For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian.<sup>5</sup>For every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire.<sup>6</sup>For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.<sup>7</sup>Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.<sup>8</sup>The Lord has sent a word against Jacob, and it will fall on Israel;<sup>9</sup>and all the people will know, Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who say in pride and in arrogance of heart:<sup>10</sup>"The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place."<sup>11</sup>But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies.<sup>12</sup>The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.<sup>13</sup>The people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD of hosts.<sup>14</sup>So the LORD cut off from Israel head and tail, palm branch and reed in one day—<sup>15</sup>the elder and honored man is the head, and the prophet who teaches lies is the tail;<sup>16</sup>for those who guide this people have been leading them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up.<sup>17</sup>Therefore the Lord does not rejoice over their young men, and has no compassion on their fatherless and widows; for everyone is godless and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.<sup>18</sup>For wickedness burns like a fire; it consumes briers and thorns; it kindles the thickets of the forest, and they roll upward in a column of smoke.<sup>19</sup>Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts the land is scorched, and the people are like fuel for the fire; no one spares another.<sup>20</sup>They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry, and they devour on the left, but are not satisfied; each devours the flesh of his own arm,<sup>21</sup>Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh; together they are against Judah. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Great Light, and the Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The darkness at the end of chapter 8 breaks. Verse 1 names the two territories that were overrun first — Zebulun and Naphtali, Galilee of the nations — and says they will be made glorious. Verse 2 has people who walked in darkness seeing a great light. Verses 3 to 5 describe the joy as harvest-joy and victory-joy, break the yoke as on the day of Midian, and burn the soldier's boots. Verses 6 and 7 give the reason for all of it: a child born, a son given, the government on his shoulder, four names, and a kingdom with no end.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 is the most compressed christology in the Old Testament. Born and given are both used, and they are not synonyms: one is how he enters, the other is where he comes from. And the second of the four names settles what is being claimed. El Gibbor, Mighty God, is not a courtly exaggeration — Isaiah uses the identical phrase of God himself fifteen verses later at 10:21. The child is called what God is called.
verseByVerse.examples: Matthew quotes verses 1 and 2 to explain why Jesus made his base in Capernaum rather than Jerusalem (Matt. 4:13-16): the light goes first to the region that was ruined first. And hold on to the guarantee at the end of verse 7 — the zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. The promise does not rest on anybody's faithfulness but on God's own determination to see it through.

verseByVerse.quote: But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations."

Chapter 8 ended in the dark — people consulting mediums, distressed and hungry, looking to the earth and seeing only "distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish" (8:22). The first word here is but, and it turns the whole book.

Then Isaiah does something you would not expect: he names a postcode. Zebulun and Naphtali, the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations.

Those two tribal territories were the far north, up against the frontier, and they were the first ground Assyria took — Tiglath-pileser stripped them and deported the population around 733 BC, years before Samaria fell. They were also the most mixed region in the country, which is what "Galilee of the nations" means: too many foreigners, too far from the temple, the part of Israel a Jerusalem man would mention with a slight tone in his voice.

First to be ruined, and Isaiah says first to be made glorious. The light does not start at the centre and work outward to the edges. It starts at the edge.

"The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone."

Note the two verbs. They walked in darkness — moving, getting on with things, living whole lives in it. And they dwelt in it: the second word is for settling, making a home. Darkness had stopped being a crisis and become an address. The phrase behind "deep darkness" is the one the twenty-third psalm uses for the valley of the shadow of death.

And what happens to them is entirely passive. They did not find the light, kindle it, or walk toward it. It shone on them. Isaiah writes it in the past tense — the prophetic perfect, a thing so certain it is reported as done — seven centuries before a carpenter from Nazareth set up in Capernaum, in Zebulun, by the way of the sea, and Matthew reached for this verse to say why (Matt. 4:13-16).

verseByVerse.quote: You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil. For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian. For every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil."

Two pictures of gladness, and both are specific. Harvest joy is the relief at the end of a year's work when the crop is actually in — the anxiety of months resolved in a week. Victory joy is the noise of soldiers dividing plunder after a battle they expected to lose. One is the joy of provision, the other of deliverance, and Isaiah wants both.

"For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian."

Three instruments, all of them things that press on a shoulder: the yoke of a draught animal, the staff used to drive it, the rod of the man in charge. That is what occupation felt like — not dramatic, just a permanent weight in the same place.

And the day of Midian is chosen with care. Gideon had thirty-two thousand men and God cut him down to three hundred, then won the battle with trumpets, jars and torches (Judg. 7). It is the standard biblical instance of a victory nobody could take credit for. Isaiah is saying the coming deliverance will be that kind: disproportionate, unearned, and plainly God's.

"For every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire."

The last image is a bonfire of military kit. Not captured, not stored for next time — burned. And the two items are chosen for what they sound and look like: the boot of a soldier tramping in step, which is the noise an occupied people hear in the street, and a cloak stiff with dried blood.

Both go on the fire. Not a ceasefire, which keeps the equipment; an end to the need for it. This is the same promise as swords beaten into ploughshares in chapter 2, and it is still outstanding, and the fire in it is real.

verseByVerse.quote: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder."

Everything in the previous verses hangs on this for. The darkness lifts, the yoke breaks, the boots burn — because of a birth.

Two verbs, and they are not saying the same thing twice. A child is born: that is the ordinary way a human being arrives, and it means this one is genuinely ours, from inside the race, with a mother. A son is given: that is not how babies come. Gifts come from somewhere else, from someone who had them first. Isaiah puts both in one line without explaining, and the two halves of the sentence are the two natures of Christ sitting side by side in the eighth century BC.

And to us, twice. Not born to a palace or given to a nation in the abstract. To us.

"The government shall be upon his shoulder." The shoulder was where a burden went — the same shoulder that carried the oppressor's yoke two verses ago. What is laid on this one is the whole weight of rule. And the only other thing Scripture puts on his shoulder is a crossbeam, on a road out of Jerusalem, which is how the government was actually obtained.

"And his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace."

Wonderful Counsellor. Not a counsellor who happens to be wonderful — the first word means a wonder, the term used for God's miraculous acts. His counsel is itself a miracle. Set that against chapter 7, where a king was offered counsel from God and took Assyria's instead.

Mighty God. El Gibbor. This is where translators and commentators have sometimes reached for softer options — "divine hero", "godlike warrior" — and the text does not allow it. Isaiah uses the identical phrase fifteen verses later, at 10:21, of God himself: "A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God." Same two words. If it means God there, it means God here.

Everlasting Father. Not a confusion of the persons of the Trinity — Isaiah is not thinking in those categories yet. It is a title of relationship and permanence: a king who fathers his people rather than using them, and who does not die and leave them to a successor. Every dynasty Judah ever had was a sequence of funerals. This one is not.

Prince of Peace. Shalom is not the absence of fighting but the presence of wholeness — everything working, everything in its place, nothing broken. He does not merely stop the war. He is the one under whom things are right.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore."

Two words carry the verse: increase and no end. Isaiah is not promising a golden age, because golden ages are the thing empires have before they decline. He is describing a kingdom on a permanent upward curve — expanding, and never at its height, because there is no height to reach.

Read that against everything the book has shown so far. Syria and Ephraim are smouldering stumps. Assyria is a hired razor that will itself be broken. Every power in these chapters is a rising thing that will fall, and the only exception is the one with a child on the throne.

"On the throne of David and over his kingdom." The promise is anchored to a specific dynasty and a specific covenant — the one under attack in chapter 7, when a coalition tried to put the son of Tabeel on that seat. It could not be broken, and this verse is why.

"To establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness." Notice what the kingdom is upheld by. Not by force, and not by legitimacy of descent, but by justice and righteousness — the two things every king in Isaiah's Judah was supposed to provide and did not. The kingdom stands because it is right, which no human government has ever managed for a generation.

"The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this."

And there is the guarantee, and it is the last line for a reason. Everything promised in verses 6 and 7 is enormous, and none of it depends on Israel, on the house of David, on political conditions, or on anybody responding well. It rests on God's zeal — his burning, jealous determination to get this done.

The chapter's next verse begins a catalogue of national failure that runs to the end, and it changes nothing. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. He is not waiting for better material, and he never was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns without warning from the child to a word sent against Jacob. Verses 8 and 9 have that word landing, and the people meeting it with pride. Verse 10 quotes them: the bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place. Verses 11 and 12 answer the boast by raising up enemies east and west, and close on the refrain that will sound three times in this chapter: his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 is the definitive picture of impenitence, and what makes it dangerous is that it sounds like courage. A blow falls and the response is to rebuild bigger — mud brick replaced with cut stone, common fig replaced with imported cedar. Not a word about why the wall came down. The discipline was meant to produce a question and produced a building programme instead.
verseByVerse.examples: The refrain is the chapter's own structure and it is easy to misread as sheer menace. A hand stretched out is the posture of striking and also the posture of reaching; the judgment continues precisely because what it was sent to produce has not happened yet. Verse 13 states it plainly: the people did not turn to him who struck them.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord has sent a word against Jacob, and it will fall on Israel; and all the people will know, Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who say in pride and in arrogance of heart: "The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The Lord has sent a word against Jacob, and it will fall on Israel; and all the people will know, Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who say in pride and in arrogance of heart."

The turn is abrupt and it is meant to be. One verse ago the government was on the child's shoulder and there was no end to peace. Now a word has been sent, and it is coming down.

The image in "it will fall" is of something thrown. God's word here is not information being circulated; it is an object in flight with a landing point, and the landing point is a nation that has already been struck once and has decided what it thinks about that.

"The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place."

This is the most quotable sentence in the chapter and the most chilling, because it sounds magnificent. It is the language of resilience. Something has knocked our buildings down, and we will rebuild them better than they were.

And the upgrade is real, not rhetoric. Mud brick was what ordinary houses were made of — cheap, quick, and what you use when you cannot afford stone. Dressed stone is quarried, cut square and expensive. Sycamore-fig was the common tree of the lowlands, useful and unimpressive; cedar came from Lebanon by ship and by ox-cart and was what kings panelled palaces with. They are answering a disaster by trading up.

Not one word about why the bricks fell.

That is the whole indictment, and it is why the sentence is so unnerving. There is no defiance of God here, no denial, no atheism — just a people who have taken a blow, absorbed it as a setback, and moved straight to the rebuild. The event was meant to produce a question. It produced a procurement plan.

Ask what the reflex is when something in a life falls down. The instinct to repair, improve and press on is a virtue nearly everywhere else. Here it is the thing that damns them, because they used it to avoid the one question the collapse was sent to raise.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies. The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies. The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth."

The answer to the building programme is not a lecture. It is more pressure. God raises and stirs up — both verbs have him as the subject, moving nations the way chapter 7 had him whistling for flies and bees.

Enemies on both sides at once: Syrians from the east, Philistines from the west. That is the shape of a nation being squeezed rather than invaded, and "devour with open mouth" is the image of an animal that does not need to hurry.

"For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still."

Here is the refrain. It closes this section, and it will close the next two as well — three times in this chapter, hammering. Isaiah wants the reader to feel the judgment not as a single event but as something that keeps not finishing.

And the image deserves care, because it is usually read as pure menace and it is more than that. A hand stretched out is the posture of a man about to strike. It is also the posture of a man reaching for someone. Both are in the picture, and the next verse tells you which is being frustrated: the people did not turn to him who struck them.

The hand stays out because the turning has not happened. Judgment continues, in this chapter, precisely because it has not yet accomplished what judgment in Scripture is nearly always sent to accomplish. It is the strangest kind of mercy — a God who will not let the consequences stop while there is still a chance they might work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Head and Tail Cut Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verse 13 gives the diagnosis in one line: they did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD. Verse 14 removes head and tail, palm branch and reed, in one day. Verse 15 identifies them — the elder and honoured man is the head, and the prophet who teaches lies is the tail. Verse 16 has the guides leading people astray and the guided swallowed up. Verse 17 reaches the point where even the young men and the fatherless and widows receive no compassion, because the corruption has gone everywhere, and sounds the refrain a second time.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment falls on leadership first and hardest, and Isaiah is careful to say that the followers go down with them rather than instead of them: the guides are culpable and the guided are swallowed. Verse 15 puts the lying prophet at the tail, which is the humiliating end of the animal — a man who speaks in God's name and points the wrong way is not merely wrong, he is the least of what a nation has.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 17 is the hardest sentence in the section, because the fatherless and widows are the very people God repeatedly commands his people to protect. When even they are outside compassion, Isaiah is not saying God has changed his mind about the vulnerable. He is saying the corruption has reached the point where there is no innocent class left to appeal to.
