'He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look to what his own fingers have made'—the double negation: not to altars, not to the handiwork of fingers. The idols of 2:8 are abandoned not because they were destroyed by the enemy but because the worshipper has turned back to the true God. 'The Asherim or the altars of incense'—the two forms of Canaanite religious apparatus most associated with syncretism: the wooden poles for Asherah (fertility goddess) and the incense altars. Both disavowed. Oswalt: the refusal to look to idols is the positive face of looking to the Maker.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights and the hilltops, which they deserted because of the children of Israel, and there will be desolation. For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge; therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine branch of a stranger, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights'—the fortified cities abandoned: the same cities that the people trusted for security become as empty as the forests the Canaanites fled at Israel's conquest. The historical reversal: Israel became like the Canaanites, and now their cities are abandoned as Canaanite cities once were. 'For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge'—the root cause of the desolation: forgetting (shakhakh) and not remembering. Spiritual amnesia produces moral collapse. 'The God of your salvation' and 'the Rock of your refuge'—two covenant-names: God as deliverer and God as protection. Both forgotten. 'Though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine branch of a stranger'—religious horticulture: planting foreign religious plants (worship-gardens for pagan deities) in place of relationship with the Rock. Childs: the garden metaphor inverts creation—instead of tending God's garden, they plant their own in honor of other gods.

verseByVerse.quote: though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain. Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow'—the frantic pace of pagan religion: even the agricultural metaphor is accelerated. The plants grow the same day they are planted; the blossoms appear the same morning. But this unnatural haste is the sign of its falseness—genuine growth takes time. 'Yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain'—what was produced by religious effort cannot be kept; the harvest of idolatry vanishes under divine judgment. 'Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea'—the next scene: nations gathering against Zion, their noise like ocean waves. The thunder of the nations is impressive and terrifying but, like the sea, bounded. Motyer: the sea-image recalls creation where God bounded the sea—the nations are no more capable of overflowing their limits than the sea is.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm. At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away'—God's rebuke is sufficient: a single word dissolves the gathered nations. 'Chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm'—two images of effortless dispersal: chaff (weightless, at the wind's mercy) and dust (insubstantial, formless). The great nations are as light as chaff before God's rebuke. 'At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more!'—the sudden dissolution: the terror of evening gone by morning. The same structure as 10:28–34 (the Assyrian advance that halts at Nob) applied universally. 'This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us'—the closing line makes the lesson explicit: this is what happens to every nation that sets itself against God's people. Webb: the oracle ends as a promise: the nations that thunder against Zion are chaff before the LORD who created and bounded the sea.

18.subtitle: The Oracle Against Cush
18.intro: Overview. Chapter 18 is a brief oracle addressed to the land of Cush (ancient Ethiopia/Sudan), the nation from which Judah might have been tempted to seek military help against Assyria. The oracle is unusual in that it contains no explicit condemnation — it is more of a description of events, addressed to the distant Cushites, announcing that God is watching events unfold from his heavenly throne and will act at the right moment. The chapter ends with the remarkable promise that Cush will one day bring gifts to the LORD on Mount Zion.

sections.title: The LORD Watches from His Dwelling
sections.commentary:
The envoys from Cush — who apparently came to seek an alliance with Judah against Assyria — are sent back home with a message: go and wait. The imagery of verse 4 is striking: “For thus the LORD said to me: I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” God is not inactive; he is watching with the quiet intensity of a farmer watching the sky in harvest season. The decisive moment will come, but not yet.

v. 4 — “I will quietly look from my dwelling.” The word quietly is the key. God does not need to be agitated or reactive. He watches with sovereign calm from his throne, knowing precisely when and how he will act. This is the posture of the God who “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph 1:11) — not hurried, not uncertain, not surprised.

Verse 7 closes with an eschatological promise: a people tall and smooth, from a land divided by rivers, will bring gifts to the LORD of hosts on Mount Zion. The oracle that begins with Cush being sent home ends with Cush making a pilgrimage. The rejected envoys become, in the end, worshippers. This anticipates Psalm 68:31 (“Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God”) and the Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8.

keyVerse.quote: “For thus the LORD said to me: I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.”
keyVerse.note: The image of God watching quietly from his dwelling is one of the most calming pictures of divine sovereignty in Scripture. It is not passivity — the harvest is coming and the pruning shears are ready (v. 5). It is the quiet confidence of one who is never caught off guard, never reactive, always working toward his own purposes at exactly the right pace.

18.reflection: Chapter 18 is a reminder that God's apparent silence is not absence. He is watching — quietly, intently, from his dwelling — and he will act at exactly the right moment. The temptation in every crisis is to rush ahead of God, to seek the Cushite alliance when God has told us to wait. The chapter invites trust in the God who watches before he acts.
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush,<sup>2</sup>which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide.<sup>3</sup>All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on the earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear!<sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me: "I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest."<sup>5</sup>For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away.<sup>6</sup>They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them.<sup>7</sup>At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 18 is one of the shorter oracles against the nations—a word to Cush (ancient Ethiopia/Sudan), the great African power of the 25th dynasty that briefly controlled Egypt. The oracle is remarkable for its restraint: God watches quietly while Cush sends its swift messengers (vv. 1–2), then at the appointed harvest time acts (vv. 5–6), and finally receives the tribute of Cush's gifts at Zion (v. 7).
verseByVerse.examples: The church in every age faces the temptation to interpret God's silence as indifference. Isaiah 18 counters this: God sees clearly from his dwelling, knows the season, and will act at the right time. The 'tall and smooth' people of Cush who come to Zion with gifts (v. 7) prefigure the Gentile ingathering of ch. 11 and 60.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush, which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush'—the wings may be the buzzing of insects (locust swarms characteristic of the region), or the metaphor of swift ambassadors dispatched like birds. Cush was modern-day Sudan, a powerful empire in Isaiah's day (25th dynasty of Egypt). 'Which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters'—the Cushite diplomatic network: papyrus boats navigating the Nile's tributaries. 'Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far'—the description of Cush: tall, smooth (perhaps smooth-skinned), feared internationally. 'A nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide'—the Nile and its branches divide the Cushite territory. Oswalt: the vivid description of Cush's power and activity sets the stage for the contrast with God's quiet watching in vv. 3–4.

verseByVerse.quote: All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear! For thus the LORD said to me: “I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear!'—the universal summons: when God acts, the signal will be unmistakable. 'For thus the LORD said to me: “I will quietly look from my dwelling”'—the surprising word: quietly. Amid all the activity of Cush's ambassadors and the world's nations, God is silently watching. His watching is not passive: it is attentive, purposeful, and prelude to decisive action. 'Like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest'—two images of the quietly relentless. The clear heat of sunshine is invisible yet scorching; the dew-cloud in harvest heat is delicate yet nourishing. Both describe God's presence as powerful without being noisy. Childs: the silence of God is a theological statement—he does not need to be active at every moment; his timing is perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: For before the harvest, when the blossom is over and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away. They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For before the harvest, when the blossom is over and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks'—God the vinedresser acts at the precise moment: not too early (before the fruit is set) and not too late (after harvest). The timing is agricultural precision applied to divine judgment. Cush's power is cut precisely when it reaches its maximum—not before, not after. 'The spreading branches he lops off and clears away'—what was spreading and expansive is cut back to nothing; the ambition of the empire is pruned. 'They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth'—the army left unburied: the ultimate dishonor and the sign of total defeat. 'The birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them'—summer and winter: the carcasses lie through all seasons, a permanent monument to the empire's fall. Motyer: the harvested vine-shoots are the people of the empire; the parallel with Israel (5:1–7) is intentional.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth'—the description of Cush from v. 2 is repeated: the same people who sent ambassadors to Zion now bring tribute. The transformation is from political diplomacy to covenant submission: they come not as equals negotiating but as those who acknowledge the LORD of hosts as supreme. 'To Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts'—Zion as the destination of all nations' tribute (cf. 2:2–4; 60:1–9). The oracle that began with Cush's impressive diplomatic activity ends with Cush's voluntary pilgrimage to Zion. Oswalt: the chapter encapsulates the movement of the nations from self-sufficiency through judgment to the acknowledgment of God—a movement that the whole of Isaiah envisions for all nations. Young: the tribute of Cush to Zion is the beginning of the Gentile ingathering that the servant songs will develop fully.

19.subtitle: The Oracle Against Egypt — and Egypt's Redemption
19.intro: Overview. Chapter 19 is one of the most astonishing chapters in all of Isaiah. It opens with a severe oracle against Egypt — civil war, failed Nile, economic collapse, foolish counsellors — and then pivots, in its second half, to one of the most remarkable promises in the Old Testament: Egypt will know the LORD, worship him, and be called “my people.” The chapter that begins with God riding on a swift cloud against Egypt ends with Egypt, Assyria, and Israel forming a threefold blessing in the earth.

sections.title: Judgment on Egypt
sections.commentary:
“Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them.” The God who dried up the Red Sea for Israel now comes against Egypt in its own land. The judgment is comprehensive: civil strife (v. 2), failed Nile (v. 5), dried-up canals, economic devastation, and — most cutting of all — counsellors made foolish. Egypt prided itself on its ancient wisdom; the princes of Zoan, sons of ancient kings, are made “utterly foolish” (v. 13).

v. 3 — “And the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers.” When divine wisdom is rejected, the vacuum is filled with the counterfeits — idols, sorcerers, mediums. The pattern is the same as in chapter 8:19. A nation that turns from God's word ends up consulting the dead for guidance.

sections.title: Egypt Will Know the LORD
sections.commentary:
The second half of the chapter is a series of “in that day” oracles that move from judgment to transformation. Five cities in Egypt will speak the language of Canaan (Hebrew) and swear allegiance to the LORD. An altar to the LORD in the heart of Egypt and a pillar at its border will be signs and witnesses to the LORD of hosts. And when Egyptians cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, he will send them a saviour and defend them — exactly as he did for Israel in Egypt.

v. 25 — “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my heritage.” These three nations — Egypt, the ancient enslaver of Israel; Assyria, the current oppressor; Israel, the covenant people — are placed side by side in a single blessing. The terms used of Israel throughout Scripture (“my people,” “the work of my hands,” “my heritage”) are distributed equally among all three. This is the most explicit anticipation of Gentile inclusion in the covenant in all of the Old Testament. Paul's mission to the nations is the fulfilment of this verse.

keyVerse.quote: “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my heritage.”
keyVerse.note: The terms “my people” and “my heritage” are covenant terms used exclusively of Israel throughout the Old Testament. Here they are extended to Egypt and Assyria. This is not the abolition of Israel's election but its expansion — the covenant blessings flowing outward to the nations, exactly as God promised Abraham: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen 12:3).

19.theology: The universal scope of salvation. Isaiah 19:18–25 is the Old Testament's most explicit preview of what the New Testament calls the inclusion of the Gentiles. The nations that were Israel's greatest enemies — Egypt, Assyria — are called by the same covenant names as Israel herself. This does not mean that national identity is erased but that the covenant community is expanded. Paul's entire theology of Jew and Gentile in Ephesians 2–3 is the New Testament commentary on Isaiah 19.
19.reflection: Chapter 19 moves from “the LORD is coming against Egypt” to “blessed be Egypt my people” — from judgment to adoption, from terror to worship. This is the arc of the gospel for every human soul. The God who rides on a swift cloud against his enemies is the same God who says to those same enemies, “You are mine.” The distance between those two verses is the cross.
19.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them.<sup>2</sup>And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against another and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom;<sup>3</sup>and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers;<sup>4</sup>and I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.<sup>5</sup>And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be dry and parched,<sup>6</sup>and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away.<sup>7</sup>There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will be parched, will be driven away, and will be no more.<sup>8</sup>The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water.<sup>9</sup>The workers in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton.<sup>10</sup>Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved.<sup>11</sup>The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, "I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings"?<sup>12</sup>Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt.<sup>13</sup>The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded; those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger.<sup>14</sup>The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit.<sup>15</sup>And there will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do.<sup>16</sup>In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them.<sup>17</sup>And the land of Judah will become a terror to the Egyptians. Everyone to whom it is mentioned will fear because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against them.<sup>18</sup>In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts. One of these will be called the City of Destruction.<sup>19</sup>In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border.<sup>20</sup>It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them.<sup>23</sup>In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians.<sup>24</sup>In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth,<sup>25</sup>whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Oracle Against Egypt and Its Remarkable Ending
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 19 is one of the most remarkable chapters in the prophetic corpus. It begins with God riding into Egypt on a swift cloud to judge it (vv. 1–15), but ends with Egypt, Assyria, and Israel forming a holy triad—'my people Egypt, my handiwork Assyria, my inheritance Israel' (v. 25). This eschatological ending is without parallel: the two great superpowers that threatened Israel become God's own people.
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah 19:24–25 is one of the most extraordinary texts in the Bible for Christian missiology: the Gentile nations included in Israel's covenant vocabulary ('my people,' 'my inheritance'). The highway between Egypt and Assyria through Israel (v. 23) prefigures the new humanity in Christ where dividing walls are broken down (Eph. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them. And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against his brother and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt'—the theophanic entry: God on a cloud (a mode of divine transportation in the ancient Near East; cf. Ps. 104:3). He comes to Egypt; Egypt is not irrelevant to him. 'The idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence'—the gods of Egypt (the most elaborate polytheism of the ancient world) shudder at the approach of the true God. What terrified the nations (God's presence) unmasks the impotence of Egypt's religious apparatus. 'The heart of the Egyptians will melt within them'—the same response as Babylon's (13:7): all human confidence dissolved at the divine approach. 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against his brother'—civil war: God's instrument of judgment against Egypt is Egypt itself. The internal conflicts that characterized Egypt's late period (the breakdown into competing dynasties) are the fulfillment. Oswalt: God need not bring an external army; he can dissolve a society from within.

verseByVerse.quote: and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers. And I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the Lord GOD of hosts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out'—the Egyptian spirit (ruakh) of wisdom and confidence vacated. Egypt was famous for its wisdom (Gen. 41; Acts 7:22); God empties that too. 'I will confound their counsel'—Egypt was known for its counselors and advisors; God confuses the very faculty Egypt trusted most. 'They will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers'—in desperation, Egypt consults every available alternative to genuine divine wisdom, all of which are condemned (8:19). 'I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them'—the ultimate judgment: Egyptian sovereignty ends. The hard master may be Assyria (Esarhaddon) or later Babylon or Persia. Childs: Egypt, which was the hard master of Israel (Ex. 1:11–14), now receives its own hard master—the covenantal principle of measure-for-measure applied at the imperial level.

verseByVerse.quote: And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be parched and dry; and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be parched and dry'—the Nile is Egypt: its flooding and retreat governed all agricultural life. To dry up the Nile is to end Egypt. 'Its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up'—the irrigation system (the canals and channels that distributed the Nile's water to the fields) becomes foul and then empty. 'Reeds and rushes will rot away'—the papyrus and reed plants that grew along the Nile's banks—the raw material of Egyptian writing, boat-building, and basket-weaving—disappear. The entire ecological foundation of Egyptian civilization is removed. Young: the judgment against the Nile reverses the plagues of Moses (Ex. 7:14–25 turned the Nile to blood); now the river simply fails. The God who controls the Nile controls Egypt's fate entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will dry up, be driven away, and be no more. The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will dry up'—the agricultural catastrophe: the fields that depended on Nile flooding and irrigation produce nothing. The Egyptian agricultural cycle—plant at the Nile's recession, harvest before the flood—breaks down entirely. 'Be driven away, and be no more'—absolute erasure: what was once productive is completely gone. 'The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water'—the fishing industry collapse: hook-fishermen and net-fishermen alike become unemployed. Fishing was a major Egyptian industry; its failure compounds the agricultural catastrophe. Motyer: the two losses (agricultural and fishing) represent the two primary food sources of Egypt—both cut off simultaneously.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who work in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton. Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Those who work in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton'—Egypt's textile industry: flax (for linen) and cotton were Egyptian specialties exported throughout the Mediterranean. The craftsmen of these industries—from raw fiber to finished cloth—face total economic collapse. 'Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed'—the 'pillars' are Egypt's foundations: its elite workers, its ruling class, those who constitute the social structure. When the pillars are crushed, the whole building falls. 'All who work for pay will be grieved'—the wage economy: everyone who depended on employment loses their livelihood. Oswalt: the judgment is socially comprehensive—it touches every economic class, from artisan to elite, from fisherfolk to linen-weavers.

verseByVerse.quote: The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings”? Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel'—Zoan (Tanis) was a Delta city that served as a royal seat; its princes represented Egypt's political intelligence. They are demolished by divine wisdom. 'How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings”?'—the claim of pedigree: Egyptian wisdom was measured by antiquity of lineage. But pedigree without the fear of the LORD produces only 'stupid counsel.' 'Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt'—the challenge: if Egypt's wise men are truly wise, they should be able to read the divine plan. Their inability to read the plan exposes the bankruptcy of their wisdom. Childs: the contest between Egyptian wisdom and divine wisdom is the prophetic counterpart to Moses' confrontation with Pharaoh's magicians (Ex. 7–9).

verseByVerse.quote: The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded; those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger. The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded'—Zoan (Delta) and Memphis (the ancient capital, near modern Cairo) represent the two poles of Egyptian political geography. Both poles produce fools and deluded men. 'Those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger'—the very leaders (cornerstones) who should stabilize the nation are the agents of its instability. 'The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion'—God is the source of the confusion: he has poured a spirit of delusion into Egypt's leadership. The divine passive reversal of wisdom. 'As a drunken man staggers in his vomit'—the most undignified image: Egypt's leadership is as incapacitated as a drunk man who cannot stand in his own mess. Young: the image deliberately humiliates the world's most sophisticated political culture.

verseByVerse.quote: And there will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do. In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do'—the vocabulary from 9:14–15 (head/tail, palm/reed) now applied to Egypt: all levels of leadership are equally impotent. No Egyptian—high or low, lofty or humble—can do anything to reverse the divine judgment. 'In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear'—the gender comparison is ancient military idiom for extreme demoralization: the warrior who trembles like a woman in battle has lost all fighting capacity. 'Before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them'—the shaking hand of God: not the stretched-out hand of judgment (9:12 etc.) but the menacing shake of warning. Even the threat of God's hand is enough to make Egypt a trembling mass. Motyer: the contrast with v. 1 (God on the swift cloud coming to Egypt) is the beginning of the chapter; its effect on Egypt is the middle; the surprising conclusion begins at v. 17.

verseByVerse.quote: And the land of Judah will become a terror to Egypt. Everyone to whom it is mentioned will fear because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against it. In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts. One of these will be called the City of Destruction. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The land of Judah will become a terror to Egypt'—a remarkable reversal: tiny Judah, which Egypt despised, becomes the source of Egypt's fear. Because God's word comes through Judah, Judah is more powerful than Egypt. 'Because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against it'—the fear is theological, not military: Egypt fears what God has said about Egypt through Judah's prophets. 'In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts'—the beginning of the conversion: Egyptian cities adopting Hebrew (the language of the covenant community) and swearing loyalty to the LORD. This is covenant language applied to Gentile cities. 'One of these will be called the City of Destruction'—possibly heliopolis (City of the Sun, altered to City of Destruction); or a city of judgment that becomes a city of conversion. Childs: five cities—a representative number—of Egypt publicly aligned with the LORD of hosts is an extraordinary sign of the nations' turning.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border. It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border'—two covenant signs planted in Egypt: an altar (the place of sacrifice and worship) at the center, a pillar (a memorial monument to God's covenant) at the border. Egypt becomes a place of legitimate Yahweh-worship. This is extraordinary given Deuteronomy's restriction of the altar to the central sanctuary. 'It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt'—the theological function: the altar and pillar testify to the LORD's reality and presence in Egypt. 'When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them'—Egypt's cry to the LORD and the LORD's response mirrors Exodus: the oppressed cry, God delivers (Ex. 3:7–9). Egypt, once the oppressor, now experiences what Israel experienced—and receives the same response. Oswalt: the covenant structure (cry, hear, send savior) is extended to Egypt—they become recipients of covenant grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them. And the LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day'—the covenantal knowledge that defines Israel's relationship with God ('know the LORD') is now extended to Egypt. 'And worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them'—the full range of covenant worship: sacrifice, offering, and vows. Egypt becomes a worshipping community indistinguishable from Israel in its posture toward God. 'The LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD'—the divine pedagogy: the judgment (striking) produces the return (healing). The striking is purposive: not destruction but the pain that leads to repentance and healing. 'He will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them'—the divine ear opens to Egypt's prayer as it opens to Israel's. Motyer: the healing of Egypt is the healing of the covenant relationship—the same grace that healed Israel is extended to Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians. In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria'—the road of enmity (the invasion route Egypt and Assyria used against each other for centuries) becomes a highway of peace. 'Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians'—not trade or diplomacy but worship: the two former enemies worship together. The shared worship of the LORD transforms political enmity into spiritual kinship. 'In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth'—the three nations form a holy triad: Egypt (south), Assyria (north-east), Israel (in the midst). Israel, long the weakest of the three militarily, is in the center—not because it is the most powerful but because it is the mediating bearer of covenant knowledge to the nations. Childs: the highway between ancient enemies is the prototype of the new humanity in Christ (Eph. 2:14–16).

verseByVerse.quote: whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance'—the most astonishing verse in the oracle against Egypt. 'My people' (ammi) was Israel's exclusive covenant designation (cf. Ex. 3:7; 6:7); now it is applied to Egypt. 'The work of my hands' (ma'aseh yadai) was Israel's description of itself as God's creation; now it applies to Assyria. 'My inheritance' (nakhalati) was Israel's title; it remains Israel's but in a context where Egypt and Assyria have been included. The three covenant-titles redistribute without diminishing Israel: Egypt and Assyria receive designations that were Israel's, and Israel still retains its own. Oswalt: this verse is the furthest reach of Isaiah's universalism—the nations not merely subdued or converted but adopted into the covenant family with Israel's own covenant names. It anticipates Romans 9–11 and the mystery of Gentile inclusion in the one people of God.

20.subtitle: The Sign of Isaiah's Nakedness
20.intro: Overview. Chapter 20 is a brief but vivid narrative. For three years, at God's command, Isaiah walked naked and barefoot as a living sign — a prophecy enacted in the prophet's own body. The sign had a specific target: Judah's temptation to rely on an Egyptian-Cushite military coalition against Assyria. Isaiah's three-year acted parable announced that Egypt and Cush would be led away by Assyria as naked prisoners, and therefore they were no foundation to build on.

sections.title: Three Years Naked and Barefoot
sections.commentary:
The chapter is anchored by the historical detail of Sargon II of Assyria's campaign against Ashdod (711 BC), confirming the oracle's specific context. Isaiah's three-year walking sign was a sustained, public, costly demonstration — not a brief prophetic gesture but a years-long embodiment of the message. The prophet's body became the sermon.

v. 3 — “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush.” The word servant here connects Isaiah to the Servant figure of chapters 40–55. Isaiah's willingness to suffer public shame to deliver God's message is itself a foreshadowing of the greater Servant who would bear far greater shame for a far greater purpose.

The practical point of the sign is verse 6: those who were looking to Egypt and Cush for help will be horrified when those powers are themselves led away as prisoners. “And we, how shall we escape?” The question is the point. If your source of security has been captured, what are you left with? Isaiah's answer, consistent throughout the book, is that the only reliable refuge has always been the LORD himself.

keyVerse.quote: “And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, ‘Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?’”
keyVerse.note: The question “how shall we escape?” is the exact question every misplaced confidence eventually produces. When the thing we trusted — whether Egypt, an alliance, a financial plan, a relationship — fails, we are left with the question Isaiah has been asking from chapter 1: to whom are you actually looking? The answer the book provides is always the same: “Look to the rock from which you were hewn” (51:1).

20.reflection: Isaiah's three-year acted sign is a reminder that God sometimes calls his servants to costly, public, apparently undignified forms of witness. The prophet did not get to choose a more respectable way to deliver this message. The question the chapter poses is both historical and personal: what is the Egypt or Cush in your own life — the security that looks impressive but will one day be led away in chains?
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it—<sup>2</sup>at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, "Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet," and he did so, walking naked and barefoot.<sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said, "As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush,<sup>4</sup>so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast.<sup>6</sup>And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Sign-Act Against Egypt and Cush
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 20 records one of the most dramatic sign-acts in prophecy: Isaiah walked stripped and barefoot for three years as a living parable of what Assyria would do to Egypt and Cush. The sign-act was directed not at Egypt but at Judah's political leaders who were counseling trust in Egypt as a counter-balance to Assyria.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign-act challenges the church's tendency to seek security in human alliances when those alliances require trust in what God has condemned. Every generation finds its Egypt—the powerful alternative to trusting God that seems safer but leads to captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it— at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, “Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet,” and he did so, walking naked and barefoot. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the year that the commander in chief... came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it'—the historical anchor: 711 BC, the Assyrian capture of Ashdod (a Philistine city allied with Egypt). Ashdod had looked to Egypt for help; Egypt did not come. This is the historical context that makes Isaiah's sign-act intelligible. 'Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet'—God commands a state of public humiliation: stripped of the garments of mourning (sackcloth) and removed from footwear. 'And he did so, walking naked and barefoot'—Isaiah obeyed without recorded protest. The nakedness was probably not total nudity but the minimal undergarment of a slave or captive. Motyer: the sign-act is costly obedience—Isaiah bears in his body the indignity of what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush, so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush'—the three years establishes the duration and the authenticating audience. 'My servant Isaiah'—the first use of the servant title in Isaiah for a human figure; it anticipates the Servant Songs of ch. 40–53. 'So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered'—what Isaiah did voluntarily, the Egyptian and Cushite captives will do involuntarily. The humiliation Isaiah adopted symbolically, they will experience actually. 'The nakedness of Egypt'—the exposure of Egypt's shame: the great power that Judah was tempted to trust will itself be stripped and paraded. Oswalt: the sign-act functions as merciful warning to Judah before the disaster becomes inevitable.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast. And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, “Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast'—two emotional states: dismayed (khathar, shattered) and ashamed (boshu, humiliated). The source of each is the object of false trust: Cush was the hope, Egypt was the boast. 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped'—the confession of failed expectation: what we relied on has been destroyed. The hope in Egypt and Cush was not merely political but quasi-religious—the kind of trust that belongs only to God. 'And we, how shall we escape?'—the coastland peoples' terrified question. If Egypt fell, they have no alternative refuge. Childs: the question exposes the theological vacuum created by misplaced trust—when the false refuge fails, there is nothing. Isaiah's answer to 'how shall we escape' is the entire remaining book: only through trust in the Holy One of Israel.

21.subtitle: Oracles Against Babylon, Edom, and Arabia
21.intro: Overview. Chapter 21 contains three short oracles, each addressed to a different nation. The first and longest (vv. 1–10) is a vision of Babylon’s fall, delivered with such physical intensity that the prophet reels under it. The second (vv. 11–12) is a night-watchman exchange with Edom — poetic, cryptic, unresolved. The third (vv. 13–17) turns to the desert caravans of Arabia, where the commerce of the ancient world will be silenced within a year. Together they form a triptych: the great empire, its anxious neighbor, and the ordinary trader — all subject to the same sovereign word.

sections.title: The Fall of Babylon
sections.commentary:
The oracle opens with a locust-like storm sweeping in from the wilderness — the image of an invading army in Isaiah’s symbolic vocabulary. God commands the Medes and Elamites to besiege, and Isaiah, caught up in the vision, reacts with physical anguish: his body shakes, his mind is dismayed, the twilight he longed for has become terror. The prophet is not a detached analyst but a participant in what he sees. He watches a banqueting table become a battlefield.

v. 3 — “My loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor.” The image of labor pains for divine judgment runs throughout Isaiah (13:8; 26:17; 66:7) and into the New Testament (Matt. 24:8). It conveys both inevitability and agony: what is coming cannot be stopped, and it will not be painless.

The watchman’s announcement — “Fallen, fallen is Babylon” — is laconic and precise. Revelation 18:2 quotes it exactly, applying it to the final fall of the city that represents human empire in all ages. Isaiah sees it as already done; the prophetic perfect collapses the distance between announcement and event. The chapter closes with a word of suffering comfort to “my threshed one, son of my threshing floor” — Israel, ground down but not destroyed, told that this vision is for them.

sections.title: The Watchman of Edom
sections.commentary: Someone calls from Seir (Edom): “Watchman, what time of the night?” The question has an anxious edge — is the darkness nearly over? The watchman’s reply is the most enigmatic in Isaiah: “Morning comes, and also the night. If you would inquire, inquire; come back again.” There is light coming, but darkness too. Not a promise of dawn without night, but a summons to keep inquiring. Edom is told it may return with its question — which is itself a mercy: the door is not closed.

sections.title: Arabia
sections.commentary: The final oracle addresses the caravans of Dedan and the people of Tema, who are called to bring water and bread to the fleeing refugees of Kedar. The judgment on Kedar — the Arabian tribes whose archers and warriors were renowned — is precise: within one year, “all the glory of Kedar will come to an end.” The timeframe is specific, and God underwrites it with his own name. Even the edges of the ancient world are within the scope of his word.

keyVerse.quote: “Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night? The watchman says: ‘Morning comes, and also the night.’”
keyVerse.note: The exchange is one of the strangest moments in prophetic literature. But its strangeness is the point: history does not move in simple arcs from darkness to light. Morning and night come together. The right response is not resignation but inquiry — keep asking, keep returning.

21.reflection: Isaiah reeled physically under the vision of Babylon’s fall. The prophets were not spectators of history but participants in God’s grief over it. Is there a situation in the world right now that you have allowed yourself to feel — not just analyze? And what does it mean to keep “inquiring” in the darkness when the watchman can only say that morning and night will both come?
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land.<sup>2</sup>A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end.<sup>3</sup>Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see.<sup>4</sup>My heart staggers; horror has appalled me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling.<sup>5</sup>They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield!<sup>6</sup>For thus the Lord said to me: "Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees.<sup>7</sup>When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently."<sup>8</sup>Then he who saw cried out: "Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights.<sup>9</sup>And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs!" And he answered, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground."<sup>10</sup>O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you.<sup>11</sup>The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, "Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?"<sup>12</sup>The watchman says: "Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again."<sup>13</sup>The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites.<sup>14</sup>To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema.<sup>15</sup>For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle.<sup>16</sup>For thus the Lord said to me, "Within a year, according to the years of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end.<sup>17</sup>And the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Oracles Against Babylon, Dumah, and Arabia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 21 contains three brief oracles: the oracle of the desert sea (Babylon's fall, vv. 1–10), the oracle of Dumah (Edom, vv. 11–12), and the oracle against Arabia (vv. 13–17). The Babylon oracle is one of the most dramatic in the book: a watchman standing on the wall reports what he sees, and what he sees is the fall of Babylon to Medo-Persian forces.
verseByVerse.examples: Revelation 18:2 quotes Isaiah 21:9 ('Fallen, fallen is Babylon') as a description of the final fall of the anti-God empire. The church's watchman role is to announce what God has declared—including the certainty of judgment and the certainty of salvation—regardless of whether the audience wants to hear it.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land. A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea'—a cryptic title: the wilderness of the sea probably refers to Babylon, surrounded by the Euphrates flood-marshes. The 'wilderness' quality may emphasize desolation to come. 'As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on'—the Negeb's desert storms are sudden, violent, and unstoppable: the image of judgment approaching. 'A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys'—the vision's character: stern, not gentle. The traitor and destroyer are probably Media and Persia, who will end Babylon. 'Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media'—the divine commission to the Medo-Persian forces. 'All the sighing she has caused I bring to an end'—the sighing of Babylon's victims (including Israel) is the grounds for judgment: God has heard the groaning and is acting. Oswalt: the oracle is dense and vivid, like the watchman's breathless report of what he sees approaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see. My heart staggers; horror has overwhelmed me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor'—the prophet's visceral response to the vision. Isaiah does not receive divine judgment as welcome news but as physical torment. The birth-pang metaphor recurs: the onset of judgment is like labor—overwhelming, involuntary, building to a climax. 'I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see'—the prophetic senses overloaded: unable to hear the vision clearly, unable to see it steadily. The intensity of divine revelation produces physical prostration. 'The twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling'—the evening rest (twilight) that the prophet anticipated as respite has become the time of trembling. Childs: the prophet's suffering is not incidental but participatory—he enters into the pain of what he announces, particularly when it involves the suffering of peoples, even enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield! For thus the Lord said to me: “Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink'—the scene of Babylon's feast: the empire at its most comfortable and self-assured. The historical parallel is Belshazzar's feast (Dan. 5), when Babylon was taken while the king feasted. 'Arise, O princes; oil the shield!'—the sudden alarm: from feasting to emergency. The shields were oiled to maintain their leather facing for combat; the command to oil them is a last-minute call to arms. 'Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees'—God commands the appointment of a watchman. The watchman is the ancient equivalent of a surveillance system: stationed on the city wall to report approaching developments. The LORD uses human observation as the medium of prophetic announcement. Motyer: the watchman motif is Isaiah's self-description—he watches, he reports, he does not determine the outcome.

verseByVerse.quote: When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently.“ Then he who saw cried out: ”Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently'—the watchman's commission to observe every category of messenger or army approaching: equestrian warriors, donkey-borne traders, camel-mounted messengers. The double 'diligently' stresses the watchman's attention: he must not miss the signal. 'Then he who saw cried out: “Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights”'—the prophet identifies himself as the watchman: stationed, faithful, day and night. 'O Lord, continually'—the continuousness of the prophetic watch. Young: the watchman who prays 'O Lord' turns his post into a prayer station; watching and praying are inseparable in the prophetic calling.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs!“ And he answered, ”Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground.“ O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground'—the watchman's report: the doubled 'fallen' is the announcement of total and irreversible collapse. The doubling signals certainty: not 'perhaps will fall' but definitively fallen. 'All the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground'—the gods of Babylon destroyed along with the city: Marduk, Bel, Nabu. The Medo-Persian conquest in 539 BC was the historical fulfillment; Revelation 18:2 applies this to the eschatological Babylon. 'O my threshed and winnowed one'—Isaiah addresses Israel as grain that has been threshed and winnowed: the painful process that separates wheat from chaff. Israel has suffered at Babylon's hand; the announcement of Babylon's fall is addressed specifically to Israel's suffering. 'What I have heard from the LORD of hosts... I announce to you'—the source: not the watchman's own assessment but the word of the LORD of hosts. Oswalt: the prophetic word is authorized precisely because it derives from the LORD of hosts, not from human observation.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, “Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?” The watchman says: “Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The oracle concerning Dumah'—Dumah may be a place in Edom or a wordplay on Edom (Edom/Dumah) with the meaning 'silence.' 'One is calling to me from Seir, “Watchman, what time of the night?”'—Seir is Edom's mountain range; the Edomites call out to the watchman (perhaps Isaiah) asking about the duration of the night of judgment. The question is urgent: how much longer? 'Morning comes, and also the night'—the watchman's cryptic answer: morning and night come together. There is both a morning (some relief, some possibility) and also night (judgment persists). 'If you will inquire, inquire; come back again'—the answer is not final; it requires further inquiry. Motyer: the Edom oracle is perhaps the most enigmatic in the book—the ambiguity of the answer matches the ambiguity of Edom's position: not completely under judgment, not yet in the light of dawn. The invitation to come back suggests the door is not permanently closed.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites'—the Dedanites were Arabian traders whose caravan routes ran through the Hejaz. They are lodging in thickets (hiding places) instead of caravanserais—fleeing something. 'To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema'—Tema was an oasis town in northwestern Arabia. The inhabitants are commanded to extend hospitality to the fleeing Dedanite refugees. The commands recall the law of the sabbath-year (Deut. 23:24–25) and the hospitality ethic of the wilderness. Childs: even in the oracles of judgment, the ethic of compassion for the vulnerable continues—the refugees fleeing Assyrian or Babylonian pressure deserve the same care as any other displaced person.

verseByVerse.quote: For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle. For thus the Lord said to me, “Within a year, according to the years of a hireling, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle'—the reason for the flight: Assyrian military advance into Arabia. The three instruments of war (drawn sword, bent bow, press of battle) catalog the full engagement of military force. 'Within a year, according to the years of a hireling, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end'—Kedar was a major Arab tribal confederation, famous for its flocks and its archers (v. 17). 'According to the years of a hireling'—the precision of the prophetic timetable; the year is contractually exact, as in 16:14. The glory (kabod) of Kedar—its power, wealth, and reputation—will be annihilated within this precise time. Young: the exact timeframe is a challenge to faith and a test of prophecy: the prophet stakes his credibility on the deadline.

verseByVerse.quote: and the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few'—Kedar was famous for its archers (49:28–29; Ps. 120:5). The warriors who defined Kedar's military reputation are reduced to a remnant. 'For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken'—the oracle's ground and authority: the LORD, God of Israel. Not a god of Arabia, not a Mesopotamian deity, but the LORD of Israel—who governs all nations, including the Arab tribal confederations of the distant desert. Motyer: the closing formula is the prophetic seal: these words are not human political analysis but divine declaration. The specificity of the prophecy (within a year, few archers) makes its fulfillment verifiable and its source unmistakable.

22.subtitle: The Valley of Vision
22.intro: Overview. Chapter 22 is unique in the oracles-against-the-nations sequence: it is addressed not to a foreign power but to Jerusalem itself, here called “the valley of vision.” The city that has received more revelation than any other is judged precisely for what it did with it. The occasion appears to be a near-miss — perhaps Sennacherib’s siege in 701 BC, when the city was threatened and then inexplicably spared. But instead of weeping and repentance, Jerusalem breaks out in celebration. The chapter also contains a striking personal oracle against the arrogant royal steward Shebna, and a promise about a better servant, Eliakim.

sections.title: The Unrepentant City
sections.commentary:
The rooftops of Jerusalem are full of noise and celebration. The prophet asks: what has happened that everyone has gone up to the housetops? The answer comes with heavy irony: your slain were not killed by the sword or in battle — they fled and were taken. The city’s leaders ran, its defenders scattered. Yet now they celebrate as if they had won.

Isaiah weeps, and asks to be left alone in his grief. He refuses to be comforted. This is not performance but prophetic solidarity with what God sees: a day of tumult, of trampling, of confusion. The Assyrian (or Babylonian) army has assembled; the siege equipment is in place; the city’s own water system has been inspected and prepared. Everything is ready for judgment — and Jerusalem parties.

v. 13 — “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” Paul quotes this exact phrase in 1 Cor. 15:32 as the logical conclusion of a life with no resurrection. Isaiah identifies it not as honest hedonism but as hardened unresponsiveness — the refusal to hear what God is saying in the events of the day.

The verdict in verse 14 is solemn: “This iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die.” Some sins have a point of no return — not because forgiveness is impossible in principle, but because the heart has crossed a threshold of deliberate, celebratory rejection of what is plainly true.

sections.title: Shebna and Eliakim
sections.commentary:
The oracle pivots from the city to one man: Shebna, the steward (literally “the one over the house”), who has been cutting himself a grand tomb on the heights. He is building his memorial while the city burns. God will take him up like a ball and hurl him into a wide land, and he will die there far from home. His grand tomb will be empty.

In his place God will call Eliakim, on whom he will hang “the key of the house of David” — authority to open and shut, to admit and exclude. Revelation 3:7 applies this language directly to Christ: “the words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens.” Eliakim is a type whose antitype fills the office perfectly.

v. 22 — “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David.” A key on the shoulder was a mark of stewardship over the royal household — physical, weighty, impossible to overlook. The image passes through Isaiah into Revelation as the defining picture of Christ’s absolute authority over access to God.

keyVerse.quote: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.”
keyVerse.note: What begins as a personnel change in Hezekiah’s court becomes one of the richest Christological images in the Old Testament. Rev. 3:7 places this language on the lips of the risen Christ. No one approaches the Father except through him; no one is excluded who comes through him.

22.reflection: Jerusalem celebrated survival without repentance. The near-miss became a party rather than a turning point. Is there a situation in your life where God has been merciful and you have responded with relief rather than return? What would true repentance look like in that situation now?

Your slain are not slain with the sword or dead in battle.<sup>3</sup>All your leaders have fled together; without the bow they were captured. All of you who were found were captured, though they had fled far away.<sup>4</sup>Therefore I said: "Look away from me; let me weep bitter tears; do not labor to comfort me concerning the destruction of the daughter of my people."<sup>5</sup>For the Lord GOD of hosts has a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the valley of vision, a battering down of walls and a shouting to the mountains.<sup>6</sup>And Elam bore the quiver with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield.<sup>7</sup>Your choicest valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen took their stand at the gates.<sup>8</sup>He has taken away the covering of Judah. In that day you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest,<sup>9</sup>and you saw that the breaches of the city of David were many.
