When you have ceased to destroy, you will be destroyed; and when you have finished betraying, they will betray you.<sup>2</sup>O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble.<sup>3</sup>At the tumultuous noise peoples flee; when you lift yourself up, nations are scattered,<sup>4</sup>and your spoil is gathered as the caterpillar gathers; as locusts leap, it is leapt upon.<sup>5</sup>The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness,<sup>6</sup>and he will be the stability of your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure.<sup>7</sup>Behold, their heroes cry in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly.<sup>8</sup>The highways lie waste; the traveler ceases. Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man.<sup>9</sup>The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is confounded and withers away; Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves.<sup>10</sup>"Now I will arise," says the LORD, "now I will lift myself up; now I will be exalted.<sup>11</sup>You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble; your breath is a fire that will consume you.<sup>12</sup>And the peoples will be as if burned to lime, like thorns cut down, that are burned in the fire."<sup>13</sup>Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and you who are near, acknowledge my might.<sup>14</sup>The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless: "Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?"<sup>15</sup>He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppressions, who shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed and shuts his eyes from looking on evil,<sup>16</sup>he will dwell on the heights; his place of defense will be the fortresses of rocks; his bread will be given him; his water will be sure.<sup>17</sup>Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land that stretches afar.<sup>18</sup>Your heart will muse on the terror: "Where is he who counted, where is he who weighed the tribute? Where is he who counted the towers?"<sup>19</sup>You will see no more the insolent people, the people of an obscure speech that you cannot comprehend, stammering in a tongue that you cannot understand.<sup>20</sup>Behold Zion, the city of our appointed feasts! Your eyes will see Jerusalem, an untroubled habitation, an immovable tent, whose stakes will never be plucked up, nor will any of its cords be broken.<sup>21</sup>But there the LORD in majesty will be for us a place of broad rivers and streams, where no galley with oars can go, nor majestic ship can pass.<sup>22</sup>For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us.<sup>23</sup>Your cords hang loose; they cannot hold the mast firm in its place or keep the sail spread out. Then prey and spoil in abundance will be divided; even the lame will take the prey.<sup>24</sup>And no inhabitant will say, "I am sick"; the people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–24 — The Destroyer Destroyed and the King in His Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 33 is a liturgical chapter—a complex psalm of lament, petition, divine response, and vision of the coming king—that functions as a hinge between the woe oracles (ch. 28–32) and the climactic judgment/restoration sequences (ch. 34–35). The woe against the destroyer (v. 1) is finally answered; God arises (v. 10); Zion's sin is burned away (vv. 11–14); and the righteous community receives a vision of the king in his beauty and the land of far horizons (vv. 17–24).
verseByVerse.examples: The vision of 'the king in his beauty' (v. 17) has sustained the church's eschatological imagination for two millennia. The king whose beauty will be seen is the one 'whom having not seen, you love' (1 Pet. 1:8). The 'land of far horizons' (v. 17) is the new creation whose dimensions exceed all earthly geography.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, you destroyer, who yourself have not been destroyed, you traitor, whom none has betrayed! When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed; and when you have ceased to betray, you will be betrayed. O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ah, you destroyer, who yourself have not been destroyed, you traitor, whom none has betrayed!'—the woe against Assyria is unique: the destroyer who has been exempt from destruction, the betrayer who has not been betrayed. The irony: its exemption is temporary. 'When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed; and when you have ceased to betray, you will be betrayed'—the divine timetable: Assyria's destruction comes when its appointed work is complete. 'O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble'—the community's prayer: grace, waiting, the divine arm as daily provision, and salvation in crisis. 'Every morning' is the rhythm of daily dependence: not a once-for-all transaction but a renewable covenant grace. Motyer: the prayer that follows the woe is the model of prophetic intercession—naming the enemy's doom while asking God for the community's grace.

verseByVerse.quote: At the tumultuous noise the peoples flee; when you lift yourself up, the nations are scattered. And your spoil is gathered as the caterpillar gathers; as locusts leap, it is leapt upon. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'At the tumultuous noise the peoples flee; when you lift yourself up, the nations are scattered'—the divine theophany causes flight: God's arising is sufficient to scatter the assembled nations. The tumultuous noise (rumbling—the sound of God's approach) is itself enough to rout the enemy. 'And your spoil is gathered as the caterpillar gathers; as locusts leap, it is leapt upon'—the reversal of Assyrian plundering: now Israel gathers Assyria's spoil as quickly and thoroughly as locusts strip vegetation. What Assyria accumulated by ravaging nations is redistributed in a moment. Oswalt: the reversal of plundering is the covenant justice of the same 'measure for measure' that operated throughout the nations' oracles—what was taken is returned.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness, and he will be the stability of your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness'—the filling of Zion with justice and righteousness is the direct consequence of the LORD's exaltation. His high dwelling produces the low-level transformation of the city. 'He will be the stability of your times'—the LORD himself as the foundation of the covenant community's stability: not military alliance, not Egypt's horses, not walls and reservoirs—but God himself as the security. 'Abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure'—the four resources of the restored community: salvation (yeshua), wisdom (khokmah), knowledge (da'at), and the fear of the LORD (yir'at YHWH). 'The fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure'—not Tyre's commercial wealth, not Egypt's military resources, but the reverential knowledge of God. Childs: the fear of the LORD as Zion's treasure is the inversion of every worldly measurement of national security and prosperity.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, their heroes cry in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly. The highways lie waste; the traveler ceases. Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Their heroes cry in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly'—the reversal of heroism: the warriors (heroes) who should be commanding are crying; the diplomats (envoys of peace) who should be negotiating are weeping. Both military and diplomatic capacities have failed. 'The highways lie waste; the traveler ceases'—the collapse of infrastructure: the roads that connected cities and enabled commerce are abandoned. The commercial interruption that began with Tyre (ch. 23) reaches its climax here. 'Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man'—the dissolution of the international order: treaties broken, cities disdained, human dignity disregarded. These are the conditions of Assyrian devastation that the community has been praying for God to end since v. 2. Motyer: the verses describe the context of the prayer—the community prays from within the ruins, not from a position of safety.

verseByVerse.quote: The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is confounded and withers away; Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves. “Now I will arise,” says the LORD, “now I will lift myself up; now I will be exalted. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is confounded and withers away; Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves'—four landscapes of desolation: Lebanon (forests), Sharon (coastal plain), Bashan (fertile plateau), Carmel (agricultural mountain). All the famous regions of fertility and beauty have been stripped. '“Now I will arise,” says the LORD, “now I will lift myself up; now I will be exalted”'—the divine response at the moment of maximum desolation: 'now.' Three times 'now' (attah): the timing of God's arising is precisely at the lowest point of the crisis. God does not act before the darkness is complete; he acts when it is darkest. Young: the triple 'now' is God's own commentary on his timing—he has waited (30:18) until the destroyer has destroyed, and now he arises with irresistible authority.

verseByVerse.quote: You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble; your breath is a fire that will consume you. And the peoples will be as if burned to lime, like thorns cut down, that are burned in the fire.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble'—the futility of the enemy's plans: Assyria's grand schemes produce only chaff and stubble—the most worthless agricultural byproducts, consumed by any fire. The labor of imperial planning (conceiving) and imperial action (giving birth) produces nothing durable. 'Your breath is a fire that will consume you'—the self-consuming nature of Assyrian pride: the breath (spirit) that animated the empire becomes the fire that destroys it. The instrument of its power is the instrument of its judgment. 'And the peoples will be as if burned to lime, like thorns cut down, that are burned in the fire'—the nations aligned with Assyria share its fate: burned to calcium oxide (lime) or consumed as quickly as cut thorns. Oswalt: the lime-burning image is particularly vivid—thorns reduced to chemical change, nothing left but mineral residue.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and you who are near, acknowledge my might. The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless: “Who among us can dwell with the devouring fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and you who are near, acknowledge my might'—the universal proclamation of divine action: far and near (the whole world) called to hear and acknowledge. 'The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless'—the unexpected audience: the sinners within Zion, not just the enemy outside. The theophanic fire that destroys Assyria terrifies those in Zion who are not right with God. '“Who among us can dwell with the devouring fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?”'—the theological crisis: the God who burns the enemy also dwells in Zion as fire (31:9). His fire cannot be compartmentalized. The question is not about the enemy's fate but about the community's own standing before the holy God. Childs: the sinners in Zion are the most surprising detail—the divine victory over Assyria does not automatically vindicate all who live in Zion; personal holiness is required to dwell with the devouring fire.

verseByVerse.quote: He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppressions, who shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed and shuts his eyes from looking on evil, he will dwell on the heights; his place of defense will be the fortresses of rocks; his bread will be given him; his water will be sure. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppressions, who shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe'—the answer to the question of v. 14: the one who can dwell with the devouring fire is characterized by six qualities: righteous walking, upright speaking, rejection of oppressive gain, refusal of bribes, stopping the ears from bloodshed, shutting the eyes from evil. These are not earning salvation but describing the character that the Spirit produces (ch. 32:15–17). 'He will dwell on the heights; his place of defense will be the fortresses of rocks'—the dwelling of the righteous: the rock-fortress that Egypt's valley-plain could not provide. 'His bread will be given him; his water will be sure'—the simplest covenant blessings: daily bread (given, not earned) and certain water. The one who can live with the fire is the one who needs only what God provides. Motyer: the six character qualities are the social face of the fear of the LORD (v. 6)—Zion's treasure visible in the daily life of the righteous person.

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land of far horizons. Your heart will muse on the terror: “Where is he who counted? Where is he who weighed the tribute? Where is he who counted the towers?” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land of far horizons'—the vision granted to the righteous: the king in his beauty. Not the king behind a veil of crisis and threat, but the king in his full, unobstructed beauty. The beautiful king is the righteous ruler of 32:1, the root of Jesse of 11:1, the child whose name is Wonderful Counselor of 9:6. 'A land of far horizons'—the land they will see is not the cramped, besieged land of Sennacherib's siege but a land whose boundaries reach to the horizon: the new creation in its spaciousness. 'Your heart will muse on the terror: “Where is he who counted? Where is he who weighed the tribute? Where is he who counted the towers?”'—the memory of Assyrian oppression: the tribute-counter, the tax-assessor, the military surveyor—all gone. The heart rehearses the vanished terror as a way of measuring the grace of their absence. Young: the questions 'where is he?' are the triumphant questions of the redeemed—the instruments of oppression have simply disappeared.

verseByVerse.quote: You will see no more the insolent people, the people of an obscure speech that you cannot comprehend, stammering in a tongue that you cannot understand. Look upon Zion, the city of our appointed feasts! Your eyes will see Jerusalem, an untroubled habitation, an immovable tent, whose stakes will never be pulled up, nor will any of its cords be broken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You will see no more the insolent people, the people of an obscure speech that you cannot comprehend'—the Assyrians with their foreign tongue (28:11) are gone: 'see no more.' The absence of the incomprehensible oppressor is itself a gift. 'Look upon Zion, the city of our appointed feasts!'—the direction of the gaze changes: from the absent enemy to the present Zion. The appointed feasts (mo'adim) return: the liturgical calendar that was interrupted by crisis resumes. 'Your eyes will see Jerusalem, an untroubled habitation, an immovable tent, whose stakes will never be pulled up, nor will any of its cords be broken'—the city as a perfect tent: the image of the wilderness tabernacle applied to the permanent city. Childs: the immovable tent is the paradox of Isaiah's eschatology—the temporary (tent) becomes the permanent; the fragile (cords) becomes the unbreakable.

verseByVerse.quote: But there the LORD in majesty will be for us a place of broad rivers and streams, where no galley with oars can go, nor majestic ship can pass. For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There the LORD in majesty will be for us a place of broad rivers and streams'—God himself as the landscape of security: Jerusalem has no major river (unlike Babylon on the Euphrates, Egypt on the Nile), but God himself provides what rivers provide—protection, supply, beauty. 'Where no galley with oars can go, nor majestic ship can pass'—the protective rivers of God are navigable for life but not for enemy warships. The security is divine, not geographical. 'For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us'—the triple divine function: judge, lawgiver, king. All three offices that were corrupted by human failure (ch. 1–5: unjust judges; ch. 8–10: scoffing leaders; ch. 28: scorner-kings) are now perfectly fulfilled by the LORD himself. 'He will save us'—the conclusion of all three offices: the Judge, Lawgiver, and King saves. Motyer: the three divine offices correspond to the executive, legislative, and judicial branches of governance—the LORD perfectly fulfills every function of the state that human institutions corrupted.

verseByVerse.quote: Your cords hang loose; they cannot hold the mast firm in its place or keep the sail spread out. Then prey and spoil in abundance will be divided; even the lame will take the prey. And no inhabitant will say, “I am sick”; the people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your cords hang loose; they cannot hold the mast firm in its place or keep the sail spread out'—the enemy's ship (Assyrian military power) is disabled: the rigging is loose, the mast unstable, the sail slack. The galley that cannot enter God's rivers cannot function at all. 'Then prey and spoil in abundance will be divided; even the lame will take the prey'—the reversal: the enemy's disabled ships are plundered, and even the most vulnerable (the lame) can participate in the division of spoil. No warrior's strength required. 'And no inhabitant will say, “I am sick”'—the healing of the eschatological community: sickness, which is the foretaste of death, is absent. 'The people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity'—the foundation of the city's healing: forgiveness. The physical absence of sickness is the outward sign of the inward reality of forgiven iniquity. Childs: the chapter that began with the community's prayer (v. 2) ends with the community's forgiveness—the fullest possible answer to prayer, reaching the deepest possible need.

34.subtitle: Judgment on the Nations
34.intro: Overview. Chapter 34 is one of the most severe judgment passages in Isaiah, serving as the dark side of the diptych completed by chapter 35. The nations are summoned to hear their sentence; Edom is the representative case — a wasteland of burning pitch and thorns, inhabited by chaos creatures. The desolation is total and permanent. The vision is eschatological in scope: it is what the end of human rebellion looks like before the new creation blooms in the next chapter.

sections.title: The Day of the LORD’s Vengeance
sections.commentary:
All nations, all peoples — draw near and hear. God is enraged against them all; their slain will be cast out, and the mountains will flow with their blood. The host of heaven will rot; the skies roll up like a scroll; all the starry host will fall like leaves from a fig tree. The cosmic-dismantling imagery here feeds directly into Revelation 6:13–14, where John uses the same images for the opening of the sixth seal. Isaiah is not predicting an astronomical event but using the only language adequate to describe the uncreating of the order that has been made to serve rebellion.

v. 4 — “All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll.” Jesus uses the same collapsing-sky language in Matt. 24:29 for the events surrounding Jerusalem’s fall, and John uses it for the last judgment. Isaiah establishes the grammar; the New Testament applies it with increasing specificity.

The specific focus falls on Edom, Israel’s perennial enemy and twin-brother nation, as the type-case of those under divine wrath. God has a day of vengeance and a year of recompense for Edom’s cause — the violence done to Jacob will be answered.

sections.title: The Desolate Inheritance
sections.commentary:
Edom’s streams will be turned to pitch, its soil to sulfur; it will not be quenched night or day. The owls and ravens, jackals and ostriches, the screech owl and the arrow snake will make their home there. It will be called “No Kingdom There.” God’s line and plumb line will be stretched over it for chaos and emptiness — the tools of creation used for de-creation.

The chapter closes with a challenge: seek and read from the book of the LORD. Not one of these creatures will be missing; not one will lack its mate. His Spirit has gathered them; his hand has sorted them. God’s word has prescribed the desolation as precisely as any survey. The chaos is not accidental but ordained.

keyVerse.quote: “Seek and read from the book of the LORD: not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them.”
keyVerse.note: Even the desolation is governed by a book — by God’s word precisely applied. This is not chaos but ordered judgment. The same God who speaks creation into existence speaks desolation into a place that has refused him. The book-of-the-LORD motif connects to Isaiah 8:16–20 and ultimately to the Book of Life in Revelation.

34.reflection: Chapter 34 is difficult to read — the severity is comprehensive and without relief until chapter 35. But Isaiah places it immediately before the greatest vision of healing and return in the book. The comfort of chapter 35 lands differently if you have stood in the desolation of chapter 34 first. What aspects of the Bible’s severity do you tend to skip past? What does reading them in full do to your understanding of what grace actually costs?
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Draw near, O nations, to hear, and give attention, O peoples! Let the earth hear, and all that fills it; the world, and all that comes from it.<sup>2</sup>For the LORD is enraged against all the nations, and furious against all their host; he has devoted them to destruction, has given them over for slaughter.<sup>3</sup>Their slain shall be cast out, and the stench of their corpses shall rise; the mountains shall flow with their blood.<sup>4</sup>All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll. All their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine, like leaves falling from the fig tree.<sup>5</sup>For my sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; behold, it descends for judgment upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction.<sup>6</sup>The LORD has a sword; it is sated with blood; it is gorged with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom.<sup>7</sup>Wild oxen shall fall with them, and young steers with the mighty bulls. Their land shall drink its fill of blood, and their soil shall be gorged with fat.<sup>8</sup>For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.<sup>9</sup>And the streams of Edom shall be turned into pitch, and her soil into sulfur; her land shall become burning pitch.<sup>10</sup>Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up forever. From generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it forever and ever.<sup>11</sup>But the hawk and the porcupine shall possess it, the owl and the raven shall dwell in it. He shall stretch the line of confusion over it, and the plumb line of emptiness.<sup>12</sup>Its nobles—there is no one there to call it a kingdom, and all its princes shall be nothing.<sup>13</sup>Thorns shall grow over its strongholds, nettles and thistles in its fortresses. It shall be the haunt of jackals, an abode for ostriches.<sup>14</sup>And wild animals shall meet with hyenas; the wild goat shall cry to his fellow; indeed, there the night bird settles and finds for herself a resting place.<sup>15</sup>There the owl nests and lays and hatches and gathers her young in her shadow; indeed, there the hawks are gathered, each one with her mate.<sup>16</sup>Seek and read from the book of the LORD: Not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them.<sup>17</sup>He has cast the lot for them; his hand has portioned it out to them with the line; they shall possess it forever; from generation to generation they shall dwell in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Judgment of Edom and All Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 34 is the dark panel before the bright panel of ch. 35—the great cosmic judgment that precedes the great cosmic redemption. Edom functions as the paradigm of all nations that opposed God and his people; its judgment is total and permanent. The chapter is one of the most vivid descriptions of divine wrath in the Old Testament, with imagery of a cosmic sacrifice, stars dissolving, and a land given to wilderness creatures forever.
verseByVerse.examples: The church reads ch. 34 in the light of Revelation 19:11–21 (the Word of God going to war) and the entire 'Babylon' complex of Revelation 14–18. Edom is the face of every human structure that persecutes God's people; its eventual and certain destruction is the ground of the church's patience in suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: Draw near, O nations, to hear, and give attention, O peoples! Let the earth hear, and all that fills it; the world, and all that comes from it. For the LORD is enraged against all the nations, and furious against all their host; he has devoted them to destruction, has given them over for slaughter. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Draw near, O nations, to hear, and give attention, O peoples! Let the earth hear, and all that fills it'—the universal summons, echoing 1:2 (hear, O heavens) but now addressed to nations and earth. The entire created order called to witness the divine judgment. 'For the LORD is enraged against all the nations, and furious against all their host; he has devoted them to destruction, has given them over for slaughter'—the divine anger is comprehensive: not selective nations but all nations and their armies. 'Devoted to destruction' (kherem): the technical term for total dedication to God, usually in the context of holy war where all captured goods and persons were destroyed rather than kept. The nations are under holy-war dedication. Oswalt: the kherem against the nations echoes the kherem of Canaan—the same God who drove out Canaan's inhabitants is now driving out all hostile nations before his people's eschatological inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: Their slain shall be cast out, and the stench of their corpses shall rise; the mountains shall flow with their blood. All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll. All their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine, like leaves falling from the fig tree. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Their slain shall be cast out, and the stench of their corpses shall rise; the mountains shall flow with their blood'—the scale of the judgment visualized in maximum terms: the volume of blood flowing down mountains. 'All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll'—the cosmic dimension: the stars (host of heaven) dissolving and the sky rolling up like a scroll being put away. This cosmic imagery appears in Revelation 6:13–14. 'All their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine, like leaves falling from the fig tree'—the armies of the nations falling like autumn leaves: naturally, inevitably, seasonally. The falling is not a battle but a seasonal event in the divine calendar. Childs: the scroll-rolling and star-rotting are the language of the de-creation that ch. 24 described—when God judges finally, the creation that witnessed human sin is also dissolved.

verseByVerse.quote: For my sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; behold, it descends for judgment upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction. The LORD has a sword; it is sated with blood; it is gorged with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; behold, it descends for judgment upon Edom'—God's sword has first been satisfied in the heavenly realm (the spiritual powers behind Edom, cf. 24:21) and now descends to the earthly nation. 'Upon the people I have devoted to destruction'—the kherem of v. 2 applied specifically to Edom: the paradigm case. 'The LORD has a sword; it is sated with blood; it is gorged with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams'—the sacrifice imagery: the slaughter of Edom is described as a sacrificial offering. The animals of sacrifice (lambs, goats, rams) are metaphors for the slaughtered Edomites. 'For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom'—Bozrah was Edom's capital. The sacrifice language is deeply disturbing: God is the priest, Edom is the offering. Young: the sacrifice-imagery insists that the judgment is not random violence but purposive, covenantally ordered action.

verseByVerse.quote: Wild oxen shall fall with them, and young steers with the mighty bulls. Their land shall drink its fill of blood, and their soil shall be gorged with fat. For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wild oxen shall fall with them, and young steers with the mighty bulls'—the spectrum of animals from the wild (wild oxen) to the domesticated (steers, bulls): all fall in the sacrifice. The entire range of Edom's livestock is included in the judgment. 'Their land shall drink its fill of blood, and their soil shall be gorged with fat'—the land itself consumes the blood and fat of the sacrifice: the ground that supported Edom's civilization becomes the altar-floor. 'For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion'—the ground of the judgment: Edom's treatment of Zion. The day of vengeance and year of recompense are God's answer to every act of hostility against his people. Motyer: the cause of Zion is the basis of God's action—not arbitrary divine violence but covenantal advocacy for the community that bears God's name.

verseByVerse.quote: And the streams of Edom shall be turned into pitch, and her soil into sulfur; her land shall become burning pitch. Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up forever. From generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it forever and ever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The streams of Edom shall be turned into pitch, and her soil into sulfur; her land shall become burning pitch'—the Sodom-and-Gomorrah imagery applied to Edom: pitch, sulfur, and eternal burning. The land that once flowed with water flows with combustibles. 'Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up forever'—the permanent fire: the desolation is eternal, not temporary. 'From generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it forever and ever'—the total absence of human habitation or transit: no commerce, no travel, no community. Revelation 19:3 quotes 'her smoke goes up forever and ever' in the context of Babylon's final judgment. Oswalt: the eternal smoke of Edom's judgment is the Old Testament's most explicit statement about the permanence of divine judgment—some things once started cannot be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: But the hawk and the porcupine shall possess it, the owl and the raven shall dwell in it. He shall stretch the line of confusion over it, and the plumb line of emptiness. Its nobles—there is no one there to call it a kingdom, and all its princes shall be nothing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The hawk and the porcupine shall possess it, the owl and the raven shall dwell in it'—four wilderness creatures inheriting Edom: bird (hawk), mammal (porcupine), bird (owl), bird (raven). The creatures of desolation inherit the land of civilization. 'He shall stretch the line of confusion over it, and the plumb line of emptiness'—the surveying instruments of construction used for deconstruction: the measuring line is tohu (chaos, Gen. 1:2) and bohu (emptiness/void, Gen. 1:2). The surveyor measures out not a new city but the primal chaos. 'Its nobles—there is no one there to call it a kingdom, and all its princes shall be nothing'—the political dissolution: no nobles, no kingdom, no princes. Childs: the application of the creation-chaos words (tohu and bohu) to Edom is deliberate—judgment de-creates, returning the land to the state before God's ordering word. What the creative word built, the judicial word undoes.

verseByVerse.quote: Thorns shall grow over its strongholds, nettles and thistles in its fortresses. It shall be the haunt of jackals, an abode for ostriches. And wild animals shall meet with hyenas; the wild goat shall cry to his fellow; indeed, there the night bird settles and finds for herself a resting place. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Thorns shall grow over its strongholds, nettles and thistles in its fortresses'—the military infrastructure (strongholds, fortresses) overgrown with thorns: the vegetation of the cursed ground (Gen. 3:18) reclaims what human effort built. 'It shall be the haunt of jackals, an abode for ostriches'—the nocturnal, desert-dwelling animals inhabit what was once populous: jackals (howlers) and ostriches (the biblical symbol of desolation). 'Wild animals shall meet with hyenas; the wild goat shall cry to his fellow'—the community of wild things: they gather and communicate in ways that parallel human social life. 'Indeed, there the night bird settles and finds for herself a resting place'—the night bird (Lilith in Hebrew, a female demon or owl) finds her home in Edom's ruins. The most feared creatures of ancient superstition dwell where Edom's civilization once stood. Young: the catalog of wilderness creatures is exhaustive because the desolation is exhaustive—every zone and every hour is inhabited by creatures of chaos.

verseByVerse.quote: There the owl nests and lays and hatches and gathers her young in her shadow; indeed, there the hawks are gathered, each one with her mate. Seek and read from the book of the LORD: Not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There the owl nests and lays and hatches and gathers her young in her shadow; indeed, there the hawks are gathered, each one with her mate'—the ecological establishment: the wilderness creatures are not merely passing through Edom's ruins but establishing permanent habitations: nesting, laying, hatching, gathering. Each has its mate—God has established even the mating of the wilderness creatures in the new order. 'Seek and read from the book of the LORD: Not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate'—the appeal to prophetic scripture: the book of the LORD confirms the completeness of what has been described. 'For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them'—the command (mouth) and execution (Spirit) of God: the same partnership that created the world (Gen. 1: God's word and Spirit) now deconstructs Edom's world. Motyer: the Spirit gathering the wilderness creatures in Edom is the anti-creation—the same Spirit who brooded over the waters of creation now assembles desolation.

verseByVerse.quote: He has cast the lot for them; his hand has portioned it out to them with the line; they shall possess it forever; from generation to generation they shall dwell in it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He has cast the lot for them; his hand has portioned it out to them with the line'—the divine allotment: God portions out the land of Edom to its new inhabitants as he once portioned out the promised land to the tribes of Israel (Josh. 18–19). The same divine action (casting lots, using the measuring line) that distributed the promised land now distributes Edom to the wilderness creatures. 'They shall possess it forever; from generation to generation they shall dwell in it'—the permanence of the wilderness inheritance: as permanent as the covenant promise to Israel. The word possess (yarash) is the technical term for Israel's inheritance of Canaan—now applied to wild creatures inheriting Edom. Childs: the ironic use of the land-inheritance vocabulary is the chapter's final statement: what Edom possessed as a proud nation is repossessed by the creatures of chaos, given to them with the same covenantal certainty with which God gave Canaan to Israel.

35.subtitle: The Highway of Holiness
35.intro: Overview. Chapter 35 is among the most luminous passages in all of Scripture — the other half of the diptych with chapter 34, and the first foretaste of the great vision of restoration in chapters 40–66. The wilderness blooms; the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, the mute sing; a highway appears in the desert called the Way of Holiness; and the ransomed return with everlasting joy. Jesus reads from this chapter to answer John the Baptist’s question about whether he is the one who was to come (Matt. 11:5).

sections.title: The Wilderness Blooms
sections.commentary:
The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus. Lebanon’s glory, Carmel’s majesty, Sharon’s beauty — the most fertile and famous landscapes of the land will be seen in the wilderness that was barren. The creation itself participates in the reversal. Strengthen the weak hands, make firm the feeble knees; say to those with an anxious heart: “Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come.”

vv. 5–6 — “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy.” Jesus quotes these verses in Matt. 11:5 as evidence that the kingdom has arrived: the miracles are not random acts of kindness but the specific signs Isaiah listed as markers of the new age. When Jesus heals, he is enacting the chapter.

Waters break forth in the wilderness; streams in the desert. The burning sand becomes a pool; the thirsty ground springs of water. Even the dwelling place of jackals — the haunt of the chaos creatures of chapter 34 — becomes a place of grass and reeds. The precise reversal of the previous chapter is not accidental.

sections.title: The Way of Holiness
sections.commentary:
A highway shall be there — the Way of Holiness. The unclean shall not pass over it; no lion shall be there, no ravenous beast. It is for those who walk on the way, even fools (simple ones) shall not err. The image of the highway cutting through the wilderness is the central metaphor of Isaiah 40–55 (“make straight in the desert a highway for our God”) and appears here in its first full form. The road is designed not for experts but for the redeemed: no special competence required, no predators waiting, just the path home.

And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away. The chapter closes the same way chapter 25 did — with tears ended, joy permanent, the destination reached. These are not metaphors of spiritual improvement; they are the promise of arrival.

keyVerse.quote: “And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it… the redeemed shall walk there.”
keyVerse.note: The Way of Holiness is the image John picks up for the New Jerusalem: nothing unclean will enter it (Rev. 21:27). But Isaiah adds what John implies: it is not the pure who travel the road — it is the redeemed, the ransomed, even the simple. Holiness here is not the qualification for the road but the character of the road itself. You travel it because you have been ransomed, not because you are already holy.

35.theology: New Creation and Bodily Redemption. Chapter 35 is the Old Testament in clearest voice about what the new creation involves: not just forgiven souls but healed bodies, redeemed creation, and a physical journey to a physical destination. The blind see, the lame walk, the mute sing — these are bodily realities. Reformed theology has consistently insisted against Gnosticism that salvation is not escape from the material world but its restoration. Chapter 35 is one of the earliest and fullest expressions of that vision in Scripture.
35.reflection: Jesus chose Isaiah 35 to answer the question “are you the one who is to come?” His answer was not a theological argument but a list of healings: look at what is happening. Where in your life have you seen glimpses of chapter 35 breaking in — wilderness blooming, weakness strengthened, joy returning where sorrow was? And what in your life still feels like chapter 34, waiting for the highway to appear?
35.text: <sup>1</sup>The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus;<sup>2</sup>it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon. They shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God.<sup>3</sup>Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees.<sup>4</sup>Say to those who have an anxious heart, "Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you."<sup>5</sup>Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped;<sup>6</sup>then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert;<sup>7</sup>the burning sand shall become a pool, and the thirsty ground springs of water; in the haunt of jackals, where they lie down, the grass shall become reeds and rushes.<sup>8</sup>And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray.<sup>9</sup>No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there, but the redeemed shall walk there.<sup>10</sup>And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Highway of Holiness: The Redeemed Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 35 is perhaps the most beautiful chapter in the book—the bright panel paired with the dark panel of ch. 34. The wilderness blossoms, the glory of Lebanon and Carmel is given to the desert, the weak are strengthened, the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, the mute sing, and the ransomed of the LORD return on the Highway of Holiness with everlasting joy upon their heads.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus' answer to John the Baptist's question ('Are you the one who is to come?') cites Isaiah 35:5–6 as evidence. The church walks the Highway of Holiness now in faith, anticipating its final and full experience at the resurrection. Every act of healing, every restored relationship, every dumb mouth opened in praise is a foretaste of the highway.

verseByVerse.quote: The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus; it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon. They shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus'—the transformation of nature: the most barren landscapes become joyful. The crocus (khavatselet) blooms in unlikely places after rain—a picture of resurrection beauty from apparent deadness. 'It shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing'—three dimensions of the desert's new life: abundant blossoming, joy, and singing. Nature participates in the salvation. 'The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon'—Edom was stripped of its glory (ch. 34); the wilderness now receives the glory of Lebanon (greatest forest), Carmel (most fertile mountain), and Sharon (richest coastal plain). The judgment of Edom (ch. 34) and the glory of the wilderness (ch. 35) are the negative and positive of the same divine action. 'They shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God'—the purpose of the transformation: the vision of divine glory. The blooming wilderness is the setting for the theophany. Oswalt: creation's transformation is not an end in itself but the context in which God's glory is revealed.

verseByVerse.quote: Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who have an anxious heart, “Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees'—the command to the community of faith to strengthen one another in the interim between promise and fulfillment. The weak hands and feeble knees are the physical expression of spiritual despair; they are to be addressed by human encouragement grounded in divine promise. 'Say to those who have an anxious heart, “Be strong; fear not!”'—the pastoral imperative: speak to the fearful. The words 'be strong, fear not' are the constant refrain of divine encouragement throughout Isaiah. 'Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you'—the two-sided coming of God: vengeance (against the enemies) and salvation (for the anxious). The same coming that destroys Edom saves the fearful remnant. Childs: the command to strengthen weak hands is the practical ecclesiology of ch. 35—before the highway is walked, the community must encourage one another along the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped'—the reversal of the judicial closing of 6:9–10 and 29:10: the eyes that judgment closed are opened; the ears that judgment stopped are unstopped. 'Then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy'—sight and hearing joined by mobility and speech: the four physical limitations reversed. The lame leaping like a deer is the image of joy-released: the leap of the deer is a leap of exuberance, not merely locomotion. 'For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert'—the water-in-the-wilderness sign of the Exodus (Ex. 17; Num. 20) renewed: God provides water where there was none. Jesus cites these four signs (blind see, deaf hear, lame walk, mute speak) in Matthew 11:5 as evidence that he is the 'coming one.' Motyer: the four physical reversals are also four spiritual reversals—the community that could not perceive, hear, walk in, or speak the truth of God now does all four.

verseByVerse.quote: the burning sand shall become a pool, and the thirsty ground springs of water; in the haunt of jackals, where they lie down, the grass shall become reeds and rushes. And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The burning sand shall become a pool, and the thirsty ground springs of water'—the continuing transformation: every form of waterlessness (burning sand, thirsty ground) becomes abundant water (pool, springs). 'In the haunt of jackals, where they lie down, the grass shall become reeds and rushes'—the habitat of the desolation-creatures (jackals, which inhabited Edom in ch. 34) transformed into lush vegetation. 'And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness'—the great promise: a road through the transformed wilderness. The Way of Holiness (derek haqodesh) is both the road and its character—holiness defines both the path and those who walk it. 'The unclean shall not pass over it'—the exclusion is not elitist but covenantal: uncleanness (moral and ritual impurity) is incompatible with the Holy Way. 'Even if they are fools, they shall not go astray'—the reassurance for the anxious traveler: even those of limited wisdom will not get lost. The Way is so clear that losing it requires determined avoidance. Childs: the Highway of Holiness is the eschatological road that 40:3–4 will announce—'prepare the way of the LORD.'

verseByVerse.quote: No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there, but the redeemed shall walk there. And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there'—the safety of the Way: the animals that threatened travel (and symbolized the powers of chaos and judgment) are absent from the highway. The lion of the divine judgment (cf. 31:4) does not threaten those on this road. 'But the redeemed shall walk there'—the exclusive travelers: the redeemed (go'ulim—those purchased back from captivity by the kinsman-redeemer). The highway is for the redeemed; no other category can walk it. 'The ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads'—the three characteristics of the arrival: singing (the highway song), everlasting joy (permanent, not temporary—elathat olam), and gladness replacing sorrow. 'Sorrow and sighing shall flee away'—the negative definition of everlasting joy: what it has expelled. Motyer: 'sorrow and sighing shall flee' is one of Isaiah's most pastoral promises—the things that have followed God's people through the darkness of judgment are finally and permanently routed. The highway ends at Zion; the journey ends in joy.

36.subtitle: Sennacherib’s Threat
36.intro: Overview. Chapters 36–39 form a historical interlude (nearly identical to 2 Kings 18–20) that shows the principles of chapters 1–35 enacted in real time. Hezekiah’s reign provides the pivot between the Assyrian threat (chs. 36–37) and the Babylonian shadow (chs. 38–39). Chapter 36 sets up the crisis: the Rabshakeh, Assyria’s chief of staff, stands before Jerusalem and delivers a masterpiece of psychological warfare — calculated to destroy faith in God and king alike.

sections.title: The Rabshakeh’s Speech
sections.commentary:
In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib has taken all the fortified cities of Judah. He sends his Rabshakeh with a great army to Jerusalem. The speech that follows is extraordinary in its sophistication. The Rabshakeh begins by attacking the rational basis of Hezekiah’s trust: Egypt is a broken reed, he says — precisely what Isaiah said. Then he attacks the religious basis: you removed the high places, so now this very LORD you trust has told me to come against this land.

When Hezekiah’s envoys ask him to speak in Aramaic rather than Hebrew so the people on the wall cannot hear, the Rabshakeh raises his voice specifically to the people on the wall. His final offer is seductive: do not listen to Hezekiah; make an agreement with me and you will eat from your own vine and drink from your own cistern — a deliberate echo of the land-of-promise language of Deuteronomy. He ends by cataloguing every god destroyed by Assyria: which of the gods of these lands has delivered his land from me?

v. 20 — “Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?” The logic is impeccable if the LORD is merely one god among others. The whole argument rests on that assumption. Isaiah has spent 35 chapters arguing the opposite: the LORD is not one among many but the maker of heaven and earth, before whom Assyria is like a drop in a bucket (40:15). The Rabshakeh is attacking a God he has no category to understand.

The people are silent. Hezekiah commanded them: do not answer him. They tore their clothes and came to Hezekiah.

keyVerse.quote: “Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’”
keyVerse.note: The Rabshakeh knows what he is attacking: not Egypt as a military ally, but trust in the LORD. He knows this is the specific ground of Jerusalem’s resistance. His entire speech is designed to make that trust seem irrational. This is the structure of every temptation that targets faith: it does not ask you to deny God exists; it asks you to stop trusting him in this specific situation.

36.reflection: The people on the wall heard everything and said nothing. Hezekiah had commanded silence, and they obeyed. Sometimes the right response to a sophisticated attack on faith is not a theological rebuttal but silence, followed by going to God in prayer. When was the last time you faced something that seemed to have a logical argument against trusting God — and what did you do with it?

And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field.<sup>3</sup>And there came out to him Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder.<sup>4</sup>And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: On what do you rest this trust of yours?<sup>5</sup>Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? In whom do you now trust, that you have rebelled against me?<sup>6</sup>Behold, you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.<sup>7</sup>But if you say to me, "We trust in the LORD our God," is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and to Jerusalem, "You shall worship before this altar"?<sup>8</sup>Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them.<sup>9</sup>How then can you repulse a single captain among the least of my master's servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?<sup>10</sup>Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"<sup>11</sup>Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall."<sup>12</sup>But the Rabshakeh said, "Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?"<sup>13</sup>Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: "Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!<sup>14</sup>Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you.<sup>15</sup>Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, "The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria."<sup>16</sup>Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of Assyria: Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern,<sup>17</sup>until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards.<sup>18</sup>Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you by saying, "The LORD will deliver us." Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?<sup>19</sup>Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?<sup>20</sup>Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?'"<sup>21</sup>But they were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him."<sup>22</sup>Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him the words of the Rabshakeh.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Sennacherib's Taunt and the Test of Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Assyrian field commander stands at Jerusalem's wall and delivers a calculated psychological assault, mocking Hezekiah's trust in Egypt and in the LORD. This historical chapter (paralleling 2 Kings 18) shows faith under siege — will Judah trust flesh or God?
verseByVerse.examples: Every believer faces a 'Rabshakeh moment' — a voice that lists your weakness and mocks your trust in God. The temptation is to argue on the enemy's terms. Isaiah calls for silence and prayer instead, taking the matter to the temple (37:1).

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem, with a great army. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The year is c. 701 BC. Sennacherib has swept through the region; only Jerusalem remains. The Rabshakeh — a title, not a name, meaning 'chief cupbearer' or high official — comes with a great army, making the political situation viscerally threatening. Oswalt notes that this chapter tests everything Isaiah has preached: will Hezekiah trust Egypt, trust his fortifications, or trust the LORD alone?

verseByVerse.quote: And there came out to him Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder. And the Rabshakeh said to them, “Say to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: On what do you rest this trust of yours? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The confrontation is public and political. The Rabshakeh demands to know the basis of Judah's confidence. His question — on what do you rest? — is the right question. Every life is built on some foundation. The Assyrian assumes it must be either military power or Egypt. He has not yet considered that the God of Israel might actually be trustworthy. Calvin sees here the universal contempt of the world for faith in God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? In whom do you trust, that you have rebelled against me? Behold, you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The broken reed image is devastating — Egypt appears strong but is hollow, and leaning on it injures the one who relies on it. Isaiah has said the same thing in chapters 30–31. The Rabshakeh is accidentally echoing the prophet's message. The spiritual lesson is profound: idols do not merely fail; they wound. What we trust wrongly becomes a source of hurt rather than help.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you say to me, 'We trust in the LORD our God,' is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, telling Judah and Jerusalem, 'You shall worship before this altar'? Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Rabshakeh misreads Hezekiah's reformation as an insult to the LORD, not understanding that Hezekiah removed syncretistic high places to purify worship, not to diminish it. His intelligence is good but his theology is wrong. Then his taunt turns contemptuous: Judah cannot even supply riders for 2,000 horses. Motyer notes that this is a picture of the church's situation in every age — outgunned by the world yet trusting an unseen Power.

verseByVerse.quote: How then can you repulse a single captain among the least of my master's servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen? Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD said to me, 'Go up against this land and destroy it.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Rabshakeh's most audacious claim: the LORD himself sent Assyria. He may be bluffing for psychological effect, or this may reflect a distorted awareness of Isaiah's earlier oracles (Isa 10:5-6, where Assyria is indeed God's rod of anger). Either way, the claim is used to paralyze faith rather than encourage it. Yet God uses even the enemy's boasts within his sovereign plan. Childs observes the bitter irony — the Rabshakeh is not entirely wrong about Assyria's role, yet entirely wrong about the outcome.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall.” But the Rabshakeh said, “Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The officials want to contain the psychological damage — keep the propaganda in Aramaic, the diplomatic language, away from common ears. The Rabshakeh refuses. His strategy is to demoralize the people directly: face siege, face famine, face horror. The graphic language of v.12 is deliberately destabilizing. Oswalt notes this is the enemy's tactic in every age: bypass leadership and sow despair among the people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria! Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you. Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, ”The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.“' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Rabshakeh now speaks directly to the people, calling Hezekiah a deceiver and faith in the LORD delusional. This is how the enemy attacks faith: not through argument alone but through the relentless suggestion that trusting God is naïve. Keller notes that the speech is sophisticated — it frames trust in God as a manipulation by human leaders, attempting to isolate the believer from the community of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, 'The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Rabshakeh continues his psychological campaign, specifically targeting Hezekiah's theological argument. He names the claim — the LORD will surely deliver us — and treats it as false hope used to manipulate the people. Yet this is precisely what faith in the living God looks like to worldly eyes: irrational optimism. The answer will come in chapter 37, when the LORD does exactly what the Rabshakeh said he could not.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of Assyria: Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern, until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The offer of peace is seductive — vine, fig tree, and cistern are images of shalom (Mic 4:4). Surrender sounds like security. Then the mask slips: until I come and take you away. Exile is the inevitable end. What the world offers as peace always carries the fine print of bondage. Webb sees this as the tempter's perennial method: offer a temporary comfort that conceals a permanent loss of freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you by saying, “The LORD will deliver us.” Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Rabshakeh's final argument is empirical: no other gods have stopped Assyria, so the LORD won't either. The logic is compelling from a purely human standpoint — the track record of defeated nations is real. But this argument treats the LORD as one deity among many. It will be answered definitively in ch37 when the LORD does what no other god could do. Oswalt: the nations' gods failed because they were nothing; the LORD will deliver because he is everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The rhetorical question that closes the first Assyrian address: no god has stopped Assyria, therefore neither will the LORD. This empirical argument seems compelling, but it misses the decisive distinction: those other gods were not real. The LORD is the Creator, not a tribal deity. Young: the Rabshakeh's logic would be valid if the LORD were merely one deity among many — but the entire message of Isaiah is that he is the only God.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, “Do not answer him.” Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and told him the words of the Rabshakeh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The silence of Hezekiah's officials is an act of obedient faith. They do not argue, do not negotiate, do not panic publicly. They bring the words to the king — torn clothes signaling mourning — and let leadership bring it to God. This is the proper response to overwhelming pressure: don't engage on the enemy's terms; bring it to the throne of grace. The chapter ends with Hezekiah about to pray, not to capitulate.

37.subtitle: Hezekiah’s Prayer and the Angel
37.intro: Overview. Chapter 37 is the climax of the Assyrian crisis — one of the greatest answered-prayer narratives in the Bible. Hezekiah receives the threatening letter, spreads it before the LORD in the temple, and prays. Isaiah delivers the divine response: Sennacherib’s arrogance will be answered, and Jerusalem will not fall. That night, 185,000 Assyrian soldiers die. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh and is killed by his own sons. Every element of the Rabshakeh’s mockery is precisely reversed.

sections.title: Hezekiah’s Prayer
sections.commentary:
Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and goes to the house of the LORD. He sends envoys to Isaiah, who answers immediately with a word of assurance: do not be afraid. Then a second letter comes from Sennacherib. And Hezekiah takes it up to the temple and spreads it before the LORD.

The prayer that follows is one of the finest in Scripture. It opens with theology — “O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made heaven and earth” — before it brings the petition. The basis for the request is not Judah’s merit but the honor of God: “so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD.” Hezekiah acknowledges the truth in the Rabshakeh’s taunt — those nations’ gods were destroyed because they were not gods. He does not dispute the military record. He simply appeals to the one who made heaven and earth.

v. 16 — “O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made heaven and earth.” Hezekiah begins with who God is before he says what he needs. This sequence — praise establishing the character of the one addressed before the petition — is the grammar of all effective prayer in Scripture. You cannot petition someone you have not first understood.

sections.title: The Answer and the Fall of Assyria
sections.commentary:
Isaiah’s oracle against Sennacherib is a taunt — the form Assyria used against the nations, turned back against them. Daughter Zion despises you; she wags her head behind you. Who have you mocked? The Holy One of Israel. Because of your pride — your chariot-roads into Lebanon, your claim that you have done all this by your own power — God will put his hook in your nose and his bit in your mouth and turn you back the way you came.

The sign given to Hezekiah is agricultural: in the third year you will sow and reap. The agricultural metaphor means: normal life will resume. And from Jerusalem a remnant will go out, a surviving remnant from Zion — the remnant theme that has threaded through the whole first section of Isaiah.

That night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. When the survivors arose early in the morning, there were only corpses. Sennacherib withdrew to Nineveh, where he was killed by his own sons while worshiping in the temple of his god. The god that could not save him from Isaiah’s God could not save him from his own family.

keyVerse.quote: “So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: The missional motive for answered prayer runs all the way from here to the Lord’s Prayer: “hallowed be your name.” Hezekiah does not pray primarily for his own comfort or survival but for the display of God’s uniqueness among the nations. The request is aligned with God’s own purposes, which is why it is answered so spectacularly.

37.reflection: Hezekiah spread the threatening letter before the LORD. He didn’t summarize it, argue with it, or strategize around it — he laid it in front of God. This is one of the most practical models of prayer in the Bible: bring the actual problem, in its full severity, and lay it before the one who made heaven and earth. What letter do you need to spread before the LORD right now?
37.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz.<sup>3</sup>They said to him, "Thus says Hezekiah, 'This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth.<sup>4</sup>It may be that the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left.'"<sup>5</sup>When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah,<sup>6</sup>Isaiah said to them, "Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the young men of the king of Assyria have reviled me.<sup>7</sup>Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'"<sup>8</sup>The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had left Lachish.<sup>9</sup>Now the king heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "He has set out to fight against you." And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.<sup>11</sup>Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered?<sup>12</sup>Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar?<sup>13</sup>Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah?'"<sup>14</sup>Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD:<sup>16</sup>"O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth.<sup>17</sup>Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God.<sup>18</sup>Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations and their lands,<sup>19</sup>and have cast their gods into the fire. For they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed.<sup>20</sup>So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD."<sup>21</sup>Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Because you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria,<sup>22</sup>this is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: "'She despises you, she scorns you— the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you— the daughter of Jerusalem.<sup>23</sup>"'Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel!<sup>24</sup>By your servants you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon, to cut down its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses, to come to its remotest height, its most fruitful forest.<sup>25</sup>I dug wells and drank waters, to dry up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt.<sup>26</sup>"'Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should make fortified cities crash into heaps of ruins,<sup>27</sup>while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown.<sup>28</sup>"'I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me.<sup>29</sup>Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come to my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came.'<sup>30</sup>"And this shall be the sign for you: this year you shall eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs from that. Then in the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.<sup>31</sup>And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward.<sup>32</sup>For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.<sup>33</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it.<sup>34</sup>By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD.<sup>35</sup>For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David."<sup>36</sup>And the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies.<sup>37</sup>Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and returned home and lived at Nineveh.<sup>38</sup>And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword. And after they escaped into the land of Ararat, Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–38 — Hezekiah's Prayer and the LORD's Deliverance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Hezekiah hears the Rabshakeh's report he goes to the temple to pray. Isaiah brings a word of assurance. A second Assyrian threat is met with Hezekiah's prayer — one of Scripture's great model prayers. The LORD's answer: a taunt against Assyria, a sign for Judah, and a deliverance so sudden and decisive that 185,000 Assyrian soldiers lie dead by morning.
verseByVerse.theology: Oswalt calls Hezekiah's prayer a model for prayer under impossible circumstances: begin with worship, acknowledge reality, ask for God's glory. The angel of the LORD striking 185,000 overnight shows that the LORD's word through his prophet cannot be stopped by any earthly army.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Hezekiah's first response to crisis is the temple — he goes to God before making any political decision. He also goes to the prophet, recognizing that the word of the LORD through Isaiah is his most critical resource. Motyer notes that unlike Ahaz (ch7), who refused to ask a sign, Hezekiah runs toward God in the hour of crisis. The sackcloth signifies genuine humility before God, not performance.
