verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, “Thus says Hezekiah, 'This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth. It may be that the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left.'” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The birth-labor metaphor is painfully vivid: strength exhausted at the critical moment. Hezekiah's message to Isaiah is saturated with theological precision — he calls the LORD your God (acknowledging Isaiah's prophetic access), notes that Assyria has mocked the living God (not a dead idol), and asks for prayer. The phrase living God is the hinge: the Rabshakeh has just argued from the silence of defeated gods; Hezekiah appeals to the God who is alive and present.

verseByVerse.quote: When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah, Isaiah said to them, “Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me. Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah's prophetic word is immediate, precise, and calm: do not be afraid. The LORD's counter-plan is already operative — a rumor, a withdrawal, a sword in his own land. God does not need to explain his mechanism. He simply states the outcome. Young notes that this confidence — the prophet speaking the LORD's outcome before it happens — is the mark of genuine prophecy. The rumor (v.9) will come from Tirhakah of Ethiopia, providing Sennacherib a pretext to withdraw.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The LORD's oracle is specific and verifiable: a spirit, a rumor, a return, a death by sword in his own land. Three successive events predicted in advance. All three happen (vv.9, 37-38). The word of the LORD is not a vague comfort but a precise promise. Motyer: this is what distinguishes the LORD from idols — he does not merely generalize; he announces specifics and they occur exactly as stated.

verseByVerse.quote: The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had left Lachish. And Sennacherib heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, “He has set out to fight against you.” When he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying, “Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The rumor from Ethiopia (v.9) does not end the threat — it produces a written ultimatum. Sennacherib escalates from verbal to written intimidation, perhaps recognizing the Rabshakeh's mission failed to produce surrender. The letter is sent to mock Hezekiah's faith one more time: do not let your God deceive you. Oswalt observes that this second assault, more formal and in writing, is designed to permanently close off the option of trusting the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The written ultimatum recycles the Rabshakeh's oral argument: do not let your God deceive you. But Hezekiah takes this letter to the temple and spreads it before the LORD. The letter represents Sennacherib's total confidence in his own power. God will answer it not with argument but with action — 185,000 dead by morning. Childs: the written threat becomes the occasion for the greatest prayer in the chapter and the greatest deliverance in Israel's history.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered? Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the children of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The letter rehearses Assyria's record of total devastation — city after city, god after god, all overcome. The litany of defeated names is meant to overwhelm by sheer historical weight. But it inadvertently makes the strongest possible case for God's uniqueness: if the LORD delivers Jerusalem, it will be uniquely and unmistakably his doing. No other power has managed it. The more Sennacherib boasts, the more dramatically God's deliverance will vindicate his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The litany of defeated kings and nations makes the empirical case against trusting Jerusalem's God. Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, Ivvah — city after city has fallen. The kings are gone. This is a real historical record, not mere boasting. But the LORD will demonstrate that he is not catalogued with these defeated local deities. His answer in v.33-35 is the response to every name in this list: he shall not come into this city.

verseByVerse.quote: Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD. And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Spread it before the LORD — one of the most moving images in Scripture. Hezekiah literally lays the threatening letter before God, as if to say: You read it; you answer it. This is the posture of faith under pressure: bring the actual problem to God rather than keeping it in human hands. Calvin: Hezekiah did not deliberate, consult advisors, or attempt a counteroffensive — he went straight to the one who alone could help. The temple is the place of encounter with the sovereign God.

verseByVerse.quote: \“O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made heaven and earth. Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Hezekiah's prayer begins with worship, not petition. He addresses the LORD as sovereign over all kingdoms, creator of heaven and earth — directly countering Sennacherib's assumption that the LORD is a local deity like the others. Then he asks God to see and hear — not because God is unaware, but as the liturgical language of appealing to the enthroned Judge. Motyer calls this a model for prayer: establish who God is before stating what you need.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations and their lands, and have cast their gods into the fire. For they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed. So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Hezekiah's prayer is remarkable for its theological honesty: yes, Assyria has destroyed the other nations and their gods — because those gods were not real. He concedes the empirical argument. But then the pivot: the LORD is not like those gods. His single petition — save us — is motivated not by self-preservation but by the glory of God among all kingdoms. Oswalt: Hezekiah prays for deliverance as a missionary act, so the nations will know the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The climax of Hezekiah's prayer: a single petition — save us — motivated not by self-preservation but by the glory of God among all nations. The prayer is missional in its deepest logic. Hezekiah does not ask for victory to vindicate himself; he asks for deliverance so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD. Oswalt: this makes Hezekiah's prayer a type of all faithful prayer — seeking God's glory first, not personal survival.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Because you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria, this is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: 'She despises you, she scorns you — the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you — the daughter of Jerusalem. Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel!' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's answer comes through the prophet, and it takes the form of a taunt against Assyria — matching taunt for taunt. Jerusalem, pictured as a virgin daughter who has not been violated, mocks the retreating Assyrian army. Young notes the dramatic reversal: the one who came to terrify ends up being laughed at. And God's charge is supreme: Sennacherib has mocked the Holy One of Israel — the one before whom seraphim veil their faces. The offense is cosmic, and the response will be cosmic.

verseByVerse.quote: Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The divine taunt against Assyria reaches its theological center: Sennacherib has mocked the Holy One of Israel. This is not merely diplomatic offense; it is cosmic rebellion. The title Holy One of Israel is Isaiah's signature name for God — the One before whom seraphim cover their faces. To mock this God is to invite the full weight of his holiness as response. Young: the punishment will be proportionate to the offense — the greater the target, the more devastating the reversal.

verseByVerse.quote: By your servants you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, 'With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon; I felled its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses; I entered its farthest lodging place, its most fruitful forest. I dug wells and drank waters, and I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of besieged places.' Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Sennacherib's boasts are reproduced and then destroyed with a single theological counter: I determined it long ago. All of Assyria's campaigns have been operating within the script God wrote before Assyria existed. The great king is not an independent agent; he is an instrument. Childs sees here the climax of Isaiah's theology of history: God's purposes precede all human action, and what appears to be autonomous power is in fact divine superintendence. Sennacherib's glory belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The decisive theological counter to Assyrian pride: God planned all of this before Assyria existed. Sennacherib's campaigns, his victories, his arrogance — all within a script God wrote in eternity. This is Isaiah's deepest historical theology: God's purposes are not reactive but proactive, not disrupted by human power but expressed through it. The implication for the exiles is immense: Babylon's power over them is also within God's plan, and so is their deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown. But I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me. Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come into my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The nations Assyria conquered were already helpless before the assault — like grass on the housetops, dried before it can grow. God allowed it. But now the hook and the bit: God uses the same language Assyria used of conquered peoples, applying it to Sennacherib himself. The great hunter is hunted; the one who led nations captive will be led. Oswalt: the imagery is both humiliating and irresistible — God does not argue with Sennacherib, he simply turns him around.

verseByVerse.quote: Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come into my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's counter-move against Sennacherib uses the same imagery Assyria used against its victims: hook in nose, bit in mouth — the equipment of conquest applied to the conqueror himself. What Sennacherib did to others, the LORD will do to him. Not by superior military force but by his word. The image is both humiliating and irresistible — God does not beg Sennacherib to leave; he simply turns him around like an animal on a leash. Motyer: the dignity of God's sovereignty is expressed in the utter simplicity of his victory.

verseByVerse.quote: And this shall be the sign for you: this year eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs from that; but in the third year sow and reap and plant vineyards and eat their fruit. And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward. For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A sign for Hezekiah: two years of eating what grows on its own (the siege will prevent normal agriculture), then in the third year normalcy restored. The remnant imagery picks up Isaiah's great theme — a faithful core will survive and flourish. The key phrase: the zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. Not Hezekiah's courage, not Egyptian alliance, not any human strategy. God's own passion for his name and people drives the deliverance. Motyer: zeal here means God's fierce, exclusive commitment to his purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The remnant theology that is central to all of Isaiah: out of disaster, a faithful core survives and produces fruit. Jerusalem will not be extinguished; out of it goes a remnant, and from that remnant blessing spreads. The final phrase is the key: the zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. Not human resilience, not military strategy — God's own passionate commitment to his purposes drives the outcome. This is the foundation of Christian hope in every age of persecution.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it. By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD. For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's protective decree is total: no arrow, no shield, no siege ramp. Jerusalem will be untouched. The motivation is twofold: for my own sake (God's name and reputation) and for the sake of my servant David (the Davidic covenant). Jerusalem's protection flows from covenant promise, not from any merit in Hezekiah or the city. Young observes that the same city Isaiah warned would face judgment (ch3) now receives divine protection — grace, not merit, is the final word.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The twin motivations for Jerusalem's protection: God's own name and the Davidic covenant. For my own sake — God's reputation among the nations is at stake; if Jerusalem falls to Sennacherib's blasphemy, it seems the LORD has been defeated. For the sake of my servant David — the covenant with David (2 Sam 7) is unconditional; God will not abandon the Davidic city. Young: the protection of Jerusalem is ultimately a Christological act — the city of David must be preserved until the Son of David comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies. Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and returned home and lived at Nineveh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The event is as sudden and complete as the word promised. The angel of the LORD — the divine warrior — acts overnight. 185,000 dead by morning. No battle description, no heroics, no human agency. God alone acts. The Assyrian annals notably do not record this defeat — conquerors rarely record their losses — but the sudden withdrawal from Jerusalem is historically established. Childs notes that the narrative's restraint (no description of the angel's action) heightens the theological point: this was entirely God's doing.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword and escaped into the land of Ararat. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The final irony: Sennacherib, who mocked the LORD while worshipping Nisroch, is murdered in Nisroch's own temple by his own sons. His god gave no protection; the LORD's word was entirely fulfilled. Isaiah's prophecy of vv.6-7 — he will return home and fall by the sword in his own land — is exactly accomplished. Motyer: the God who is mocked always has the last word, and that word is always precisely what he said it would be.

38.subtitle: Hezekiah’s Illness and Recovery
38.intro: Overview. Chapter 38 begins the Babylonian shadow that will darken the second movement of Isaiah. Hezekiah falls ill and is told he will die. He prays; God gives him fifteen more years. The sundial goes back ten steps as a sign. Hezekiah writes a song of thanksgiving (vv. 9–20) that is one of the most honest accounts of the experience of near-death in the Bible — moving from lament to praise by way of a genuine wrestling with what had seemed certain.

sections.title: Illness, Prayer, and Extension
sections.commentary: Hezekiah is told by Isaiah: set your house in order, for you shall die. He turns his face to the wall and weeps bitterly — his prayer is not resignation but protest, grounded in his record of faithful living. Before Isaiah has left the court God sends him back: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears; I will add fifteen years to your life. The sign — the shadow on the sundial going back ten steps — is one of the stranger miracles in the historical books. Its significance is theological: the God who governs time can reverse its apparent movement to confirm his word.

sections.title: Hezekiah’s Song
sections.commentary:
The song is remarkable for its honesty. Hezekiah describes what it felt like to look at death: he thought he would see God no more in the land of the living, be cut off like a shepherd’s tent, consumed like a weaver who rolls up his cloth. He moaned like a dove; his eyes were weary looking heavenward. The lament is not sanitized. He walked in the bitterness of his soul.

v. 17 — “It was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.” The retrospect is stunning: the suffering was for his welfare. Not despite God’s love but because of it. And the forgiveness — “cast all my sins behind your back” — is placed at the center of the recovery, not as an afterthought but as the deepest gift in the whole experience.

The song ends with commitment: “The living, the living, he praises you, as I do this day. The father makes known to the children your faithfulness.” The extension of life is not primarily about more time but about more witness — more fathers telling children what God has done.

keyVerse.quote: “It was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.”
keyVerse.note: The theological logic of suffering-for-welfare is the logic of the cross: the deepest bitterness becomes the vehicle of the deepest love. Hezekiah does not explain how this works; he simply reports that it was so. The forgiveness placed at the center — not healing, not the sundial miracle, but “you have cast all my sins behind your back” — suggests that what he most needed was not years but pardon.

38.reflection: Hezekiah’s prayer was heard, his life was extended, and then — in chapter 39 — he will make the worst decision of his reign. The fifteen years included the birth of Manasseh (2 Kings 21:1), Judah’s most wicked king. God’s answer to prayer is not a guarantee of what we will do with the gift. How does that complicate your understanding of answered prayer? And what does “casting sins behind the back” mean for what you are carrying right now?
38.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, "Thus says the LORD: Set your house in order, for you shall die, you shall not recover."<sup>2</sup>Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD,<sup>3</sup>and said, "Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And Hezekiah wept bitterly.<sup>4</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Isaiah:<sup>5</sup>"Go and say to Hezekiah, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.<sup>6</sup>I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and will defend this city.<sup>7</sup>"This shall be the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do this thing that he has promised:<sup>8</sup>Behold, I will make the shadow cast by the declining sun on the dial of Ahaz turn back ten steps." So the sun turned back on the dial the ten steps by which it had declined.<sup>9</sup>A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, after he had been sick and had recovered from his sickness:<sup>10</sup>I said, In the middle of my days I must depart; I am consigned to the gates of Sheol for the rest of my years.<sup>11</sup>I said, I shall not see the LORD, the LORD in the land of the living; I shall look on man no more among the inhabitants of the world.<sup>12</sup>My dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent; like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom; from day to night you bring me to an end;<sup>13</sup>I calmed myself until morning; like a lion he breaks all my bones; from day to night you bring me to an end.<sup>14</sup>Like a swallow or a crane I chirp; I moan like a dove. My eyes are weary with looking upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my pledge of safety!<sup>15</sup>What shall I say? For he has spoken to me, and he himself has done it. I walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul.<sup>16</sup>O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these is the life of my spirit. Oh restore me to health and make me live!<sup>17</sup>Behold, it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.<sup>18</sup>For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your faithfulness.<sup>19</sup>The living, the living, he thanks you, as I do this day; the father makes known to the children your faithfulness.<sup>20</sup>The LORD will save me, and we will play my music on stringed instruments all the days of our lives, at the house of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>Now Isaiah had said, "Let them take a cake of figs and apply it to the boil, that he may recover."<sup>22</sup>Hezekiah also had said, "What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Hezekiah's Illness and the Song of the Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah falls mortally ill and receives a death sentence from Isaiah. He prays, weeping bitterly, and the LORD reverses the sentence, adding fifteen years to his life and giving the sundial sign as confirmation. Hezekiah's psalm (vv.9-20) is a profound meditation on death, suffering, and the grace of restoration — the song of one who has been brought back from the gates of Sheol.
verseByVerse.theology: Oswalt notes the psalm in vv.9-20 is one of the richest personal laments in Scripture, moving from lament through wrestling to praise. It models honest prayer that does not hide grief from God but ultimately arrives at trust: 'the living, the living, he thanks you' (v.19).

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, “Thus says the LORD: Set your house in order, for you shall die, you shall not recover.” Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The death sentence is unqualified: you shall die, you shall not recover. God speaks clearly, and yet the story does not end there. Hezekiah's response is immediate prayer — turning toward the wall, perhaps toward the temple (1 Kings 8:44), shutting out all distractions. Calvin: Hezekiah did not resign himself to fate; he brought his case before the Judge who had pronounced the sentence. This is not rebellion against God's will but faith that the God who speaks is also the God who hears.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly. Then the word of the LORD came to Isaiah: “Go and say to Hezekiah, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Hezekiah's appeal to his faithfulness is not self-righteousness but covenant language — he appeals to his covenant relationship with God. His bitter weeping reveals genuine human anguish. And God responds: I have heard… I have seen your tears. God is moved by human grief. Motyer notes this reveals something profound about God: he is not unmoved by our sorrow. The fifteen years are pure grace — not earned but given in response to prayer and compassion.

verseByVerse.quote: Go and say to Hezekiah, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The word of the LORD reverses the death sentence. I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears — God acknowledges both the verbal petition and the emotional reality. The fifteen-year extension is pure grace. But Motyer notes the sobering sequel in chapter 39: Manasseh (Isaiah 3:12's worst king) will be born in those fifteen years. God's compassionate gifts sometimes carry complex providential implications we cannot anticipate. The gift of life was real; what Hezekiah did with it mixed.

verseByVerse.quote: I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and defend this city. This shall be the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do this thing that he has promised: Behold, I will make the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz go back ten steps.“ So the sun turned back on the sundial the ten steps it had gone down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The deliverance of the city and the healing of Hezekiah are linked — both come from God's sovereign grace. The sundial sign is extraordinary: the shadow reverses ten steps. Whether this involved a localized optical phenomenon or a cosmic event, it is a sign that the God who controls time and creation is the one who speaks. Young: the sign confirms that the impossible word of God will come to pass. God binds himself to what he says by performing the impossible.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz go back ten steps. So the sun turned back on the sundial the ten steps it had gone down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The sundial sign is one of Scripture's most remarkable miracles: the sun reverses its position by ten steps on the sundial of Ahaz (perhaps a staircase serving as a sundial). Whether this was a localized refraction or a cosmic event is less important than its meaning: God who controls time and creation stands behind this word. Oswalt: the sign binds God to his promise publicly and visibly, giving Hezekiah a lasting memorial of divine faithfulness every time he sees the sundial. The God who reverses shadow reverses death sentences.

verseByVerse.quote: A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, after he had been sick and had recovered from his sickness: I said, In the middle of my days I must depart; I am consigned to the gates of Sheol for the rest of my years. I said, I shall not see the LORD, the LORD in the land of the living; I shall look on man no more among the inhabitants of the world. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalm opens with the raw grief of one facing death in mid-life. In the middle of my days — not at the end of a full life but cut short. The greatest loss Hezekiah anticipates is not personal but relational: he will not see the LORD in the land of the living. This reflects the OT's understanding of Sheol as a realm of diminished existence, where the praise of God is not sung (v.18). It is honest, not faithless, to grieve the loss of present worship and fellowship.

verseByVerse.quote: I said, I shall not see the LORD, the LORD in the land of the living; I shall look on man no more among the inhabitants of the world. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The lament reaches its deepest expression of grief: not merely physical death but the loss of the LORD's presence in the land of the living. The OT anticipation of afterlife was limited compared to NT revelation; Hezekiah's grief is genuine — he cannot see how his relationship with God continues beyond the grave. Yet his prayer is itself a refutation of that fear: even in the shadow of death, he addresses the LORD. Motyer: the very act of prayer to God in the midst of despair about losing God is a form of faith that the despair does not destroy.

verseByVerse.quote: My dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent; like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom; from day to night you bring me to an end; I calmed myself until morning; like a lion he breaks all my bones; from day to night you bring me to an end. Like a swallow or a crane I chirp; I moan like a dove. My eyes are weary with looking upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my pledge of safety! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalm's imagery is vivid and anguished: a tent pulled up, a weaving cut off, bones crushed like a lion's prey. Hezekiah does not spiritualize his suffering; he names it graphically. The chirping and moaning are sounds of helplessness — the sick man reduced to animal-like crying. Yet the final cry — be my pledge of safety! — is addressed to God. Even in extremity, Hezekiah addresses the LORD. Motyer: this is the essence of faith under suffering — not suppressing the pain but directing it toward God.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a swallow or a crane I chirp; I moan like a dove. My eyes are weary with looking upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my pledge of safety! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The plaintive bird-sounds — swallow-like chirping, dove-like moaning — capture the helplessness of severe illness. The sick man is reduced to inarticulate cries, his upward gaze exhausted, his strength gone. Then the petition: be my pledge of safety! — literally, be surety for me. Hezekiah asks God to take personal responsibility for his case, to be his advocate before the divine court. This is a deep legal metaphor for intercession. Oswalt: it anticipates the NT understanding of Christ as our surety before the Father (Heb 7:22).

verseByVerse.quote: What shall I say? For he has spoken to me, and he himself has done it. I walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul. O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these is the life of my spirit. Oh restore me to health and make me live! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A turning point: Hezekiah acknowledges that God himself brought this suffering (he himself has done it), yet paradoxically appeals to that same God for restoration. The bitterness is real; the appeal is genuine. By these things men live — perhaps meaning that suffering itself teaches life's true meaning, or that God's word and discipline are the source of real life. Oswalt: Hezekiah has moved from protest to submission to appeal, the full arc of lament prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; it is you who have kept my soul from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back. For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your faithfulness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: For my welfare that I had great bitterness — the retrospective view of grace through suffering. God's purpose in the illness was goodness, not punishment. The glorious addition: you have cast all my sins behind your back. This is forgiveness at its most radical — sins placed where God himself does not see them, out of his own view. The motivation for wanting to live: Sheol cannot praise God. Hezekiah wants to live so he can keep worshipping. This is a profound motivation for existence.

verseByVerse.quote: The living, the living, he thanks you, as I do this day; the father makes known to your children your faithfulness. The LORD will save me, and we will play my music on stringed instruments all the days of our lives, at the house of the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalm's resolution: the living praise God. Hezekiah's motivation for recovery is doxological — to praise, to tell his children, to make music in the temple all his remaining days. Calvin notes the communal dimension: faith is not private. What God does for one believer is passed down to the next generation as testimony of his faithfulness. The final image — music at the house of the LORD — restores what the illness threatened to remove forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Isaiah had said, “Let them take a cake of figs and apply it to the boil, that he may recover.” Hezekiah also had said, “What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The appendix is historically grounding: God's healing comes through a fig poultice — a known ancient medical remedy. Divine healing does not exclude natural means; God works through both. The question about a sign shows Hezekiah's faith seeking confirmation, not doubting God's promise. Motyer: God graciously accommodates our human need for assurance. The sign of the sundial (given before the psalm) is now requested here — the narrative in 2 Kings 20 and Isaiah 38 use slightly different ordering, but the theological point holds: God confirms his word to those who ask.

39.subtitle: The Shadow of Babylon
39.intro: Overview. Chapter 39 is brief and devastating. Babylon’s king sends envoys to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery, and Hezekiah, in a moment of pride, shows them everything — every treasure of his palace, every weapon in his armory. Isaiah pronounces the consequence: all of this will be carried to Babylon; your own sons will be eunuchs in the king’s palace. Hezekiah’s response — “there will be peace and security in my days” — is one of the saddest lines in the whole book. The chapter pivots the entire book from Assyrian crisis to Babylonian captivity.

sections.title: The Folly of the Open Treasury
sections.commentary:
The delegation from Babylon is a diplomatic opportunity that becomes a spiritual test. Merodach-baladan sends letters and a gift to congratulate the recovered king — and Hezekiah is pleased with them and shows them everything. There was nothing in his house or his whole realm that he did not show them. Isaiah’s question is clinical: what did they see? Everything, Hezekiah replies, and adds nothing.

The oracle is direct: the days are coming when all this will be carried to Babylon. Nothing will be left. Some of your sons will be taken, and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. This is not a vague future threat but the specific shape of the exile — announced before Isaiah 40 begins its great consolation.

v. 8 — “Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, ‘The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.’ For he thought, ‘There will be peace and security in my days.’” This is perhaps the most chilling line in Isaiah’s historical section. Hezekiah receives a judgment oracle on his descendants and calls it good because he himself will be unaffected. John MacArthur noted that the comfort of “not in my time” is the comfort of someone who has confused his personal peace with God’s peace — a category error with enormous consequences.

And yet: the chapter serves a structural purpose. The shadow of Babylon that falls here makes the comfort of chapter 40 necessary. “Comfort, comfort my people” is addressed to those who will be exactly where chapter 39 describes — in Babylon, stripped, far from home. The darkness at the end of chapter 39 is what makes the dawn of chapter 40 so luminous.

keyVerse.quote: “Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, ‘The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.’ For he thought, ‘There will be peace and security in my days.’”
keyVerse.note: The contrast with chapter 37’s prayer is stark. There, Hezekiah interceded for others and future generations; here, he accepts judgment on his descendants with private relief. The chapter stands as a warning about the way personal comfort can corrupt what began as genuine faith. Hezekiah did not lose his faith; he privatized it.

39.reflection: Hezekiah showed the Babylonians everything. Pride after a great deliverance is one of the most common patterns in the spiritual life — the recovery that becomes an occasion for display rather than gratitude. What has God delivered you from that you are now tempted to exhibit for your own credit? And whose future are you shaping by choices you’re making today?
39.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been sick and had recovered.<sup>2</sup>And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.<sup>3</sup>Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, "What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?" Hezekiah said, "They have come to me from a far country, from Babylon."<sup>4</sup>He said, "What have they seen in your house?" Hezekiah answered, "They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."<sup>5</sup>Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD of hosts:<sup>6</sup>Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD.<sup>7</sup>And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."<sup>8</sup>Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "There will be peace and security in my days."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Hezekiah's Folly and the Babylonian Prophecy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylonian envoys arrive to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery. Hezekiah, flushed with pride, shows them everything in his treasury. Isaiah comes with a devastating oracle: all Hezekiah has shown will one day go to Babylon, and his sons will be eunuchs in the Babylonian palace. Hezekiah's response — 'the word of the LORD is good' — is either genuine faith or troubling complacency. The chapter pivots Isaiah from his Assyrian context to the Babylonian exile.
verseByVerse.theology: Childs sees ch39 as the hinge of the entire book: it explains why Babylon replaces Assyria as the threat in chs40-66 and introduces the exile that makes the 'comfort' of ch40 necessary. The final verse's ambiguity — is Hezekiah's response faithful resignation or selfish relief? — is intentional. Keller notes the chapter warns against the pride that comes with answered prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been sick and had recovered. And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Merodach-baladan was a historical Babylonian king who resisted Assyrian domination — his interest in Hezekiah may have had political-military motives (forming an anti-Assyrian alliance). Hezekiah is flattered by the attention and shows everything. The word gladly signals the problem: he delights in being noticed by a great power, the very temptation Isaiah warned against in relying on Egypt. Oswalt: after all the lessons about trusting the LORD rather than human power, Hezekiah reverts to the old pattern — impressing the world rather than glorifying God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, “What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?” Hezekiah said, “They have come to me from a far country, from Babylon.” He said, “What have they seen in your house?” Hezekiah answered, “They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them.” Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah's questioning is pastoral and probing — he already knows the answer but he asks, leading Hezekiah to confess the extent of his display. Nothing that I did not show them — the admission reveals pride. The prophet then introduces the divine word: what has been so proudly displayed will become spoil for the very nation whose envoys admired it. Young notes the irony: Hezekiah's attempt to impress Babylon guarantees Babylon's eventual claim on his wealth.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah introduces the divine oracle with the full weight of prophetic authority: Hear the word of the LORD of hosts. What follows (vv.6-7) is the most direct prophecy of the Babylonian exile in chapters 1-39. The title LORD of hosts — used over 60 times in Isaiah — emphasizes the God who commands the armies of heaven. Childs: the juxtaposition of vv.1-4 (Hezekiah's pride) and v.5 (the LORD's word) shows the prophetic function: God breaks into human pride with the word of truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD. And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The oracle is a watershed in Isaiah's book. Everything Hezekiah showed will go to Babylon — treasure and descendants alike. The mention of eunuchs in Babylon's palace anticipates Daniel and his companions (Dan 1). Childs: this prophecy was not inevitable from Hezekiah's sin alone — the exile was a long time coming from accumulated national sin — but Hezekiah's action becomes the occasion for announcing it. The chapter is designed to explain why the second half of Isaiah addresses Babylonian exile rather than Assyrian threat.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “There will be peace and security in my days.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The response is deeply ambiguous. On the surface, the word of the LORD is good sounds like faithful submission. But the editorial comment — for he thought, there will be peace in my days — suggests troubling self-focus: the disaster will come, but not to me. Motyer wrestles with whether this is courageous faith or selfish relief; most commentators (Oswalt, Young) see it as the latter, a failure of compassion for future generations. Yet the chapter ends without further condemnation — God's word stands, and the pivot to ch40's comfort begins immediately.

40.subtitle: Comfort, Comfort My People
40.intro:
Overview. Chapter 40 is the great turn of the book. After thirty-nine chapters of indictment and the shadow of Babylon, God commissions a company of heralds with one word said twice — comfort — and three announcements: the sentence is served, the iniquity is pardoned, the debt is settled in full. Then a voice is sent into the wilderness to build a road, because God is coming in person, and the glory that arrives on it will be seen by all flesh at once.

The middle of the chapter resets the scale for people whose whole horizon had become an empire: oceans measured in a cupped hand, the nations weighed and found to be dust on a balance, idols that have to be kept from falling over, and stars that answer a roll call by name. The last five verses bring all of it down onto one complaint — my way is hidden from the LORD — and answer it not with sympathy but with God himself: the everlasting God does not faint or grow weary, and those who wait for him exchange their spent strength for his. All four Gospels quote verse 3 of John the Baptist, and Peter grounds Christian assurance on verse 8.

keyVerse.quote: “But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.”
keyVerse.note: The word wait (qavah) means to bind together, to strain toward — it is not passive waiting but directed, tethered hoping. The renewal is not a restoration of natural energy but a supernatural infusion. R.C. Sproul called this the great promise of the second section of Isaiah: what human strength cannot sustain, divine grace can renew.

40.theology:
The incomparability of God. Everything in chapters 40 to 55 rests on the claim made here: the God who speaks is not the largest item in a list of powerful things but the ground of everything that exists. Later theology calls this aseity — God’s existence from himself, depending on nothing and taught by nobody — and verses 13 and 14 state it as bluntly as Scripture ever does. The pastoral force is exact: only an infinite God can offer an infinite comfort, so the tenderness of verses 1 and 2 and the cosmic scale of verses 12 to 26 are not two subjects but one argument.

The road built for the LORD. Verse 3 prepares a way for Yahweh, and all four Gospels assign that road-building to John the Baptist, whose road was walked by Jesus of Nazareth (Matt. 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4-6; John 1:23). The New Testament does not argue the identification; it assumes it. Verse 5 promises that the glory of the LORD will be revealed to all flesh, and John reports the sighting: we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

Grace to the empty-handed. The chapter’s last movement is the whole economy of grace in miniature. Human strength is measured at its peak and found to fail (v. 30); the strength that does not fail is given to the faint and to the man with no might at all (v. 29); and the verb for renewing it in verse 31 means to exchange. Nothing is topped up. The spent thing is handed over and something else is received in its place, which is how every other gift of God has ever worked.
40.reflection: The chapter begins with double comfort for people who feel their sin has been answered double. It ends with renewal for people who have grown weary waiting. Which of those two do you need most right now — the assurance of pardon, or the renewal of strength? And what does “waiting for the LORD” actually look like in the specific weariness you are carrying this week?
40.text: <sup>1</sup>Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.<sup>2</sup>Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins.<sup>3</sup>A voice cries: "In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God.<sup>4</sup>Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain.<sup>5</sup>And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."<sup>6</sup>A voice says, "Cry!" And I said, "What shall I cry?" All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field.<sup>7</sup>The grass withers, the flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass.<sup>8</sup>The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.<sup>9</sup>Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, "Behold your God!"<sup>10</sup>Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and his arm rules for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him.<sup>11</sup>He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.<sup>12</sup>Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?<sup>13</sup>Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?<sup>14</sup>Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding?<sup>15</sup>Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as the dust on the scales; behold, he takes up the coastlands like fine dust.<sup>16</sup>Lebanon would not suffice for fuel, nor are its beasts enough for a burnt offering.<sup>17</sup>All the nations are as nothing before him, they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness.<sup>18</sup>To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him?<sup>19</sup>An idol! A craftsman casts it, and a goldsmith overlays it with gold and casts for it silver chains.<sup>20</sup>He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move.<sup>21</sup>Do you not know? Do you not hear? Has it not been told you from the beginning? Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth?<sup>22</sup>It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in;<sup>23</sup>who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness.<sup>24</sup>Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble.<sup>25</sup>To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One.<sup>26</sup>Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name; by the greatness of his might and because he is strong in power, not one is missing.<sup>27</sup>Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, "My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God"?<sup>28</sup>Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable.<sup>29</sup>He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength.<sup>30</sup>Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted;<sup>31</sup>but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Comfort, and the Road for God to Come On
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Isaiah opens, and after thirty-nine chapters of indictment the first word is comfort, spoken twice. Verses 1 and 2 announce a sentence served, a pardon granted and a debt settled. Verses 3 to 5 send a voice into the wilderness to build a road, because God is coming in person and the glory that arrives will be seen by all flesh at once. Verses 6 to 8 measure that promise against human frailty — all flesh is grass, and the only thing that outlasts the withering is the word of God. Verses 9 to 11 put a herald on a mountain with two pictures of the God she announces: a warrior whose arm rules, and a shepherd carrying lambs.
verseByVerse.theology: The comfort of this chapter is not encouragement; it is the announcement of an accomplished settlement, which is why it can be commanded rather than merely hoped. And the road in verse 3 is built for the LORD himself. When all four Gospels apply that verse to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus of Nazareth, they are not borrowing a convenient phrase — they are identifying the one whose road it was. The two images of verses 10 and 11 are not in tension: omnipotence in the service of tenderness is what the arm of God is for.
verseByVerse.examples: John the Baptist, asked directly who he was, answered by quoting verse 3 — I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness (John 1:23). Peter grounds Christian assurance on verse 8 and then names the abiding word: it is the good news that was preached to you (1 Pet. 1:24-25). And the herald's message in verse 9 is still the shortest summary of Christian proclamation available: Behold your God.

verseByVerse.quote: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Comfort, comfort my people, says your God."

Thirty-nine chapters of indictment stop here. The last thing said before this was that everything in Hezekiah's house would be carried to Babylon, and the first word after it is comfort, said twice. In Hebrew the imperative is plural — God is not speaking to one prophet but commissioning a company of heralds, and the doubling is how the language shouts.

Then two possessives that have been missing for a long time. My people. Your God. Through the first half of the book they have mostly been "this people," which is what you call a nation you are addressing at arm's length. The relationship is being spoken back into place before anything is explained.

"Speak tenderly to Jerusalem." The Hebrew is dabberu al-lev — speak to the heart of Jerusalem — and it is not a general instruction to be gentle. It is the idiom for courtship. It is what Shechem does when he loves Dinah, what Boaz does when Ruth is frightened, what God says he will do when he takes his unfaithful wife into the wilderness to win her back (Hos. 2:14). God is not merely informing his people that the punishment is over. He is wooing them.

Three things are then cried over the city. Her warfare is ended — the word is the one used for compulsory military service, a term of hard duty with a fixed end. Her iniquity is pardoned. And she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins.

That last phrase troubles readers, and it should not. It does not mean God overcharged her. The word means the matching half of something folded over — the second panel that exactly answers the first — so the sense is that the sentence has been served in full, right to the last day of it, with nothing outstanding. Nothing is still owing. There is no residue to be collected later.

Which is why comfort can be commanded here rather than merely offered. Christian comfort has never been a mood worked up in the face of trouble; it is the proper response to a settled account. If the debt is paid, cheer is not optimism but accuracy — and the double that fell on the head of the servant in chapter 53 is what makes the arithmetic work.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice cries: "In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain. And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A voice cries: 'In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God.'"

The picture is a road gang. When an eastern king travelled, men went ahead of him to make the route passable — filling holes, cutting through spurs, levelling the surface — because the road had to be ready before the king would come. Isaiah takes that ordinary piece of imperial logistics and puts it in the desert between Babylon and home, and the king being announced is God.

"Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain." Nothing is left in the way. Not the mountains, which is to say not the obstacles that cannot ordinarily be moved.

Then verse 5, which is the point of the roadworks: "And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken." Not a rumour of God, and not a report brought back by specialists. The glory itself, in the open, seen by everybody at once.

Now hold that against the Gospels, because all four of them quote this verse, and they quote it about one man. Matthew, Mark and Luke apply it to John the Baptist (Matt. 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4-6), and when the delegation from Jerusalem asked John directly who he was, he refused every title they offered him and answered with this verse: "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord'" (John 1:23).

Follow what that does. Isaiah says the road is being built for the LORD — the covenant name, the God whose glory fills the earth. John built his road, and then Jesus of Nazareth walked up it. The Gospel writers do not argue this; they simply take a sentence about the coming of God and hand it to a carpenter's son, and expect the reader to notice.

And what the road-builders were told to expect, John saw. "We have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father" (John 1:14). The valleys had been filled and the mountains taken down, and what came along the finished road was a man they could touch.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice says, "Cry!" And I said, "What shall I cry?" All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A voice says, 'Cry!' And I said, 'What shall I cry?'"

The herald is willing and does not know what the message is. The answer he gets is not the one he expects: before the comfort can be preached, something has to be said about the people being comforted.

"All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass."

The image is exact, and anyone who has lived in that country knows it. After the rains the hills go green and the wildflowers come, and it is genuinely lovely, and then the east wind arrives off the desert — the sirocco, hot and dry — and in a day or two the whole hillside is brown. Not weeks. Days.

And Isaiah does not say all flesh is weak. He says all flesh is grass, and specifies that what goes first is the beauty. Not the ugliness of human life but its loveliness: strength, looks, competence, the years when everything works. Read the obituaries of the people who ran the world eighty years ago. Look up the books everyone was required to have an opinion about in the decade you were born. The withering is not a threat hanging over human glory. It is the ordinary weather of it.

And notice who does the withering. Not time, not bad luck, not the market. "The breath of the LORD blows on it." The same breath that gave the grass its life takes it, on a schedule that belongs to God and not to us — which is a harder thought than mortality in the abstract, and a better one, because a wind that is God's breath is not a random wind.

verseByVerse.quote: The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever."

The whole architecture of the chapter rests on this one sentence. Two clauses of the verse repeat what has just been said, so the third lands with everything behind it: one thing in the picture is not grass.

Take the comfort of verses 1 and 2 and ask what it is standing on. If the pardon were built on national recovery, or on a change of imperial policy, or on the exiles finding new resolve, then it would be grass and it would go the way of grass — beautiful for a season and brown by summer. It is built on something God said. And what God has said outlasts the people he said it to, the empire that overheard it, and the language it was first spoken in.

That is a specific kind of security, and its precise shape matters. It is not the promise that the believer will feel certain. Feelings are grass; they were in the list. It is the promise that the thing believed does not depend on the believer to hold it up.

Peter takes these two verses to Christians scattered across five provinces and under real pressure, quotes them in full, and then does something remarkable: "And this word is the good news that was preached to you" (1 Pet. 1:24-25). The abiding, unwithering, imperishable word is not left as an abstraction hovering over history. Peter puts his finger on it and says: you have already heard it. It was the gospel, in a room, out of somebody's mouth, and it is the one thing in your life that is not grass.

verseByVerse.quote: Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, "Behold your God!" Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and his arm rules for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him. He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, 'Behold your God!'"

The city that has spent thirty-nine chapters being preached at is handed the microphone. Zion is now the herald, sent up a hill so the sound will carry, told twice to lift her voice and once not to be afraid — which suggests that the natural instinct of a recently disgraced people with good news is to say it quietly.

And the message she is given is two words long. Not behold your deliverance, or behold your restored fortunes, though both are coming. Behold your God. Everything the exiles wanted was downstream of that, and Isaiah will not let the gift be announced ahead of the giver.

Then, in two verses, two pictures of the God being pointed at, and they do not sit together comfortably.

"Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and his arm rules for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him." That is a conqueror coming home — the arm that does the ruling, the spoils carried in front of the column. It is the image that terrifies the enemies of God, and it is meant to.

"He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young." Same God, next sentence. The arm that rules for him in verse 10 is the arm the lambs are carried in in verse 11.

Notice the last clause especially, because it is the most practical thing in the chapter. Gently lead those that are with young. A flock moves at the speed of its slowest member, and a shepherd who drives it at the pace of the strongest will kill the pregnant ewes. Jacob knew it and said so to Esau: if the flocks are driven hard for one day, all of them will die (Gen. 33:13-14). God sets the pace of his people by the weakest one in it.

Two images and one God. The arm that will not be resisted is the arm that carries lambs; the might that comes with recompense is the tenderness that slows down for a pregnant animal. There is no tension in it and never was. This is what omnipotence looks like when it belongs to a shepherd, and it is the same one who said, centuries later, that he was the good shepherd and would lay down his life for the sheep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — To Whom Then Will You Compare Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The middle movement resets the scale for people whose whole horizon had become Babylon. Verses 12 to 14 ask who measured the oceans in a cupped hand and who taught God anything. Verses 15 to 17 weigh the nations and find them a drop and a speck of dust. Verses 18 to 20 turn to the alternative and follow an idol from the timber yard to the workshop, ending on the specification that matters most to its owner: that it will not fall over. Verses 21 to 24 have God stretching the sky like a tent and blowing on princes until they go like stubble. Verses 25 and 26 close the movement by summoning the stars and finding all of them present.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the doctrine later theology calls aseity — that God exists of himself, depending on nothing, taught by nobody. The polemic is precise rather than sneering: the nations and their gods are not God's rivals but his creation, and an idol is a category mistake before it is a sin. Verse 17 uses the word for the formless void of Genesis 1:2 of the nations, which is the point exactly — apart from God nothing has standing of its own.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul quotes verse 13 twice, at Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16, both times to stop an argument in front of the unsearchable wisdom of God. And the idol of verses 19 and 20 has never gone out of production. Every age builds something impressive with real skill, gives it the weight of its trust, and then has to take steps to stop it toppling over.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance? Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?"

Four measurements, and the units are the point. The hollow of the hand is the cupped palm — every ocean on earth held the way you would hold a mouthful of water. A span is the distance from thumb-tip to little finger on a spread hand, about nine inches, and it is being used to measure the sky. The dust of the earth goes into a grain scoop. The mountains go on the kitchen scales.

These are not images of a very large God. They are images of a God who is not on the same scale at all — who handles the whole created order with the casual gestures of a merchant checking a quantity.

"Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding?"

The questions turn from power to wisdom, and every one of them expects the answer nobody. God has never taken advice. He has never had a teacher, never revised a position in the light of better information, never been shown something he had not considered. Paul quotes verse 13 twice — at the end of eleven chapters of argument in Romans (11:34), and again in 1 Corinthians (2:16) — both times at the moment where the right response to God is to stop talking.

To an exile this is intensely practical. Babylon was full of professional advisers — astrologers, diviners, wise men whose whole trade was telling a king what was coming. The God directing the history that had swept them into that city had not consulted any of them, and did not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as the dust on the scales; behold, he takes up the coastlands like fine dust. Lebanon would not suffice for fuel, nor are its beasts enough for a burnt offering. All the nations are as nothing before him, they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as the dust on the scales."

Watch how precisely that is chosen. Not a bucket — a drop from a bucket: the single bead of water that hangs on the rim and falls when you lift it, which nobody notices and nobody counts. Not a load of dust — the dust that has settled on the pan of a balance and is not enough to move the needle.

"Lebanon would not suffice for fuel, nor are its beasts enough for a burnt offering." Lebanon meant the great cedar forests, the timber kings sent for when they wanted a temple or a palace. Isaiah says: burn the whole forest, put every animal in it on the altar, and you still have not made an offering big enough to be adequate to this God.

"All the nations are as nothing before him, they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness." The last word is tohu — the same word used of the formless void in the second verse of the Bible, before anything had been shaped.

Remember who is being told this and where they are standing. These are people living inside the Babylonian empire, for whom Babylon is not one nation among several but the entire horizon: its army, its gods, its processions, its buildings, the sheer daily weight of it. Isaiah is not insulting them and he is not exaggerating for effect. He is resetting the scale, because a captive's real problem is usually not that he has too high a view of God but that he has an accurate view of his captor and no idea what to set beside it.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him? An idol! A craftsman casts it, and a goldsmith overlays it with gold and casts for it silver chains. He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him?"

The question is not rhetorical padding; it is the hinge of chapters 40 to 48, and Isaiah will keep asking it. Having described a God who measures oceans in his palm, he now turns and looks at the competition.

"An idol! A craftsman casts it, and a goldsmith overlays it with gold and casts for it silver chains." The sequence is followed like a work order. Somebody founds it, somebody gilds it, somebody chains it — and then verse 20 goes down the market to the customer who cannot afford that: "He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skilled craftsman to set up an idol that will not move."

Read the last clause again, because it is the sharpest sentence in the passage. After the timber selection and the hiring of a specialist, the specification that matters — the thing the whole investment is for — is that the finished god will stay upright. That is the ambition. Not that it will act, or hear, or save. That it will not fall over.

Two verses ago the nations were dust on a balance. Here the gods of those nations are objects that have to be steadied. They are not God's rivals. They are his furniture.

And the error Isaiah is exposing is a category mistake before it is a wickedness: treating a made thing as though it were the Maker. That reaches a good deal further than carved wood. Anything that gets a person's ultimate trust while remaining something he himself built — a portfolio, a reputation, a marriage, a body, a career, a church building — will need propping up, and the propping is the tell. Ask what in your life you spend most effort keeping upright. Whatever that is, you are its shipwright and not the other way round.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know? Do you not hear? Has it not been told you from the beginning? Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth? It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Have you not known? Have you not heard? Has it not been told you from the beginning? Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth?"

Four questions, and not one of them offers new information. Isaiah is not introducing a doctrine; he is charging his hearers with forgetting something that has been in plain view since the world began. That is the same argument Paul makes about the whole human race — what can be known about God is evident, and the problem is suppression rather than shortage (Rom. 1:18-20). Nobody in this chapter is short of evidence. They are short of attention.

"It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in."

The tent is the striking picture, and it is domestic. Anyone in that world had watched one go up: the cloth shaken out, hauled over the poles, the guys pegged into the ground, and a household living underneath it by evening. Isaiah says that is what God did with the sky. One unhurried gesture, performed at the beginning, and every human being who has ever lived has lived inside it.

And grasshoppers is not contempt. Isaiah has just called the nations dust on a balance; if he wanted to insult us he had better material. It is scale. An insect on the floor of a very large tent is not worthless — it is alive, it is fed, it is provided for — it is simply very small in a very big room. The verse is not asking the reader to despise himself. It is asking him to stop imagining that the room is the size of his own concerns.

He sits above the circle of the earth. Not perched on it, not managing it from within it, not one of the forces operating inside the system — above it, seated, which is the posture of a king who is not worried.

verseByVerse.quote: who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness. Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness."

Isaiah now applies the scale to the one thing an exile could not stop thinking about: power. Not power in general — princes, rulers of the earth, named individuals with armies and treasuries and the ability to decide where a family would live and whether it would live.

"Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble."

Three times scarcely, hammered. The dynasties that seemed permanent are seedlings that have not got their roots down yet. And read what God actually does to them: he does not send an army, or raise up a rival, or uproot them. He blows on them. The gesture is the smallest one in the chapter.

It is also the same gesture as verse 7, where the breath of the LORD blows on the grass. Isaiah has now used one image twice, deliberately: what happens to a wildflower in the sirocco is what happens to an empire. The difference between them is size, not kind — both are vegetation, both are seasonal, and both go down before the same breath.

Nebuchadnezzar was the most powerful man alive when these words were being read by people he had deported. There is a photograph of that empire in the British Museum and nothing else left of it. That is not a comfort about politics being unimportant; the exiles' suffering under it was real and God takes a whole book to say so. It is a comfort about proportion. A believer who is frightened of a government is frightened of stubble in a wind — and the wind belongs to his Father.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name; by the greatness of his might and because he is strong in power, not one is missing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"'To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him?' says the Holy One."

The question comes back, and this time God asks it himself, in his own voice, using the title that has run through the whole book: the Holy One. The claim inside the question is not that God wins the comparison. It is that there is no category to run the comparison in. He is not the best of a kind; there is no kind.
