verseByVerse.commentary: The indictment is subtle and devastating: Israel uses all the right language — swearing by the LORD, confessing the God of Israel, calling themselves after the holy city — but not in truth or right. Formal religious identity without genuine commitment. Oswalt: this is the perennial danger of covenant religion — inheriting the vocabulary of faith without the reality. The people who claim God's name most loudly may be most insulated from actually knowing him.

verseByVerse.quote: The former things I declared of old; they went out from my mouth, and I announced them; then suddenly I did them, and they came to pass. Because I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God declared events in advance and fulfilled them — so Israel could not claim the idols did it. But the reason for this advance declaration is Israel's stubbornness: the obstinate, brass-forehead people needed extra evidence. Motyer: God's predictive prophecy is not merely an apologetic tool but a pastoral accommodation to human hardness of heart. He builds the evidential case for those who would otherwise refuse to believe. The hardness is real and God knows it; the grace works around and through it.

verseByVerse.quote: I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass I announced them to you, lest you should say, 'My idol did them, my carved image and my metal image commanded them.' You have heard; now see all this; and will you not declare it? I announce to you new things from this time, things hidden and you have not known. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose of advance prophecy: to deny idols any credit for fulfilled events. Now new things are announced — things hidden, not previously revealed. The new exodus, Cyrus, the servant — things unprecedented. Childs: the distinction between former things (announced and fulfilled) and new things (now being announced) structures the entire argument of Isaiah 40-48. The former things prove God's prophetic power; the new things are the substance of the gospel announcement.

verseByVerse.quote: They are created now, not long ago; before today you have not heard of them, lest you should say, 'Behold, I knew them.' You have never heard, you have never known, from of old your ear has not been opened. For I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that from before birth you were called a rebel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The new things are genuinely new — not extensions of old patterns but unprecedented acts. God withheld them precisely so Israel could not claim prior knowledge and thereby dismiss the grace. The accusation intensifies: from before birth you were called a rebel. The stubbornness is not circumstantial but constitutional — Israel's rebellion is original, not acquired. Young: this is not pessimism about human nature but realism — the grace that works with such deep obstinacy must be all the more powerful and sovereign.

verseByVerse.quote: For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off. Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: For my name's sake I defer my anger — the foundation of grace is God's own character, not Israel's merit. The restraint of judgment is for his praise — God's reputation as Redeemer requires that he not abandon the people he has called. The furnace of affliction (exile) is a refining process, but not as silver: silver is refined to purity; Israel's refining produces survivors who know their dependence on God. Motyer: the exile is simultaneously judgment and grace — God judges Israel's sin but preserves the remnant for his purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I will not give to another. Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called! I am he; I am the first, and I am the last. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The doubled for my own sake is emphatic: God's action in redemption is self-motivated. This is not cold or selfish — it means redemption is grounded in the most reliable foundation possible, God's own honor. My glory I will not give to another — the covenant commitment that makes rescue certain. Then: I am the first and I am the last — the Alpha and Omega declaration that encompasses all time within God's being. Childs: the First and Last encompasses every moment of Israel's history within God's sovereign care.

verseByVerse.quote: My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand forth together. Assemble, all of you, and listen! Who among them has declared these things? The LORD loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon, and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Creator who spoke creation into being by name — stars obeying his call — is the same God who speaks Cyrus into action. The personification is striking: creation has a worshipper's response to God's voice (they stand forth together). Then the court is reconvened: who among the idol-worshippers predicted Cyrus? None. The LORD loves him — Cyrus is an object of divine affection in the sense of divine purpose. Young: God's love for Cyrus is instrumental, purposive love — he loves him for what he will accomplish for Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: I, even I, have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and he will prosper in his way. Draw near to me, hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret, from the time it was, there I was. And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: V.16b is one of the most remarkable statements in Isaiah: the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit — a three-person dynamic: the LORD (Father), the speaker (the servant/prophet), and the Spirit. Many commentators (Childs, Motyer, Young) see this as a transition from prophetic speech to servant speech, with trinitarian overtones. Motyer: whether referring to the prophet or the Servant, the three-person formula anticipates the NT revelation of Trinity and the Spirit-anointed mission of the Servant.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go. Oh that you had listened to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The lament is one of Scripture's great what ifs: Oh that you had listened! Peace like a river, righteousness like ocean waves — these are what obedience would have produced. The images convey abundance, persistence, and irresistible flow. But Israel did not listen. The lament is not resignation but passion: God is grieved by the peace his people forfeited. Oswalt: the oh that of v.18 is the divine ache — God who could not be forced to feel anything feels the loss of what might have been.

verseByVerse.quote: your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains; their name would never be cut off or destroyed from before me. Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, 'The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: After the lament comes the command: Go out from Babylon! The new exodus begins with a shout rather than a flight. Declare this… proclaim it… send it to the end of the earth — the redemption of Jacob is news for all nations. The scope of the announcement makes the return from exile the prototype of the universal gospel proclamation. Childs: the command to go out from Babylon is echoed in Rev 18:4 (Come out of her, my people) — the spiritual Babylon of any age is to be abandoned by God's people.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock; he split the rock and the water gushed out. There is no peace, says the LORD, for the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The water-from-the-rock miracle (Ex 17:1-7; Num 20:7-11) is recalled as promise: the God who provided in the first wilderness will provide in the new wilderness of the return journey. Then the jarring close: there is no peace for the wicked. This refrain (repeated in 57:21) closes the section with a warning: the comfort and the new exodus are for those who come out of Babylon — the wicked who remain outside the covenant of grace have no access to the peace that the LORD gives. Young: the hinge verse points forward to ch53, where the servant's suffering produces the peace that the wicked cannot have.

49.subtitle: The Second Servant Song
49.intro:
Overview. The second Servant Song (vv. 1-6) has the servant speak for himself, and he addresses the coastlands rather than Israel. He was called before he was born and prepared in concealment — a sword hidden in the shadow of God’s hand, an arrow hidden in a quiver. He is given Israel’s own name and sent to bring Israel back, which is the puzzle the song exists to pose. And then, extraordinarily, he says his work has come to nothing: I have labored in vain. God’s answer is not reassurance but a larger commission — restoring Israel is too light a thing, and the salvation is to reach the end of the earth.

The rest of the chapter answers Zion, who interrupts the singing of heaven and earth to say that the LORD has forsaken and forgotten her. God does not rebuke the complaint. He measures his commitment against a nursing mother’s, concedes that hers can fail, and puts his own past it — and then holds out his hands, with her name cut into the palms. The chapter closes with builders outstripping destroyers, a bereaved woman bewildered by the number of her children, and God contending in person with those who contend with his people.

keyVerse.quote: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands.”
keyVerse.note: The argument moves from the most reliable human attachment — mother to nursing infant — to something more reliable still. God does not merely match maternal love; he exceeds it. The engraving-on-palms image anticipates the wounds in the hands of Christ — the permanent bodily record of what it cost to keep the promise.

49.reflection: The Servant confessed that he had labored in vain — and God immediately expanded his commission. The experience of apparent futility preceded the revelation of greater purpose. Where in your life have you been most tempted to conclude that your faithfulness has been wasted? And what would it mean to respond with the Servant’s posture: “yet my right is with the LORD”?
49.text: <sup>1</sup>Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar. The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name.<sup>2</sup>He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away.<sup>3</sup>And he said to me, "You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified."<sup>4</sup>But I said, "I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God."<sup>5</sup>And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him; and that Israel might be gathered to him— for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength—<sup>6</sup>he says: "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth."<sup>7</sup>Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers: "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you."<sup>8</sup>Thus says the LORD: "In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you; I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages,<sup>9</sup>saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.' They shall feed along the ways; on all bare heights shall be their pasture;<sup>10</sup>they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them.<sup>11</sup>And I will make all my mountains a road, and my highways shall be raised up.<sup>12</sup>Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Syene."<sup>13</sup>Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted.<sup>14</sup>But Zion said, "The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me."<sup>15</sup>"Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.<sup>16</sup>Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me.<sup>17</sup>Your builders make haste; your destroyers and those who laid you waste go out from you.<sup>18</sup>Lift up your eyes around and see; they all gather, they come to you. As I live, declares the LORD, you shall put them all on as an ornament; you shall bind them on as a bride does.<sup>19</sup>"Surely your waste and your desolate places and your devastated land— surely now you will be too narrow for your inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up will be far away.<sup>20</sup>The children of your bereavement will yet say in your ears: 'The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell in.'<sup>21</sup>Then you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? I was bereaved and barren, exiled and put away, but who has brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; from where have these come?'"<sup>22</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and raise my signal to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders.<sup>23</sup>Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. With their faces to the ground they shall bow down to you, and lick the dust of your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who wait for me shall not be put to shame."<sup>24</sup>Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued?<sup>25</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued, for I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children.<sup>26</sup>I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with wine. Then all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Called from the Womb, and Sent Further Than He Knew
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The servant speaks for himself, and he addresses the coastlands rather than Israel. Verses 1 and 2 describe a calling that predates his birth and a preparation spent entirely in concealment — a sword hidden in the shadow of God's hand, an arrow hidden in a quiver. Verse 3 names him Israel. Verse 4 is his own confession that the work has come to nothing. Verses 5 and 6 are God's answer, which enlarges the commission instead of consoling him: restoring Israel is too small a thing, and the salvation is to reach the end of the earth. Verse 7 promises that the despised one will be stood up before kings.
verseByVerse.theology: The song makes the identification of the servant unavoidable. He is called Israel in verse 3 and sent to bring Jacob back in verse 5 — so he is Israel and he is not Israel, which means he is the true Israel doing what the nation could not do for itself. Verse 4 adds something the first song did not: this servant experiences the work as failure from the inside, and holds on by entrusting the verdict to God rather than by seeing results.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul and Barnabas, turned out of a synagogue, quote verse 6 as their own marching orders — I have made you a light for the Gentiles (Acts 13:47) — which is a striking use of a verse about the servant. What was said to Christ is applied to the church sent out in his name. And verse 4 has kept more discouraged ministers, parents and missionaries at their posts than almost any other sentence in the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar. The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name. He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar."

The servant speaks for himself for the first time, and notice who he is speaking to. Not Jerusalem. The coastlands and distant peoples — the far edge of the map, the places that had never heard of the covenant. The second song is addressed outward from its opening word, before it has said anything at all about what the servant is for.

"The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name."

His vocation is older than he is. Jeremiah was told the same (Jer. 1:5), and Paul said it of himself (Gal. 1:15), and both of them were echoing a pattern that belongs most exactly to one man — the only one whose name was announced by an angel to his mother before he was conceived (Luke 1:31).

"He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away."

Two weapons, and both of them are the mouth. The word is the sword and the word is the arrow; nothing here is metal. The New Testament keeps the image exactly — the word of God living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb. 4:12), and a risen Christ with a sharp two-edged sword coming out of his mouth (Rev. 1:16).

But the striking thing is that both weapons are described as hidden. A sword in the shadow of a hand, an arrow shut in a quiver. Isaiah spends half the verse on concealment, and the concealment is not failure — it is what you do with a weapon you intend to use. A polished arrow is polished in the dark, and then it is kept in the dark until the moment it is wanted.

Which is the honest description of nearly every life God is preparing for something. Thirty years in a carpenter's shop is the shadow of the hand. Nobody watching would have called it preparation; from the inside it does not feel like being sharpened, it feels like being shelved. It was neither.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And he said to me, 'You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified.'"

God names the servant, and the name he gives him is the name of the nation.

Hold that beside verse 5, two sentences later, where the same servant is formed in the womb "to bring Jacob back to him, and that Israel might be gathered to him." He is called Israel, and he is sent to Israel. He cannot simply be the nation, because he has a mission to the nation. And he cannot simply be a private individual either, because God has given him the nation's own name.

The resolution is the one the whole book has been moving toward. Israel was called to be God's son, God's servant, God's light; Israel failed at all three, as chapter 42 said with painful directness. So one comes who is everything Israel was supposed to be — carrying the name, doing the work, succeeding at the calling — and then does for Israel what Israel could not do for itself.

Everything the New Testament says about being in Christ stands on this verse. A believer is not saved by becoming a better Israelite. He is saved by being joined to the one who wears the name and kept the covenant, so that what is true of him becomes true of those attached to him. Isaiah 49:3 is where the grammar of that begins.

"In whom I will be glorified." The purpose is not first the rescue. It is the glory of God displayed in a person, and the rescue is how the display happens.

verseByVerse.quote: But I said, "I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But I said, 'I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity.'"

This is the servant speaking, and it is one of the most unexpected sentences in the Old Testament. Not the nation complaining, not the prophet despairing — the chosen servant, in the middle of his own song, saying that the work has come to nothing.

Read what he actually claims. Not that the work was hard. Not that it took longer than he hoped. In vain. For nothing. Vanity — the word is the one Ecclesiastes uses for vapour, breath, the thing that will not stay in your hand. He has spent his strength, all of it, and there is nothing to show.

Anyone who has taught the same child the same thing for eleven years, or prayed for a marriage that got worse, or preached faithfully in a place that emptied, knows the temperature of that sentence. What it is not is unbelief. It is the honest report of a faithful worker's eyes.

"Yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God."

And there is the turn, and it is the whole art of persevering. He does not talk himself out of the assessment. He does not find a hidden fruitfulness to console himself with. He moves the verdict to a different court. My right — my case, my vindication — is with the LORD: it is not lying about unresolved, it is lodged somewhere, held by somebody, and it will be given.

Which is what makes the next two verses so extraordinary. A man says his life's work has failed, and God's answer is not to reassure him that it has not.

verseByVerse.quote: And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him; and that Israel might be gathered to him— for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength— he says: "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him, and that Israel might be gathered to him — for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength."

Before the commission is enlarged, the servant is told what he already is. I am honoured in the eyes of the LORD. The man who has just said he laboured for nothing is told that in the only eyes that assess anything he is honoured — which is not a contradiction of his experience but a correction of the court he had been reporting to.

"He says: 'It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.'"

Consider what God does not say. He does not say the labour was fruitful after all. He does not explain the apparent failure or offer evidence that it went better than it looked. He says the job is too small.

Restoring an entire nation from exile — the thing the servant has been pouring his strength into and believes he has failed at — is described as too light a thing, a load not worth the strength of the man carrying it. So it is doubled. Not Israel: the nations. Not the return: salvation to the end of the earth.

That is God's characteristic answer to the sense of futility, and it should be remembered by anyone who is ready to give something up. He rarely responds by shrinking the assignment to fit our discouragement. Paul and Barnabas, thrown out of the synagogue at Antioch, took this verse as theirs and turned to the Gentiles with it in their mouths (Acts 13:47) — which is what a rejection looked like when God got hold of it.

And the reach of the promise is total. Not many nations. Not most. The end of the earth, which in a book written for a small people pinned between empires is the most implausible sentence available, and which has since been fulfilled in front of everybody for two thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers: "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers."

Three descriptions, and each is worse than the last. Deeply despised — the Hebrew is a despising of the whole soul, contempt without qualification. Abhorred by the nation — not by foreigners but by his own people. The servant of rulers — a man with no standing, at the disposal of whoever holds power.

Every one of the three landed. He came to his own and his own people did not receive him. He was handed between a Sanhedrin, a governor and a tetrarch in the space of one morning, each of them free to do as they liked with him.

"Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves."

And there is the reversal, in the same sentence as the contempt. The men before whom he stood as a prisoner will stand up when he comes into the room, and then go down on their faces. Note the sequence: they see, and then they rise. Nothing has to be argued to them. What overturns their judgment is the sight of him.

"Because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you." The grounds of the reversal are stated and they are not in the servant. It is not that he earns his way back up, or that public opinion eventually comes round. It is that God is faithful and God chose him, and those two facts will finish what they started regardless of how the middle of the story looks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Day of Salvation and the Road Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the servant with a timetable and a task. Verse 8 sets a time of favour and a day of salvation, and makes the servant a covenant to the people. Verses 9 to 11 have him saying two words to prisoners — come out — and then shepherding them home along roads made out of mountains, with no hunger, no thirst, and nothing scorching them on the way. Verse 12 gathers them from every direction of the compass. Verse 13 calls on the heavens and the earth and the mountains to sing about it.
verseByVerse.theology: The comfort here is covenantal rather than circumstantial: it rests on an appointed day that God has fixed, not on an improvement in conditions. Paul takes verse 8 and applies it to the present moment of gospel opportunity — behold, now is the favourable time, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2) — reading the servant's appointed day as having arrived.
verseByVerse.examples: The promises of verses 9 and 10 turn up almost word for word at the end of the Bible, said of a multitude nobody could number: they shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more, the sun shall not strike them, and the Lamb will be their shepherd and guide them to springs of living water (Rev. 7:16-17). The road home in Isaiah 49 and the arrival in Revelation 7 are the same journey.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you; I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages, saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.' They shall feed along the ways; on all bare heights shall be their pasture;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD: 'In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you.'"

The servant said his right was with the LORD and left it there. Here is the answer, and it comes with a time attached — a set moment, chosen by God, when the case is taken up. Not if, and not eventually. In a time of favour I have answered you, spoken in the past tense over something not yet visible.

Paul takes this verse and does something remarkable with it. Quoting it to the Corinthians, he adds: "Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor. 6:2). The appointed day the servant was told to wait for has, in Paul's reading, arrived — and the window it opened is the one his readers are standing in while he writes.

"I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages."

The title from the first song comes back: he does not deliver the covenant, he is it (42:6). And the work attached to it is oddly practical — establishing land, parcelling out ruined inheritances, the business of a surveyor after a war. Salvation in Isaiah is never purely interior. It ends with people back on their own ground.

"Saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.'"

Two words to each group, and no procedure attached to either. No ransom named at the door, no conditions read out, no interview. The prison is opened by an imperative. It is the same voice that would one day stand outside a tomb in Bethany and use three words, and the same authority that makes the gospel an announcement rather than an offer of terms.

verseByVerse.quote: they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them. And I will make all my mountains a road, and my highways shall be raised up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them."

The prisoners are out, and now they have to get home, and the road runs through desert. Isaiah names the four things that kill people on that journey — hunger, thirst, the desert wind, the sun — and rules out all four.

The reason given is not that the route is easy. It is a person: he who has pity on them will lead them. The word is the one for a mother's compassion, the deep physical tenderness that has its root in the womb. What gets them across the desert is not provisioning but the character of the one walking in front.

Turn to the last book of the Bible and this promise is there almost word for word, said of a crowd out of every nation that nobody could number: "They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water" (Rev. 7:16-17). John is not borrowing a nice phrase. He is reporting the arrival of this journey.

"And I will make all my mountains a road, and my highways shall be raised up."

The obstacles are not gone round. They are turned into the road. What stood in the way becomes the way — which is not a general principle about adversity, but it is exactly what God did with the worst thing that ever happened, and anyone who has looked back at a hard year and found it was the road has met this verse from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Syene." Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Syene."

Three times behold, as though the prophet were standing on a rise pointing at different horizons as the columns appear. From far away. From the north and the west. And from Syene, which is Aswan, the southern frontier of Egypt — the far end of the known world in that direction.

What is being described is bigger than the return from Babylon, and Isaiah has made it too big on purpose. Exiles came home from one direction. This is a homecoming from every direction there is, which is how the New Testament will describe the final gathering: people from east and west and north and south, sitting down at table in the kingdom of God (Luke 13:29).

"Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his afflicted."

The command goes out to the whole creation, which is what Isaiah does when the subject is too large for human voices: the sky, the ground, and the hills are told to make the noise. And the reason given for the singing is not the scale of the rescue or the defeat of the enemy. It is one word — comforted — and one more: he will have compassion on his afflicted.

The universe is called to sing because God has been tender with hurt people. That is the announcement the mountains are told to carry, and it tells you a great deal about the God being sung to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–26 — The Mother Who Cannot Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zion interrupts the singing to say that the LORD has forsaken her and forgotten her, and God does not rebuke the complaint — he answers it. Verse 15 measures his commitment against the strongest natural bond there is and goes past it. Verse 16 gives the answer a body: her name is cut into his palms. Verses 17 to 21 have the builders outstripping the destroyers and a bereaved woman bewildered by the number of her children. Verses 22 and 23 turn the nations from captors into couriers. Verses 24 to 26 answer the last objection — that prey cannot be taken back from the strong — with a flat promise that it will be.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology of this passage is that God's faithfulness is not a disposition but a commitment with a cost attached, and verse 16 says so in the most physical terms available: engraved, not written. What is cut into a hand cannot be removed from it without injury. Zion's fear is not answered by an argument that she is lovable; it is answered by a mark on God.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 is one of the places Scripture reaches for a mother rather than a father to say what God is like, and it does so at the exact point where the reader most needs it. And the palms of verse 16 acquired a further meaning on a Friday outside Jerusalem: the hands that carry the names of God's people are hands that can be shown, with the marks still in them, to a man who needed to touch them before he could believe.

verseByVerse.quote: But Zion said, "The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But Zion said, 'The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me.'"

The heavens have just been told to sing. The earth has been told to exult. The mountains have been told to break forth. And in the very next sentence, one voice cuts straight across all of it and says that God has gone.

Isaiah has placed that deliberately, and the placement is a kindness. It is one of the most accurate things in Scripture about how faith actually works. It is entirely possible to know that God is good, to be surrounded by people singing that he is good, to have the sky and the mountains agreeing that he is good, and to be unable to feel that any of it applies to you. The doxology and the desolation are in adjacent verses because in real lives they are in adjacent minutes.

Read the two verbs. Forsaken — he has left. Forgotten — worse, he did not leave on purpose, I simply went out of his mind. The second is the one that does the real damage, because it does not even grant her the dignity of being rejected.

And now watch what God does not do. He does not rebuke her. He does not correct her theology, though her theology is wrong. He does not point out that he has just spent thirteen verses promising the exact opposite, though he has. There is not a word of reproach anywhere in the answer that follows.

God takes the complaint seriously enough to answer it, which is the first thing anybody in that condition needs to know about him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb?"

The answer to feeling forgotten is a question about a mother, and God picks the strongest attachment in human experience to make his comparison with. Not a mother and a grown son. A nursing mother and the infant at her breast — a bond that is not only emotional but physical, where the woman's own body will remind her if she forgets, and where the child's survival depends hour by hour on her attention.

The expected answer is no. And God does not give the expected answer.

"Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you."

He concedes the point. Sometimes she does forget — through illness, through poverty, through the collapse of a mind, through the thousand ways human beings fail at the things they would die for. The strongest natural love available is not unbreakable, and God says so plainly rather than building his comfort on a sentimental picture of motherhood that would fall apart the moment somebody's own mother came to mind.

He takes the highest human love, grants that it can fail, and puts himself past it. That is the whole argument, and it is stronger for the concession than it would have been without it.

And note where God is willing to be found in this image. He does not reach for a king, a general or a judge to say what his commitment is like. He reaches for a woman feeding a baby, and then says he is more constant than she is.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me."

Zion said she had been forgotten. God's final answer is not an argument. It is a gesture — he holds out his hands.

The verb is not written. It is engraved, cut in, incised. Writing can be washed off a hand at the end of a day; the whole point of the image is a mark made by a blade in flesh, which does not come off because the hand has been altered to carry it. God has done something permanent to himself in order to make forgetting impossible.

And the location is not accidental. Not on a wall in heaven, not in a book, not on a list. On the palms — the working surface, the part of a hand that is used. Every act of God in history is performed by hands with his people's names cut into them. He cannot lift a finger without the names moving.

"Your walls are continually before me." She is looking at rubble; God says her walls are permanently in his sight. He is not looking at the ruin. He is looking at the finished city, and has been all along.

Seven hundred years later a man will stand in a locked room and hold out his hands to somebody who cannot believe he is there, and the marks in them will be the argument that settles it. The palms of Isaiah 49 turned out to be more literal than anyone reading them in exile could have guessed. He has our names cut into his hands, and he did not get them in a workshop.

verseByVerse.quote: Your builders make haste; your destroyers and those who laid you waste go out from you. Lift up your eyes around and see; they all gather, they come to you. As I live, declares the LORD, you shall put them all on as an ornament; you shall bind them on as a bride does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Your builders make haste; your destroyers and those who laid you waste go out from you."

The two crews pass each other in the gate. One is going out, the other is hurrying in, and Isaiah puts them in a single line so that the reader sees the exchange happen. The demolition men are still leaving as the masons arrive.

What she is looking at is a ruin, and what he describes is a building site. That is not optimism about the rubble; it is a different point in time being reported as though it were present, which is how prophets talk when the thing is certain.

"Lift up your eyes around and see; they all gather, they come to you. As I live, declares the LORD, you shall put them all on as an ornament; you shall bind them on as a bride does."

First the instruction: lift up your eyes. Zion has been looking down, at the stones and at herself. She is told to look at the horizon, where people are already coming.

Then the oath. As I live — God swearing by his own existence, the strongest undertaking available to him, since there is nothing greater to swear by. The pledge that her children are coming home is secured on the fact that God is alive.

And the image at the end is unexpectedly warm. The returning exiles are not counted as a population or a workforce. They are jewellery — put on the way a bride puts on her ornaments on the morning of a wedding, for no reason except delight. The woman who thought she was forgotten is being dressed.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely your waste and your desolate places and your devastated land— surely now you will be too narrow for your inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up will be far away. The children of your bereavement will yet say in your ears: 'The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell in.' Then you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? I was bereaved and barren, exiled and put away, but who has brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; from where have these come?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Surely your waste and your desolate places and your devastated land — surely now you will be too narrow for your inhabitants."

The reversal is pressed until it becomes funny. The city's complaint has been emptiness; its complaint will be overcrowding. The bereaved children of verse 20 will say in her hearing, "The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell in" — the sound of a household outgrowing its house.

"Then you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? I was bereaved and barren, exiled and put away, but who has brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; from where have these come?'"

This is the best sentence in the chapter, and it is the sound of grace arriving in a quantity nobody asked for. She is not grateful yet; she is bewildered. She counts the children and cannot make the arithmetic work, because she knows exactly what she had — nothing — and here is a crowd calling her mother.

Four words describe her former state and they should be read slowly: bereaved, barren, exiled, put away. She had lost children, could have no more, was removed from her land, and had been divorced. There was no route from that condition to this one, and she is right that there was not. That is why the question is the correct response.

Anyone who has been given more than his life had any capacity to produce will recognise the feeling. The right reaction to grace, at the start, is not thankfulness. It is arithmetic that does not work.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and raise my signal to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders. Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. With their faces to the ground they shall bow down to you, and lick the dust of your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who wait for me shall not be put to shame."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and raise my signal to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders."

The answer to from where have these come? is that the nations are bringing them. The empires that carried Israel away are going to carry Israel's children back, and the detail is domestic rather than political: sons held in the arms, daughters up on the shoulders, the way an adult carries a tired child who cannot walk the last mile.

"Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers."

The reversal is complete. The powers that treated her as a resource become her household staff — and not distant patrons either, but foster fathers and wet nurses, the people who get up in the night. Isaiah keeps choosing images of physical care rather than of political triumph, and the choice is the meaning.

"With their faces to the ground they shall bow down to you, and lick the dust of your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who wait for me shall not be put to shame."

And there is the line to hold. Those who wait for me shall not be put to shame. The waiting is the thing Zion has been doing badly and complaining about, and God does not promise that it will be short. He promises what it will not end in.

Shame is the specific fear of everyone who has staked a life on God and watched nothing happen — not that God will punish them, but that they will look foolish, that the whole thing will turn out to have been a misplaced confidence held in public. That is the fear this sentence closes. Nobody who waited will be embarrassed at the end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued? For thus says the LORD: "Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued, for I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children. I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with wine. Then all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued?"

Zion raises the last objection, and it is the practical one. Everything promised has assumed that the people can be got back. But prey is not returned by predators, and tyrants do not release the men they hold; that is what the words mean. Anyone who has ever watched an addiction, or a regime, or a death, hold onto somebody has asked this question in exactly this form.

"Surely, thus says the LORD: 'Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued, for I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children.'"

God does not soften the question. He agrees that nobody takes prey from the strong, and then says that this is precisely what he will do — and, crucially, that he will do it in person. I will contend with those who contend with you. Not send help. Not raise up a deliverer. He steps into the dispute himself and makes his people's opponents his own.

Verse 26 describes the outcome in language that is deliberately hard to read — the oppressors made to eat their own flesh and drink their own blood as with wine. It is the Old Testament's way of saying that violence turns back on the violent; the machinery they built to consume other people finishes by consuming them.

"Then all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob."

The chapter began with a servant who thought he had laboured for nothing and it ends with all flesh knowing who God is. Between those two points nothing changed except that God kept going. He is the Redeemer, the near kinsman with the right to buy his relatives out of slavery, and the Mighty One of Jacob, which is the title Jacob himself used after a night of wrestling — and the hands that pay the price have the names cut into them.

49.theology:
The servant who is Israel and is sent to Israel. Verse 3 calls him Israel; verse 5 sends him to bring Jacob back. He therefore cannot simply be the nation, and cannot simply be a private individual carrying his own name. He is the true Israel — wearing the name, keeping the covenant, and doing for the nation what the nation could not do for itself. Everything the New Testament means by being in Christ rests on that structure: a believer is not saved by becoming a better Israelite but by being joined to the one who kept it all.

Futility answered by enlargement. The servant’s confession in verse 4 is not unbelief but an honest report, and his recovery is not a re-assessment of the evidence — he moves the verdict to another court: my right is with the LORD. God’s reply neither disputes the assessment nor shrinks the assignment. It doubles it. This is the standing pattern of God’s dealing with discouraged servants, and Paul and Barnabas read it that way when a synagogue expelled them (Acts 13:47).

Assurance with a body. Zion’s fear in verse 14 is answered in three movements: a comparison she can feel (v. 15), a mark she can look at (v. 16), and a promise about waiting (v. 23 — those who wait for me shall not be put to shame). The middle one is the ground of the other two. Engraved, not written: God has altered his own hands so that forgetting is not available to him, and the palms of this verse were shown to a doubting disciple with the marks still in them.

54.subtitle: Sing, O Barren One
54.intro: Overview. Chapter 54 is the song of the covenant renewed after the Servant’s work in chapter 53. The barren woman who is called to sing is Israel, and the grounds for the singing are the husband’s return. God was angry for a moment but will have everlasting love. The chapter closes with a promise that no weapon formed against God’s people shall prosper — not because they are invincible but because God is their champion.

sections.title: The Barren Woman Sings
sections.commentary:
Sing, O barren one, who did not bear; break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not been in labor! Paul quotes verse 1 in Galatians 4:27, applying it to the new covenant community — the children of the free woman, born not through natural descent but through promise. Enlarge your tent; lengthen your cords; strengthen your stakes. You will spread abroad to the right and to the left.

vv. 7–8 — “For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you. In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you.” The proportion is startling: a brief moment of anger against everlasting love. The exile felt like eternity; God sees it as a moment. The everlasting love is not the same quantity as the anger; it is categorically different in kind and duration.

The covenant of peace — berith shalom — will not be removed. As God swore to Noah that the waters would never again cover the earth, so he swears that his steadfast love will not depart from his people. The Noah comparison is deliberate: this is a covenant with creation-level permanence.

sections.title: The City of Righteousness
sections.commentary:
O afflicted city, storm-tossed and not comforted: I will set your stones in antimony, your foundations in sapphires, your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles. All your children will be taught by the LORD, and great will be their peace. This is the city of chapter 35 and the new Jerusalem of Revelation 21 — the same precious stones, the same divine instruction, the same peace.

And the climax: “No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD and their vindication from me.” The promise is specific: not that no weapons will be fashioned — they will be — but that none will succeed. God guarantees the outcome without removing the conflict.

keyVerse.quote: “For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed, says the LORD, who has compassion on you.”
keyVerse.note: The geological stability of mountains is the benchmark for everything we consider permanent — and God places his love above it. Mountains will move before his love departs. This is the answer to chapter 39’s shadow and every experience of divine absence: the absence was a moment; the love is permanent.

54.reflection: God describes the exile as a “brief moment” of anger against which he sets “everlasting love.” What season of God’s apparent absence are you in or have you been in? What would it mean to let God re-proportion your experience — to see the moment in the light of the everlasting, rather than letting the moment obscure the everlasting?

For the children of the desolate one will be more than the children of her who is married," says the LORD.<sup>2</sup>"Enlarge the place of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes.<sup>3</sup>For you will spread abroad to the right and to the left, and your offspring will possess the nations and will people the desolate cities.<sup>4</sup>"Fear not, for you will not be ashamed; This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD and their vindication from me, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Sing, Barren Woman: the Everlasting Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Following the servant's atoning work, the barren woman (Zion) is called to sing, for she will have more children than the married woman. The husband who seemed to abandon her returns with everlasting love and great compassion. The covenant of peace is as sure as the covenant with Noah. God will build Jerusalem with precious stones, and no weapon formed against her will prosper.
verseByVerse.theology: Grace through the servant's work: ch54 flows directly from the servant's sacrifice in ch53. The barren woman who is suddenly fruitful, the forsaken wife who is reclaimed — these are pictures of the community that benefits from the servant's atoning death. Paul quotes v.1 in Galatians 4:27 as describing the freedom of the gospel over against the bondage of the law: the barren (Gentile) church has more children than the established synagogue.
verseByVerse.examples: The everlasting covenant of peace (v.10) is one of Isaiah's terms for the new covenant (also 55:3; 61:8). Unlike the Mosaic covenant which could be broken (Jer 31:32), this covenant of peace will never be removed. It rests on God's love and compassion, not human faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing, O barren one, who did not bear; break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not been in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than the children of her who is married, says the LORD. Enlarge the place of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The barren woman — Zion in exile, desolate and childless — is commanded to sing before the children arrive. Faith anticipates the gift. Enlarge the tent — expect overflow, not merely a modest restoration. Sarah was the original barren woman (51:2); Zion now receives the same promise in an expanded key. Paul quotes v.1 in Gal 4:27 to show that the barren church (Gentiles, outside the covenant) is becoming more populous than the established covenant community. Motyer: the command to enlarge before seeing the children is the posture of faith — acting on the promise before the evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: For you will spread abroad to the right and to the left, and your offspring will possess the nations and will people the desolate cities. Fear not, for you will not be ashamed; be not confounded, for you will not be disgraced; for you will forget the shame of your youth, and the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The expansion is geographic and missiological: left, right, possessing nations, repopulating desolate cities. The community formed by the servant's work is inherently outward-moving. Shame and disgrace — the marks of the exile — will be forgotten: the shame of Egypt (Israel's youth), the disgrace of Babylon (the widowhood). Oswalt: the complete forgetting of shame is one of the most distinctive promises of Isaiah. God does not merely reduce shame; he eliminates its power over the community's identity. New identity in redemption requires the release of old shame.

verseByVerse.quote: For your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name; and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer, the God of the whole earth he is called. For the LORD has called you like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit, like a wife of youth when she is cast off, says your God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Your Maker is your husband — the intimacy of the Creator-Redeemer relationship expressed in marital language. The God of the whole earth stoops to be the husband of a deserted, grieving community. Wife of youth when she is cast off — the most vulnerable, most painful marital situation. This is the condition God addresses: not the proud or the established but the abandoned. Young: the marriage metaphor throughout Isaiah (and Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea) grounds the covenant relationship in the most intimate human bond, showing that God's commitment is relational, not merely contractual.

verseByVerse.quote: For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you. In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you, says the LORD, your Redeemer. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The exile is placed in perspective: a brief moment of desertion, a moment of overflowing anger. But the other side is disproportionate: great compassion, everlasting love. The contrast of brief versus everlasting is the key. Oswalt: God is not equating his anger and his love as equal forces; the anger was momentary, the love is eternal. The exile reveals the temporary consequence of sin; the return reveals the permanent priority of grace. Paul's logic in Romans 8:18 is parallel: present suffering is not worth comparing to coming glory.

verseByVerse.quote: This is like the days of Noah to me: as I swore that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so I have sworn that I will not be angry with you and will not rebuke you. For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed, says the LORD, who has compassion on you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant of peace is as permanent as the Noahic covenant. The rainbow promise — no more flood — stands as the analogy: just as certain as God's promise to Noah (which has held for all of human history) is his promise to never again be angry with his people. Mountains may depart and hills be removed — geological catastrophe — but the steadfast love (hesed) will not depart. The new covenant is unconditional and eternal: not based on Israel's faithfulness but God's character. Childs: the everlasting covenant of peace is the new covenant in Jeremiah 31:31-34, grounded in the servant's atoning work.

verseByVerse.quote: O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted, behold, I will set your stones in antimony, and lay your foundations with sapphires. I will make your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles, and all your wall of precious stones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The storm-tossed, uncomforted city will be rebuilt in precious stones — antimony, sapphires, agate, carbuncles. This is the New Jerusalem vision that Revelation 21:18-21 develops explicitly, with its twelve foundations adorned with every jewel. The desolate exile who had rubble for walls receives gem-studded walls instead. Motyer: the architectural extravagance is not literal urban planning but the language of incomparable beauty — the restored community will be visibly, unmistakably glorious. What was shamed will be splendid.

verseByVerse.quote: All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children. In righteousness you shall be established; you shall be far from oppression, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: All your children shall be taught by the LORD — the new covenant community will be characterized by direct divine instruction (Jer 31:34: they shall all know me). Jesus quotes this in John 6:45 as evidence that those who come to him are the fulfillment of this promise: everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. The stability of this community — established in righteousness, far from oppression, free from terror — is the social expression of the servant's atoning work. Young: peace is the fruit of righteousness (32:17), which is the fruit of the servant's suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone stirs up strife, it is not from me; whoever stirs up strife with you shall fall because of you. Behold, I have created the smith who blows the fire of coals and produces a weapon for its purpose. I have also created the ravager to destroy; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God asserts sovereignty even over the makers of weapons and the agents of destruction. The smith who forges weapons exists within God's creative order. The ravager is not an independent power; God created him. This is not divine approval of destruction but assertion of divine control over it: what appears to be random violence or organized oppression is within the scope of God's sovereign ordering. Oswalt: the assurance to Zion is grounded not in the absence of threats but in the truth that no threat originates outside God's awareness and control.

verseByVerse.quote: no weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD and their vindication from me, declares the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: No weapon formed against you shall succeed — the covenant protection of the servant's community is total. This is not a promise of the absence of attack but of the failure of every attack. The tongue that rises in accusation will be refuted. Then the glorious designation: the servants of the LORD — plural, the community formed by the servant's work. Their vindication comes not from their own strength but from God. Motyer: the heritage of the servants is the inheritance won by the one Servant — what he purchased, they receive as their permanent possession.

55.subtitle: Come, Everyone Who Thirsts
55.intro:
Overview. Chapter 55 closes the central movement of the book (chs. 40-55) with an open invitation, and it opens at a market stall. Everyone who is thirsty is called, and so is everyone with no money — and then comes the sentence that should not work: he who has no money, come, buy. Water, milk and wine are on offer at no price, which means the only people who go without are those who insist on paying. What is handed to that penniless crowd turns out to be a covenant, and not a new one: the sure mercies promised to David.

The middle of the chapter puts a horizon on the offer — seek him while he may be found — and promises a pardon the Hebrew describes as multiplied, then defends that promise with the famous verses about God’s thoughts being higher than ours. Those verses are about forgiveness, not about the mysteries of providence. The chapter ends with rain that never goes back up unused, a word that always completes its errand, and a landscape in which the thorns of Genesis 3 have been replaced by cypress and myrtle.

keyVerse.quote: “So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.”
keyVerse.note: This is Isaiah’s doctrine of the word: it is not contingent on human reception. It goes, it works, it returns with the harvest of its purpose. The whole of chapters 40–55 has been one extended word-act — comfort, promise, prediction, invitation — and this verse stands at the end of it as the guarantee of everything that was spoken.

55.reflection: God asks: why do you spend your money for what is not bread? This is one of the most diagnostic questions in Scripture. What are you currently investing time, money, or emotional energy in that does not satisfy — while the free feast sits unattended? What would it actually cost you to “come to the waters” today?
55.text: <sup>1</sup>"Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.<sup>2</sup>Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food.<sup>3</sup>Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live; and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David.<sup>4</sup>Behold, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples.<sup>5</sup>Behold, you shall call a nation that you do not know, and a nation that did not know you shall run to you, because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you.<sup>6</sup>"Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near;<sup>7</sup>let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.<sup>8</sup>For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD.<sup>9</sup>For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts.<sup>10</sup>"For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater,<sup>11</sup>so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.<sup>12</sup>"For you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and the hills before you shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.<sup>13</sup>Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle; and it shall make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Come and Buy Without Money
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens at a market stall with a vendor shouting. Verse 1 calls everyone who is thirsty and everyone with no money, and offers water, wine and milk at no price. Verse 2 asks the diagnostic question — why spend money on what is not bread and labour on what does not satisfy? Verse 3 turns the invitation into a covenant, and an everlasting one, made of the steadfast love promised to David. Verse 4 recalls what David was given to be, and verse 5 hands the same role to the people: nations they have never heard of will come running.
verseByVerse.theology: The paradox in verse 1 is deliberate — buy, and without money — and it is the exact shape of grace. The transaction is real, so something is genuinely received; the price is nil, so nothing is contributed. The only people who go without at this stall are those who insist on paying. And verse 3 makes the offer covenantal rather than casual: what is being handed to ordinary thirsty people is the sure mercies promised to David.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul quotes verse 3 in a synagogue at Antioch and applies the sure mercies of David to the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 13:34) — the promises made to a king are kept in a risen one. And verse 2 is a question worth putting to a diary and a bank statement rather than only to a conscience: what is currently being paid for that has never once satisfied?

verseByVerse.quote: "Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price."

The scene is a market, and the voice is a stallholder's. The Hebrew opens with hoy — the same syllable that began the six woes of chapter 5, now used as a street trader's shout to get attention. Ho, over here.

Read who is being called. Everyone who is thirsty. And everyone who has no money. Those are the only two qualifications, and the second one is a disqualification everywhere else in the world. In every actual market, the man with nothing in his purse is the one who walks past.

And then the sentence that should not work: he who has no money, come, buy. Buy with what? Isaiah keeps the commercial verb and removes the price, and the contradiction is the point. Something is genuinely transacted here — a person really receives goods and walks away with them — and nothing whatever is contributed. Which means the only people who go hungry at this stall are the ones who insist on paying.

Three things are on offer, and together they cover a life. Water, without which you die. Milk, the staple that feeds and builds. And wine, which nobody needs and which exists for gladness. God does not stock the stall with bare necessities. He puts the celebration out where the survival rations are.

"Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?"

Now the question, and it is diagnostic rather than rhetorical. Not why do you sin. Why do you keep paying for things that have never once fed you? God's description of a wasted life is not primarily wickedness; it is bad economics — real money, real effort, spent on what has a proven record of not working.

The honest way to take that question is not to reach for a general answer. Look at where last month's money actually went, and at what the hours after work were actually spent on, and ask of each item whether it delivered what it promised. Most people already know. The tragedy in verse 2 is not ignorance about what satisfies. It is going back to the same stall.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live; and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David. Behold, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live."

Three imperatives and they are all about listening. Tilt the head. Come. Hear. And the result attached to hearing is not information or improvement but life — hear, that your soul may live. In this chapter the ear is the organ of survival, which is what Paul means when he says faith comes by hearing (Rom. 10:17).

"And I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David."

The invitation has just changed character. What began as a free meal turns out to be a covenant, and not a new one — the covenant made with David, the promise of a throne and a son and a kingdom that would not end.

Consider who is being offered it. Not a king. Not a dynasty. The thirsty, penniless crowd at the stall in verse 1. The promises that once ran to one royal family are being handed out to anyone who will come and eat, and the word attached to them is sure — the covenant version of the word for what is reliable, faithful, the root behind amen.

Paul stood up in a synagogue at Antioch and quoted this line to explain the empty tomb. God raised Jesus from the dead, he said, and this is what was meant by "I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David" (Acts 13:34). The sure mercies could not be kept in a man who stayed dead; they are kept in a son of David who did not.

"Behold, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples." And that is what David was for — not a private blessing but a public exhibit, a man through whom the nations were meant to learn something about God. The role is about to be handed over in the very next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you shall call a nation that you do not know, and a nation that did not know you shall run to you, because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, you shall call a nation that you do not know, and a nation that did not know you shall run to you, because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you."

What David was in verse 4, the people become in verse 5. The witness to the peoples is now a whole community, and the traffic runs both ways: they will call nations they have never heard of, and nations who have never heard of them will come running.

Notice the verb. Not walk, not consider, not be persuaded. Run. Isaiah keeps using it for the nations in this book — streaming uphill to the mountain of the LORD in chapter 2, coming with their gifts in chapter 60 — and it always has the same energy in it. Nobody is being dragged.

And the reason is given twice over, so that no one mistakes what the attraction is: because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you. They are not running toward Israel's culture or its record or its virtue. They are running because something has visibly happened to these people, and the something has a name.

That is the honest shape of Christian witness, and it removes a great deal of anxiety about technique. The community is not asked to be impressive. It is asked to be a people to whom God has plainly done something, and the running starts when that becomes visible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Seek Him While He May Be Found
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verse 6 puts a horizon on the invitation: seek him while he may be found, call while he is near. Verse 7 says what returning involves — forsaking a way and forsaking thoughts — and promises a pardon that the Hebrew describes as multiplied. Verses 8 and 9 ground that promise in the distance between God's thoughts and ours, measured as the height of the sky over the ground. Verses 10 and 11 close the movement with rain and snow that do not go back up until they have done their work, and a word that behaves the same way.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 8 and 9 are constantly quoted about the mysteries of providence, and that is not what they are doing here. The subject of the paragraph is forgiveness: God will abundantly pardon, and the reason given is that his thoughts are not ours. What is being said is that our arithmetic about what can be forgiven, and at what cost, and how many times, is earthbound — and his is not.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 11 is the promise every discouraged teacher, parent and preacher needs and the one most often misread as a guarantee of visible results. What is promised is that the word accomplishes what God purposed by it, which is not always what we purposed by it. Rain does not negotiate its effectiveness, and it does not always fall where the farmer was looking.

verseByVerse.quote: "Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near; let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near."

Two little words hold the urgency of the whole chapter: while, and while. The invitation of verse 1 is free, unlimited in scope, and open to anybody — and it has a horizon. Isaiah does not say when the window closes and gives no way of calculating it, which is exactly what makes delay a bad bet rather than a manageable risk.

Notice too what is assumed: right now he may be found, and right now he is near. The verse is not principally a threat. It is the announcement that the door is currently open, said by someone who can see the door.

"Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon."

Two things are to be forsaken and the second is the harder. The way is what a man does, and it can be changed by a decision. The thoughts are what he privately believes about the whole arrangement — what he thinks he can get away with, what he thinks he is owed, what he thinks God is like. Repentance in this verse goes past behaviour into the reasoning that produced it.

And then the promise, which in Hebrew is more extravagant than the English shows: he will multiply to pardon. Not pardon reluctantly, not pardon within limits. Pardon, and pardon, and go on pardoning past the point where any accountant would have closed the account.

Everything in the next two verses exists to defend that clause against the reader's instinct to disbelieve it.

verseByVerse.quote: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts."

These are two of the best-known verses in the Old Testament and they are very often used for something they are not doing here. They are usually quoted to a person in bewildering trouble, to say that God's providence is beyond our understanding. That is true, and Scripture teaches it elsewhere, and it is not what this paragraph is about.

Look at the word that opens verse 8: for. It is attached to what has just been said, and what has just been said is that God will abundantly pardon. The subject of these verses is not suffering. It is forgiveness.

So read them in their own context and they say something far more useful. Your thoughts about pardon are not God's thoughts about pardon. Your calculation of what can be forgiven, and how often, and after how long, and at what cost, and whether a person who has done that can really be received — every one of those calculations is being made at ground level, and his are made at the height of the sky.
