Which turns the verse from a rebuke into a rescue. The reason a returning sinner cannot believe the offer is that he has correctly assessed the case using human arithmetic. He knows what he did. He knows what he would think of somebody else who did it. Isaiah's answer is not that the offence is smaller than he thinks. It is that the mercy is running on a completely different scale, and his ceiling is not God's floor.

The gap between heaven and earth is not first a measure of how much God knows that we do not. In this passage it is a measure of how much more willing he is to forgive than we would ever be.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth."

The picture is a complete circuit. Water leaves the sky, falls, soaks in, and does not go back up as it came — it goes back up having been through a wheat field. The rain returns as evaporation only after it has become a crop, and the crop becomes seed for next year and bread on a table this year. Nothing is wasted and nothing comes back unchanged.

"It shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it."

God's word is described as that kind of rain. It is not information issued in the hope of a response; it is an agent with an assignment, and the assignment is completed. That is the guarantee standing under the whole of chapters 40 to 55 — every promise of comfort, every announcement about the servant, every invitation in this chapter — and it is why Isaiah can speak of a future restoration in the past tense.

But read the promise precisely, because it is frequently misused. It does not say the word accomplishes what we purposed by it. It says it accomplishes what God purposed by it. A parent who has said true things to a son for fifteen years and seen nothing is not holding a failed promise; he is holding rain that has gone into ground he cannot see into, on a schedule that was never shown to him.

Rain does not ask permission and does not negotiate its effectiveness. It also does not always fall where the farmer happened to be standing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–13 — Out in Joy, and the Thorns Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last two verses take the invitation outdoors. Verse 12 has the people going out in joy and being led in peace, with the mountains and hills breaking into song in front of them and the trees of the field clapping their hands. Verse 13 replaces the thorn with the cypress and the brier with the myrtle, and says the change will stand as a name for the LORD and an everlasting sign that cannot be cut off.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is new-creation language and it is precise about which curse is being reversed. Thorns and briers are what the ground produced when it was cursed in Genesis 3:18; here they are replaced, not cleared. The invitation that began at a market stall ends with the soil itself changed, which is Isaiah's way of saying that salvation is not the rescue of souls out of a ruined world but the mending of the world they were made for.
verseByVerse.examples: Creation singing is not decoration in Scripture. Paul says the creation waits with eager longing and groans, and will be set free from its bondage to decay when the children of God are revealed (Rom. 8:19-22). Isaiah 55:12 is what that release sounds like: the landscape, at last, in tune.

verseByVerse.quote: "For you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and the hills before you shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and the hills before you shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands."

The invitation that began at a market stall ends outdoors, on a road, with the whole landscape making a noise.

Two verbs describe the people, and they should be kept apart. They go out — that is their own action, walking out of exile on their own feet. And they are led forth — that is somebody else's action, and the word is the one for leading livestock or a child. They are walking and they are being walked. Both are true at once, which is a fair account of how a Christian actually gets anywhere.

Then the hills sing and the trees applaud. It is easy to read that as decorative poetry, and Scripture will not let it stay decorative. Paul says the creation itself waits with eager longing, groans, and is going to be set free from its bondage to decay when the children of God are revealed (Rom. 8:19-22). The world is not scenery to the story of redemption; it is a participant with an interest in the outcome.

So the singing is not the poet dressing up a homecoming. It is the sound of a creation that has been groaning since Genesis 3 hearing that the thing it was waiting for has started.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle; and it shall make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle; and it shall make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off."

Two plants out, two plants in, and the choice of the first pair is not random. Thorns and briers are what the ground was told to produce when it was cursed: "thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you" (Gen. 3:18). Isaiah has reached all the way back to the third chapter of the Bible for the thing being reversed.

And notice that the thorns are not weeded. They are replaced — where the thorn was, a cypress comes up. The soil that produced the curse is now producing timber and fragrance out of the same ground. This is not the tidying of a ruined world but the mending of it.

Which is exactly the difference between the Christian hope and a general hope of going somewhere better. Isaiah does not promise escape from a thorny world. He promises that the thorns themselves will be gone from the actual ground, and the last chapters of the Bible say the same thing in different words: no more curse, and the leaves of the tree for the healing of the nations.

"An everlasting sign that shall not be cut off." The chapter that opened by shouting at a crowd of penniless people closes with a permanent monument, and the monument is a landscape. The evidence that God did this will not be a text or a memory. It will be the world itself, growing the right things at last, with his name on it forever.

55.theology:
Free, and therefore real. Verse 1 keeps the commercial verb and removes the price, and the paradox is the doctrine: something is genuinely received and nothing is contributed. Verse 3 raises the offer from a meal to a covenant — and an everlasting one, made of the steadfast love promised to David, which Paul preaches as kept in the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 13:34). Grace here is free at the point of use because it was never free to provide.

Verses 8-9 are about pardon. They are almost always quoted to someone bewildered by providence, and the word that opens verse 8 is for — attaching them to the promise immediately before, that God will abundantly pardon. The claim is that our arithmetic about what can be forgiven, how often, and for whom, is earthbound, and his is not. Read that way the passage stops being a rebuke to curiosity and becomes the answer to the returning sinner’s strongest objection, which is his own accurate assessment of his case.

The word as agent. Verse 11 makes God’s word an errand-runner rather than a communication: it goes, it works, it comes back having done what it was sent for. That is the guarantee under everything promised in chapters 40-55. It is also frequently misquoted — what is promised is that the word accomplishes what God purposed by it, which is not always what the speaker purposed by it, and rain does not always fall where the farmer was standing.

56.subtitle: My House Shall Be a House of Prayer for All Peoples
56.intro: Overview. Chapter 56 opens the final section of Isaiah (chs. 56–66), which applies the great promises of chapters 40–55 to the community returning from exile. Two groups who were excluded from the assembly under the Mosaic law — eunuchs and foreigners — are explicitly included in God’s coming house. The chapter is the Old Testament ground for Jesus’ cleansing of the temple: “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

sections.title: The Included Outsiders
sections.commentary:
Keep justice and do righteousness, for my salvation is about to come. Blessed is the man who does this — who keeps the Sabbath, who keeps his hand from evil. And then two expansions that must have been startling to the original hearers.

Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, “The LORD will surely separate me from his people.” And let not the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” The eunuch who keeps the Sabbath and holds fast to the covenant will be given “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; an everlasting name that shall not be cut off.” The foreigners who join themselves to the LORD — to serve him, to love his name, to be his servants — these God will bring to his holy mountain. Their offerings will be accepted on his altar.

v. 7 — “For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” Jesus quotes this verse in Matt. 21:13 when he overturns the money changers’ tables. His point is not merely about commerce but about access: the outer courts — the only place Gentiles were permitted — had been taken over by the very commerce that made worship transactional and excluded the outsiders Isaiah said God had already included.

sections.title: Blind Watchmen
sections.commentary: The chapter pivots to a biting critique of Israel’s own leaders: the watchmen are blind, knowing nothing, silent dogs who cannot bark. They dream, lie down, love to slumber. They are shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain. The contrast is severe: God is expanding his house to include all nations while the leaders of the house are asleep. The ones most responsible for keeping watch are the ones least alert.

keyVerse.quote: “For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
keyVerse.note: The text Jesus quotes when he cleanses the temple. The inclusivity is the point: God’s house was always designed for all peoples, not just Israel. The commerce that Jesus disrupted was not incidental but structural — it was physically occupying the only space available to outsiders. To clear it out was to enact Isaiah 56.

56.reflection: The two groups God explicitly includes — eunuchs and foreigners — were both defined by what they lacked or what they were not. God offers them something better than biological legacy or ethnic membership: an everlasting name. Who in your community occupies the place of the “excluded outsider”? And what does God’s explicit inclusion of the eunuch and the foreigner say about the shape of his house?
56.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Keep justice, and do righteousness, for soon my salvation will come, and my righteousness be revealed.<sup>2</sup>Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath, not profaning it, and keeps his hand from doing any evil."<sup>3</sup>Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, "The LORD will surely separate me from his people"; and let not the eunuch say, "Behold, I am a dry tree."<sup>4</sup>For thus says the LORD: "To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant,<sup>5</sup>I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off.<sup>6</sup>"And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, to minister to him, to love the name of the LORD, and to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath and does not profane it, and holds fast my covenant—<sup>7</sup>these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples."<sup>8</sup>The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, declares, "I will gather yet others to him besides those already gathered."<sup>9</sup>All you beasts of the field, come to devour— all you beasts in the forest.<sup>10</sup>His watchmen are blind; they are all without knowledge; they are all silent dogs; they cannot bark, dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber.<sup>11</sup>The dogs have a mighty appetite; they never have enough. But they are shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain, one and all.<sup>12</sup>"Come," they say, "let me get wine; let us fill ourselves with strong drink; and tomorrow will be like this day, great beyond measure."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The House of Prayer for All Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third major section of Isaiah begins (chs 56-66). God declares his salvation is near and calls for justice and righteousness. Foreigners and eunuchs — those excluded from the Mosaic assembly (Deut 23:1-8) — are explicitly included in the new covenant community. God's house will be a house of prayer for all nations. But the chapter ends with a harsh rebuke of Israel's blind and greedy leaders.
verseByVerse.theology: Inclusion and the eschatological community: Isaiah 56 is one of the most explicit inclusivity texts in the Old Testament. Those who were excluded by the Mosaic law's purity codes are included in the new covenant based on one criterion: holding fast to the covenant, loving the LORD's name, keeping the sabbath. Jesus quotes v.7 ('a house of prayer for all nations') when cleansing the temple (Mark 11:17), identifying his action as the beginning of the fulfillment of this promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer sees chs 56-66 as the application of the servant's atoning work to the life of the community. The servant suffers in 52:13-53:12; the community reaps the benefits in chs 54-66. The inclusion of foreigners and eunuchs in ch56 is the direct consequence: the servant's sacrifice breaks down every wall of separation.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: 'Keep justice, and do righteousness, for soon my salvation will come, and my righteousness be revealed. Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath, not profaning it, and keeps his hand from doing any evil.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens with ethical imperatives grounded in eschatological imminence: keep justice and do righteousness because salvation is coming soon. The ethical life is not the basis of salvation but its anticipatory response. The sabbath-keeper is blessed — the sabbath becomes a synecdoche for covenantal faithfulness generally. Oswalt: the call to justice in light of coming salvation is the structure of NT ethics as well — in view of God's mercies, present your bodies (Rom 12:1). Eschatology energizes ethics.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, 'The LORD will surely separate me from his people'; and let not the eunuch say, 'Behold, I am a dry tree.' For thus says the LORD: 'To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Two groups who feared exclusion are explicitly addressed. The foreigner joined to the LORD fears second-class status; the eunuch (excluded from the assembly in Deut 23:1) fears permanent exclusion (a dry tree = no descendants, no future). God speaks directly to each fear. The criterion for full inclusion is not ethnicity or physical wholeness but covenant faithfulness: keeping sabbath, choosing what pleases God, holding fast the covenant. Childs: the eschatological community is defined not by biological or ethnic identity but by covenant loyalty.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off. And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, to minister to him, to love the name of the LORD, and to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath and does not profane it, and holds fast my covenant— (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: To the eunuch who feared a dry tree: an everlasting name better than sons and daughters. The monument within the walls of God's house is permanent memorial — a name that cannot be cut off, unlike biological lineage that ends with childlessness. For the foreigner: full membership, ministry, love of God's name, servant status. Three criteria for the foreigner (v.6): keeping sabbath, not profaning it, holding fast the covenant. Motyer: the three criteria are intensive and complementary — active observance, avoidance of violation, and covenantal commitment — covering the whole of covenant life.

verseByVerse.quote: these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, declares, I will gather yet others to them besides those already gathered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A house of prayer for all peoples — the climax of the inclusion promise. The temple, which had become an exclusively Israelite space, is declared God's universal place of access. Jesus quotes this in Mark 11:17 when cleansing the temple — the money-changers had turned it from a house of prayer into a commercial zone, reversing the inclusivity God intended. Young: God gathers not only the outcasts of Israel but also the Gentile others — the already-gathered plus more to be gathered. The community of grace is always expanding outward.

verseByVerse.quote: All you beasts of the field, come to devour — all you beasts in the forest. His watchmen are blind; they are all without knowledge; they are all silent dogs; they cannot bark, sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A dramatic tonal shift: the watchmen (prophets, priests, leaders) are blind dogs who cannot bark. The beasts of prey are invited to devour — God himself opens the gate to destruction because the shepherds have failed. The silence of watchmen who should warn is the church's perennial failure in every age. Childs: the contrast between the coming global community (vv.1-8) and the corrupt present leadership (vv.9-12) reveals the gap that only the servant's renewal can bridge.

verseByVerse.quote: The dogs have a mighty appetite; they never have enough. But they are shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain, one and all. 'Come,' they say, 'let me get wine; let us fill ourselves with strong drink; and tomorrow will be like this day, great beyond measure.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The corrupt shepherds: insatiable appetite, no understanding, self-serving, greedy, given to drunken complacency. Tomorrow will be like today — the willful blindness to coming judgment. This is the pastoral failure that precedes every national disaster in Scripture — leaders who look after themselves rather than the flock. Oswalt: the rebuke of corrupt shepherds in vv.9-12 is the shadow side of the inclusion promise in vv.1-8. Until the servants of God are transformed (the work of the Spirit in chs 59-66), the community's leaders will remain the obstacle to the very inclusion God promises.

57.subtitle: The High and Holy One Who Dwells with the Contrite
57.intro: Overview. Chapter 57 contains a scathing critique of Israel’s idolatrous practices — sexual fertility rites, child sacrifice, pagan deal-making — before arriving at one of Isaiah’s most theologically surprising statements: the high and exalted God, who inhabits eternity, chooses to dwell with the lowly and contrite in spirit. The chapter ends with the peace that is for the contrite and the restlessness that awaits the wicked.

sections.title: Idolatry’s Exhausting Program
sections.commentary:
The righteous perish and no one lays it to heart — the devout are taken away while the wicked prosper and no one understands. Then God indicts: you who mock, you offspring of the adulterer and the prostitute. Behind every idol there is a journey: you journeyed far, going to Sheol, wearing yourself out. The idol program is exhausting. You were wearied by the length of your way, but you did not say “It is hopeless.”

v. 10 — “You were wearied by the length of your way, but you did not say ‘It is hopeless.’” This is one of the saddest diagnoses in Isaiah: the people are exhausted by idolatry but refuse to acknowledge it is not working. The energy to keep trying substitutes for the honesty to stop and return. Idolatry is primarily characterized not by blasphemy but by stubbornness in the face of evidence.

sections.title: With the Contrite and Lowly
sections.commentary:
And it shall be said: build up, build up, prepare the way; remove every obstruction. God will revive the heart of the contrite ones. For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.”

The two addresses — the eternal heights and the lowly spirit — are not in tension but in design. God is not condescending when he comes to the lowly; he is fulfilling the same character that makes him exalted. His holiness and his humility are two expressions of the same nature. The chapter closes: “There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked” — the wicked are always in motion (v. 20: like the tossing sea). The contrite are still; the wicked cannot stop.

keyVerse.quote: “For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit.”
keyVerse.note: This verse holds together what would seem like opposites: the infinite God and the broken person. The condition for the divine indwelling is not religious achievement but contrition. Jesus’ first beatitude (“blessed are the poor in spirit”) is the New Testament form of this verse. The throne and the broken heart are the same address.

57.reflection: God inhabits eternity and chooses to dwell with the contrite in spirit. Not with the successful, the together, the impressive — with the contrite. What would it mean for you to stop managing your spiritual life well enough to avoid contrition, and instead to let yourself be small enough for God to actually dwell there?
57.text: <sup>1</sup>The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one understands. For the righteous man is taken away from calamity;<sup>2</sup>he enters into peace; they rest in their beds who walk in their uprightness.<sup>3</sup>But you, draw near, sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer and the loose woman.<sup>4</sup>Whom are you mocking? Against whom do you open your mouth wide and stick out your tongue? Are you not children of transgression, the offspring of deceit,<sup>5</sup>you who burn with lust among the oaks, under every green tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks?<sup>6</sup>Among the smooth stones of the valley is your portion; they, they, are your lot; to them you have poured out a drink offering, you have brought a grain offering. Shall I relent for these things?<sup>7</sup>On a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed, and there you went up to offer sacrifice.<sup>8</sup>Behind the door and the doorpost you have set up your memorial; for, deserting me, you have uncovered your bed, you have gone up to it, you have made it wide; and you have made a covenant for yourself with them, you have loved their bed, you have looked on nakedness.<sup>9</sup>You journeyed to the king with oil and multiplied your perfumes; you sent your envoys far off, and sent down even to Sheol.<sup>10</sup>You were wearied with the length of your way, but you did not say, "It is hopeless"; you found new life for your strength, and so you were not faint.<sup>11</sup>Whom did you dread and fear, so that you lied, and did not remember me, did not lay it to heart? Have I not held my peace, even for a long time, and you do not fear me?<sup>12</sup>I will declare your righteousness and your deeds, but they will not profit you.<sup>13</sup>When you cry out, let your collection of idols deliver you! The wind will carry them all off, a breath will take them away. But he who takes refuge in me shall possess the land and shall inherit my holy mountain.<sup>14</sup>And it shall be said, "Build up, build up, prepare the way, remove every obstruction from my people's way."<sup>15</sup>For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.<sup>16</sup>For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made.<sup>17</sup>Because of the iniquity of his unjust gain I was angry, I struck him; I hid my face and was angry, but he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart.<sup>18</sup>I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will lead him and restore comfort to him and his mourners,<sup>19</sup>creating the fruit of the lips. Peace, peace, to the far and to the near," says the LORD, "and I will heal him.<sup>20</sup>But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt.<sup>21</sup>There is no peace," says my God, "for the wicked."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — God Dwells with the Contrite
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous perish and no one understands why (v.1). The wicked pursue their idolatrous ways — child sacrifice, bed-making on hilltops, visiting foreign gods. Then the divine reversal: God dwells not with the mighty or the proud but with the contrite and lowly in spirit, to revive them. The chapter closes with the offer of peace and healing, and the solemn restatement: there is no peace for the wicked.
verseByVerse.theology: Contriteness and divine indwelling: the central theological claim of the chapter — that the High and Lofty One who inhabits eternity also dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit (v.15) — is one of Isaiah's most paradoxical statements. Infinity and humility, eternity and brokenness, are the chosen companions of the same God. This is the incarnation anticipated: God entering the lowly, small, broken space of human need.
verseByVerse.examples: Childs notes that 57:15 is one of the greatest verse in Isaiah, combining the transcendence of God (high and lofty, inhabits eternity, Holy One) with the most intimate divine condescension (dwells with the contrite and lowly to revive their spirit). This is the theological center of what the servant's work accomplishes: it makes God accessible to the broken.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one understands. For the righteous man is taken away from calamity; he enters into peace; they rest in their beds who walk in their uprightness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The righteous die and no one understands why. The answer given: they are taken from coming calamity — God removes the devout before the judgment falls, like Lot from Sodom. They enter peace; they rest in their beds. This is Isaiah's clearest suggestion of a blessed afterlife for the righteous: they rest in peace while the storm gathers. Motyer: the death of the righteous is not tragedy but protective mercy — God takes his people home before the worst arrives. This is not cynicism but deep pastoral confidence in God's governance of timing.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, draw near, sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer and the loose woman. Whom are you mocking? Against whom do you open your mouth wide and stick out your tongue? Are you not children of transgression, the offspring of deceit, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast is stark: the righteous rest in peace; the wicked are confronted with their identity. Sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer — Israel's idolatry is described in terms of sexual and spiritual unfaithfulness. The mockery they direct at the righteous (open mouth, stuck-out tongue) is now reversed — God addresses the mockers. Oswalt: the irony is that the wicked mocked the righteous for their apparent foolishness in trusting God; now God shows that it was the wicked's confidence in idols that was foolish.

verseByVerse.quote: you who burn with lust among the oaks, under every green tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks? Among the smooth stones of the valley is your portion; they, they are your lot; to them you have poured out a drink offering, you have brought a grain offering. Shall I relent for these things? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The indictment of syncretistic worship becomes darkest here: child sacrifice in the valleys. The sacred trees, the clefts in rocks used for Canaanite worship, the smooth stones (perhaps cairn altars) — all of these are Israel's actual worship practices condemned throughout Kings and Jeremiah. The drink offerings and grain offerings poured to idols were intended for the LORD. God's question — shall I relent for these things? — is rhetorical and devastating. Young: the specificity of the indictment (place, practice, victim) makes it impossible to miss. There is no softening here — this is Israel's actual religious life exposed.

verseByVerse.quote: On a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed, and there you went up to offer sacrifice. Behind the door and the doorpost you have set up your memorial; for, deserting me, you have uncovered your bed, you have gone up to it, you have made it wide; you have made a covenant with them, you have loved their bed, you have looked on nakedness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The idolatry is described in overtly sexual terms — bed on the mountain, uncovered bed, love of the idol-bed. The pagan high places were often associated with ritual prostitution; Isaiah uses the sexual metaphor to expose the inner logic of idolatry: it is unfaithfulness to the covenant husband (54:5). The memorial behind the door may be mezuzah-like inscriptions to pagan gods. Childs: the sexual language is not prurient but theologically precise — idolatry is covenant adultery, betraying the most intimate relationship for a false one.

verseByVerse.quote: You journeyed to the king with oil and multiplied your perfumes; you sent your envoys far away, and sent down even to Sheol. You were wearied with the length of your way, but you did not say, 'It is hopeless'; you found new life for your strength, and so you were not faint. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The king may be Molech (the idol-king) or a foreign power sought through diplomatic idolatry. The journeying to Sheol suggests consulting the dead — prohibited by the Torah (Deut 18:10-11). The irony: Israel was so energized by its idolatry that it found new life for its strength — the same energy it refused to spend in seeking the LORD. Oswalt: the exhausting pursuit of idols is the mirror image of the weary pursuit of God that produces eagle wings (40:31). The same human energy, invested in opposite directions, produces opposite results.

verseByVerse.quote: Whom did you dread and fear, so that you lied, and did not remember me, did not lay it to heart? Have I not held my peace, even for a long time, and you do not fear me? I will declare your righteousness and your deeds, but they will not profit you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's diagnostic question: whom did you dread and fear? — someone other than God. The fear of something other than God (foreign powers, human opinion, social pressure) produces the lies and the forgetting. God's long silence was misread as indifference; it was actually patience. When he declares their righteousness — meaning, he will display their deeds publicly in the light of his judgment — those deeds will not profit them. Motyer: the righteous deeds done in idolatry's service are not assets but liabilities; their true nature exposed in God's courtroom.

verseByVerse.quote: When you cry out, let your collection of idols deliver you! The wind will carry them off, a breath will take them away. But he who takes refuge in me shall possess the land and shall inherit my holy mountain. And it shall be said, 'Build up, build up, prepare the way; remove every obstruction from my people's way.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The ultimate bankruptcy of idols: at the moment of crisis, they are carried off by wind and breath. The contrast with the refuge in the LORD: inheritance of the land, possession of the holy mountain. Then the gospel road: build up, prepare the way, remove obstructions. The same highway language of 40:3-5 recurs — the path made clear for God's people to travel home. Childs: the call to prepare the way in v.14 signals that the community's repentance and the idols' failure are the conditions for the new exodus to begin.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: 'I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The theological summit of the chapter — and one of the greatest verses in Isaiah. The One who is high and lifted up (language of 6:1 and 52:13) inhabits eternity and is Holy — absolute transcendence. Yet this same God dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit. High and holy, yet low and broken: both at once. The purpose is active: to revive the lowly and contrite. God descends not merely to be with the broken but to restore them. Motyer: the incarnation is here in principle — the eternal, holy, transcendent God choosing the space of human brokenness as his dwelling place.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made. Because of the sin of his unjust gain I was angry; I struck him; I hid my face and was angry, but he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's anger is self-limited: he will not contend forever or always be angry, because sustained divine anger would destroy the frail creature he made. The restraint is mercy within judgment. Then the explanation of the exile: unjust gain, idol-serving sin. I struck him… he went on backsliding — judgment did not produce repentance. Oswalt: the stubbornness of human sin in the face of divine discipline is the deepest problem of fallen humanity. The exile warned, judged, and yet Israel kept going in the way of its own heart. This is why only a new heart can solve the problem (Ezek 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will lead him and restore comfort to him and his mourners, creating the fruit of the lips. Peace, peace, to the far and to the near, says the LORD, and I will heal him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: I have seen his ways — God knows the full extent of the sin — but I will heal him. The grace comes after full knowledge, not in ignorance of the problem. The healing is comprehensive: leading, comfort, mourners consoled. Creating the fruit of the lips — the praise that will spring from healed hearts. Peace, peace, to the far and to the near — the doubled peace, universal in scope: those already near and those far off (Eph 2:17 — he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near). Young: the gospel of peace is precisely this — God healing those who deserve only his anger.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt. There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The closing refrain of the second major section of Trito-Isaiah (repeated from 48:22, closing the first). The wicked are like the restless sea — tossing up mire and dirt, incapable of quiet. No peace is possible for those who remain in the idolatry and injustice described in vv.3-12. The peace offered to the near and far in v.19 is contingent on the repentance that v.15 enables — the contrite and lowly receive God's dwelling; the wicked remain without peace. Childs: the two endings of major sections (48:22; 57:21) mark the absolute divide between those who receive God's comfort and those who refuse it.

58.subtitle: The Fast That God Chooses
58.intro: Overview. Chapter 58 is one of the most practically searching chapters in Isaiah. The people fast and pray and perform religious duties — and they cannot understand why God does not notice. God’s answer: you are fasting for yourselves. The fast he chooses looks nothing like religious theater; it looks like loose bonds, free people, shared bread, covered nakedness. And then one of the richest promises in the book: your light will rise in the darkness.

sections.title: Why Does God Not See?
sections.commentary:
They seek God daily and delight to know his ways; they ask for righteous judgments and delight in God’s nearness. But when they fast, they fast for themselves: they quarrel and fight; they fast to make their voice heard on high. Is such the fast that I choose? God’s question dismantles the religious performance entirely. The fast was not wrong as a category; it was wrong as an offering, because it was primarily about them.

v. 6 — “Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?” The chosen fast is horizontal, not vertical. It is not primarily an act of personal piety toward God but of justice toward the neighbor. Jesus’ parable of the sheep and goats (Matt. 25:31–46) is the New Testament version of this principle: the service rendered to “the least of these” is service rendered to God himself.

sections.title: Light Rising in Darkness
sections.commentary:
Then shall your light break forth like the dawn; your healing shall spring up speedily; your righteousness shall go before you; the glory of the LORD shall be your rear guard. Then you shall call and the LORD will answer; you shall cry and he will say, ‘Here I am.’ The conditions: remove the yoke, the pointing of the finger, the speaking of wickedness; offer yourself to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted. The promised results: light in darkness, guided continually, watered like a garden, the ancient ruins rebuilt.

The chapter ends with the Sabbath: if you turn back your foot from the Sabbath, calling it a delight, then you shall take delight in the LORD, and I will make you ride on the heights of the earth. The Sabbath is the enacted declaration that God provides; the fast is the enacted declaration that I give to others. Both are acts of trust that something greater than my effort governs the world.

keyVerse.quote: “If you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness and your gloom be as the noonday.”
keyVerse.note: The image of light rising in darkness is the fruit of self-giving, not self-improvement. The person who pours themselves out — who gives what they need rather than what they can spare — discovers that the light that rises is not their own light but the LORD’s. Self-denial becomes illumination; the loss of comfort becomes the gain of presence.

58.reflection: God diagnoses their fasting as self-serving without them knowing it. Their religious sincerity was real — they genuinely sought God, genuinely performed the fasts. But sincerity does not make a misdirected offering acceptable. What religious activities in your life might be primarily serving your own spiritual comfort rather than the justice God actually wants? And where might he be asking you to pour yourself out rather than merely perform?
58.text: <sup>1</sup>"Cry aloud; do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet; declare to my people their transgression, to the house of Jacob their sins.<sup>2</sup>Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God.<sup>3</sup>'Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?' Behold, in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers.<sup>4</sup>Behold, you fast only to quarrel and to fight and to hit with a wicked fist. Fasting like yours this day will not make your voice to be heard on high.<sup>5</sup>Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself? Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the LORD?<sup>6</sup>"Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?<sup>7</sup>Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him, and not to hide yourself from your own flesh?<sup>8</sup>Then shall your light break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up speedily; your righteousness shall go before you; the glory of the LORD shall be your rear guard.<sup>9</sup>Then you shall call, and the LORD will answer; you shall cry, and he will say, 'Here I am.' If you take away the yoke from your midst, the pointing of the finger, and speaking wickedness,<sup>10</sup>if you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness and your gloom be as the noonday.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD will guide you continually and satisfy your desire in scorched places and make your bones strong; and you shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water, whose waters do not fail.<sup>12</sup>And your ancient ruins shall be rebuilt; you shall raise up the foundations of many generations; you shall be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer of streets to dwell in.<sup>13</sup>"If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight and the holy day of the LORD honorable; if you honor it, not going your own ways, or seeking your own pleasure, or talking idly;<sup>14</sup>then you shall take delight in the LORD, and I will make you ride on the heights of the earth; I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — True Fasting and the Light of Dawn
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel complains that God does not respond to their fasting. God's answer: their fasting is performative, not transformative — they fast while exploiting workers and quarreling. True fasting is releasing the oppressed, feeding the hungry, housing the wanderer, clothing the naked. When Israel practices justice, light breaks forth like the dawn, healing springs up, and the glory of the LORD becomes the rear guard.
verseByVerse.theology: Justice as worship: the chapter is one of the most direct connections in Scripture between religious practice and social ethics. God refuses to accept worship that is disconnected from justice. The fasting he chooses (v.6) is not liturgical abstinence but socioeconomic liberation — releasing oppressed workers, breaking unjust structures. The connection to Isaiah 1:10-17 is direct: 'cease to do evil; learn to do good; seek justice' is the prerequisite for acceptable worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus reads the parallel passage from Isaiah 61 in Luke 4:18-19 as the definition of his own ministry. The sabbath dispute in Luke 13:10-17 echoes ch58 directly — Jesus heals a woman 'bound for eighteen years' on the sabbath, and his defense uses the logic of ch58: ought this daughter of Abraham not be loosened on the sabbath day?

verseByVerse.quote: Cry aloud; do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet; declare to my people their transgression, to the house of Jacob their sins. Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The trumpet-call (cf. 58:1 with Lev 25:9 — the jubilee trumpet) summons Isaiah to blunt proclamation. The irony is devastating: the people are superficially devout — seeking God daily, delighting in his ways, asking for righteous judgments — while practicing injustice. Motyer: the description of v.2 could be a positive portrait of a godly community, but the context reveals it as performance without substance. Religious regularity and theological curiosity can coexist with complete failure in the social ethics that flow from genuine faith.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?' Behold, in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure and oppress all your workers. Behold, you fast only to quarrel and to fight and to hit with a wicked fist. Fasting like yours this day will not make your voice to be heard on high. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel's complaint: we fasted and God ignored it. God's diagnostic: on your fast day, you exploit your workers and quarrel. The fast that humbles the body while the hand oppresses the poor is not fasting at all — it is spiritual theater. The voice lifted in fasting is not heard on high because the hands are stained with injustice. Oswalt: the problem is not the ritual of fasting per se but its use as a substitute for the justice God requires. Religious practice that coexists with social exploitation is a form of hypocrisy that God will not reward.

verseByVerse.quote: Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself? Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the LORD? Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God defines his chosen fast: not liturgical posture (bowing like a reed, sackcloth and ashes) but socioeconomic action (loose bonds of wickedness, break every yoke, let the oppressed go free). This is jubilee language — the year of release when debts are forgiven and slaves freed (Lev 25). Jesus applies this language to his own mission in Luke 4:18. Childs: the fast God chooses is not an addition to justice but its expression — true worship cannot be separated from the treatment of human beings made in God's image.

verseByVerse.quote: Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him, and not to hide yourself from your own flesh? Then shall your light break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up speedily; your righteousness shall go before you; the glory of the LORD shall be your rear guard. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The social practices of true fasting: bread for the hungry, housing for the homeless poor, clothing for the naked. Not to hide yourself from your own flesh — seeing the needy as family, as kin, not strangers. Then the promise: light like the dawn, healing springing up, righteousness going before, glory as rear guard. The community that practices justice becomes luminous — its light is not self-generated but the reflection of the God whose glory guards from behind. Young: the imagery of light, healing, and divine escort covers every dimension of communal flourishing — physical, relational, and spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you shall call, and the LORD will answer; you shall cry, and he will say, 'Here I am.' If you take away the yoke from your midst, the pointing of the finger, and speaking wickedness, if you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness and your gloom be as the noonday. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Then you shall call, and the LORD will answer… here I am — the most immediate divine responsiveness. The condition: remove the yoke, stop pointing the finger (the gesture of accusation and contempt), stop speaking wickedness; pour yourself out for the hungry. The pouring out — exhaustive generosity — echoes the servant's self-giving (53:12 — he poured out his soul). Motyer: the community formed by the servant learns to give as the servant gave. The light that rises is not earned but is the overflow of genuine, servant-like love.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD will guide you continually and satisfy your desire in scorched places and make your bones strong; and you shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water, whose waters do not fail. And your ancient ruins shall be rebuilt; you shall raise up the foundations of many generations; you shall be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer of streets to dwell in. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The watered garden (Eden restored), the unfailing spring — images of abundance in the midst of drought. The rebuilder of ruins, raiser of foundations, repairer of breaches — the just community becomes the agent of social restoration. Repairer of the breach — one of Scripture's most beautiful titles. The community that practices ch58's justice becomes the community that mends what is broken in society. Oswalt: the church that practices genuine justice does not merely avoid exploitation but actively rebuilds what exploitation has destroyed — streets, foundations, ancient ruins.

verseByVerse.quote: If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight and the holy day of the LORD honorable; if you honor it, not going your own ways, or seeking your own pleasure, or talking idly; then you shall take delight in the LORD, and I will make you ride on the heights of the earth; I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter concludes with the sabbath — the bookend to the fasting theme. Just as fasting is corrupted by self-seeking, so the sabbath is corrupted by treating it as an opportunity for personal pleasure. The sabbath, rightly kept, is a delight in the LORD — an anticipation of the eschatological rest (Heb 4:9-11). The promise: riding on the heights of the earth, fed with Jacob's heritage. Motyer: the sabbath principle — one day surrendered fully to God — is the training in delight that transforms the whole week. The person who truly delights in the LORD on the sabbath cannot oppress workers on Monday.

59.subtitle: Your Iniquities Have Separated You
59.intro: Overview. Chapter 59 begins with one of Isaiah’s most honest diagnoses: God’s hand is not too short to save, his ear not too heavy to hear — the problem is Israel’s iniquities, which have made a separation between them and God. The chapter moves from communal confession to divine intervention, and ends with the arrival of the Redeemer and the promise of the Spirit resting on God’s people forever.

sections.title: The Separation
sections.commentary:
Behold, the LORD’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God. The catalog that follows is extensive: lying, injustice, violence, oppression, empty pleas, no justice, truth stumbling in the public square. The snake-egg-and-spider-web images (vv. 5–6) are vivid: the schemes of the wicked hatch vipers and weave webs that cannot clothe anyone.

A communal confession follows: we grope like the blind; we have transgressed and denied the LORD; justice is far from us. Truth has stumbled in the public square; honesty cannot enter. The corporate nature of the confession — we, not they — is the precondition for what comes next.

sections.title: The Redeemer Comes
sections.commentary:
The LORD saw it, and it displeased him that there was no justice. He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation, and his righteousness upheld him. When no human justice is available, God himself becomes the warrior. He puts on righteousness as a breastplate, a helmet of salvation, garments of vengeance for clothing, a cloak of zeal. Paul takes this armor and gives it to the church in Ephesians 6: the armor of God is the armor God himself wore into battle.

v. 20 — “And a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression.” Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:26 as the promise of Israel’s ultimate salvation: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; he will banish ungodliness from Jacob.” The Redeemer of Isaiah 59 is the Christ of Romans 11 — coming to those who turn from transgression, which is itself a gift of the Spirit promised in the final verse.

“My Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth… from this time forth and forevermore.” The chapter that began with separation ends with permanent indwelling. The iniquity that made the gap is dealt with by the Redeemer; the Spirit fills the space the sin had occupied.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, the LORD’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God.”
keyVerse.note: The two verses together diagnose the human spiritual condition with precision: the problem is never God’s ability or willingness, always the sin that creates the gap. And the rest of the chapter shows that God’s response to the gap is not to demand it be bridged from the human side but to cross it himself, dressed for battle, as Redeemer.

59.reflection: The people in this chapter were not irreligious — they expected God to notice their prayers (v. 1). They were surprised he didn’t. The diagnosis was separation created by iniquity they had not addressed. Is there a separation in your own experience of God right now? What would honest communal confession — we, not they — look like in your life?
59.text: <sup>1</sup>Behold, the LORD's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear;<sup>2</sup>but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear.<sup>3</sup>For your hands are defiled with blood and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies; your tongue mutters wickedness.<sup>4</sup>No one enters suit justly; no one goes to law honestly; they rely on empty pleas, they speak lies, they conceive mischief and give birth to iniquity.<sup>5</sup>They hatch adders' eggs; they weave the spider's web; he who eats their eggs dies, and from one that is crushed a viper is hatched.<sup>6</sup>Their webs will not serve as clothing; men will not cover themselves with what they make. Their works are works of iniquity, and deeds of violence are in their hands.<sup>7</sup>Their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed innocent blood; their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; desolation and destruction are in their highways.<sup>8</sup>The way of peace they do not know, and there is no justice in their paths; they have made their roads crooked; no one who treads on them knows peace.<sup>9</sup>Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness does not overtake us; we hope for light, and behold, darkness, and for brightness, but we walk in gloom.<sup>10</sup>We grope for the wall like the blind; we grope like those who have no eyes; we stumble at noon as in the twilight, among those in full vigor we are like dead men.<sup>11</sup>We all growl like bears; we moan and moan like doves; we hope for justice, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far from us.<sup>12</sup>For our transgressions are multiplied before you, and our sins testify against us; for our transgressions are with us, and we know our iniquities:<sup>13</sup>transgressing, and denying the LORD, and turning back from following our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering from the heart lying words.<sup>14</sup>Justice is turned back, and righteousness stands far away; for truth has stumbled in the public squares, and uprightness cannot enter.<sup>15</sup>Truth is lacking, and he who departs from evil makes himself a prey. The LORD saw it, and it displeased him that there was no justice.<sup>16</sup>He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation, and his righteousness upheld him.<sup>17</sup>He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and wrapped himself in zeal as a cloak.<sup>18</sup>According to their deeds, so will he repay, wrath to his adversaries, repayment to his enemies; to the coastlands he will render repayment.<sup>19</sup>So they shall fear the name of the LORD from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun; for he will come like a rushing stream, which the wind of the LORD drives.<sup>20</sup>"And a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression," declares the LORD.<sup>21</sup>"And as for me, this is my covenant with them," says the LORD: "My Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, or out of the mouth of your offspring, or out of the mouth of your children's offspring," says the LORD, "from this time forth and forevermore."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Sin Confessed and the Warrior God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The community confesses that their separation from God is not due to his inability to hear but to their own iniquities. A comprehensive indictment of social and moral failure follows. No one intercedes; no one stands in the gap. So God himself puts on righteousness as armor and comes as a warrior to bring salvation to Zion. The chapter ends with the promise of God's Spirit and words never departing from the redeemed community.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin, intercession, and divine initiative: the chapter's logic mirrors Romans 3:9-26. All have sinned; no one seeks God; God himself provides the righteousness that no human can supply. The divine warrior who puts on salvation as a helmet and righteousness as a breastplate anticipates Paul's armor of God in Ephesians 6:13-17. The Spirit and word promised in v.21 are the new covenant gifts of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer sees ch59 as the darkest chapter in the last section of Isaiah — the comprehensive exposure of sin that makes the new covenant promise of ch60 all the more glorious. Keller uses vv.1-2 in pastoral ministry: God's silence is never due to his inability to hear or act; when God seems distant, the first question is always the state of the approaching heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the LORD's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter's foundational diagnosis: God's power and attentiveness are not the problem. The hand that parted the Red Sea is not shortened; the ear that heard Israel's cry in Egypt is not dull. The separation is created by sin, not divine distance. Iniquities have built a wall between the community and God. Oswalt: the pastoral implication is both sobering and hopeful. Sobering: the absence of answered prayer is not God's failure but our condition. Hopeful: if sin is the cause, repentance is the remedy — the way back exists.

verseByVerse.quote: For your hands are defiled with blood and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies; your tongue mutters wickedness. No one enters suit justly; no one goes to law honestly; they rely on empty pleas, they speak lies, they conceive mischief and give birth to iniquity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The indictment is bodily and specific: hands, fingers, lips, tongue — every member implicated. Then the social dimension: courts corrupted, justice absent, lies standard practice. Isaiah 1:15-17 comes full circle — the hands God would not look at in prayer are the same hands defiled with blood. Childs: the catalog of bodily sin (vv.3-8) echoes Psalm 14's description of universal corruption, which Paul quotes in Romans 3:10-18 as the diagnosis of all humanity, Jew and Gentile alike.

verseByVerse.quote: They hatch adders' eggs; they weave the spider's web; he who eats their eggs dies, and from one that is hatched a viper is born. Their webs will not serve as clothing; men will not cover themselves with what they make. Their works are works of iniquity, and deeds of violence are in their hands. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The imagery is venomous and futile: eggs that hatch vipers, webs that cannot clothe. Evil is both deadly (vipers) and useless (webs). The works of the unjust harm others and profit no one, not even the workers themselves. Motyer: sin is always self-defeating as well as other-destructive. The spider's web that cannot clothe the spider-spinner captures the ultimate bankruptcy of a life built on wickedness — it looks like work but produces nothing durable.

verseByVerse.quote: Their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed innocent blood; their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; desolation and destruction are in their highways. The way of peace they do not know, and there is no justice in their paths; they have made their roads crooked; no one who treads on them knows peace. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes vv.7-8 in Romans 3:15-17 as part of the universal indictment of human sin. The way of peace they do not know — this connects directly to the peacelessness of 48:22 and 57:21. The crooked roads, the unknowing of peace — these are not accidental characteristics but the fruit of the choices catalogued in vv.3-6. Young: the absence of peace in human society is a direct consequence of the absence of righteousness. The crooked road cannot lead to a straight destination.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness does not overtake us; we hope for light, and behold, darkness, and for brightness, but we walk in gloom. We grope for the wall like the blind; we grope like those who have no eyes; we stumble at noon as in the twilight, among those in full vigor we are like dead men. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The community's first-person confession begins: we — a communal ownership of the sin just described. Justice far away, righteousness elusive, light hoped for but darkness experienced, groping like the blind. The noon-blindness (stumbling in full daylight) is the darkest image of spiritual incapacity. Oswalt: this is Israel's Gethsemane moment — the full recognition that the problem is internal, not external. The darkness is not Babylon's but their own sin's shadow. This confession is the prerequisite for the divine action of v.16.

verseByVerse.quote: We all growl like bears; we moan and moan like doves; we hope for justice, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far from us. For our transgressions are multiplied before you, and our sins testify against us; for our transgressions are with us, and we know our iniquities: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The animal sounds — bear's growl, dove's moan — capture the inarticulate grief of a community that knows something is deeply wrong. The confession deepens: our transgressions are with us, we know our iniquities. Self-knowledge of sin without external accusation is the beginning of genuine repentance. The transgressions testify against them — they are their own witnesses. Motyer: the most dangerous sins are the unacknowledged ones; these people at least know what they have done, which is the painful beginning of honesty before God.

verseByVerse.quote: transgressing, and denying the LORD, and turning back from following our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering from the heart lying words. Justice is turned back, and righteousness stands far away; for truth has stumbled in the public squares, and uprightness cannot enter. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The confession catalogues the sins at their root: transgression, denial, departure from God — spiritual sins — and oppression, revolt, lying — social sins. Then the result in public life: justice turned back, truth stumbling in the city squares, uprightness unable to enter the gates. When personal faith collapses, public justice collapses with it. Young: the public square reflects the interior condition of a society's souls. A community that has privately denied the LORD will publicly deny justice to its neighbors.

verseByVerse.quote: Truth has stumbled in the public squares, and uprightness cannot enter. Truth is lacking, and he who departs from evil makes himself a prey. The LORD saw it, and it displeased him that there was no justice. He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation, and his righteousness upheld him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The pivotal moment: God looks for an intercessor and finds none. No human being steps up to address the situation. He wondered that there was no one to intercede — the surprise of divine grief at human moral failure. So God acts himself: his own arm brought him salvation. The arm of the LORD (51:9; 52:10; 53:1) acts when no human arm can. This is the gospel principle: human inability triggers divine initiative. Childs: the intercessor God cannot find in ch59 is the intercessor the servant becomes — making intercession for the transgressors (53:12).

verseByVerse.quote: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and wrapped himself in zeal as a cloak. According to their deeds, so will he repay, wrath to his adversaries, repayment to his enemies; to the coastlands he will render repayment. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God arms himself as a warrior — righteousness as breastplate, salvation as helmet. Paul copies this imagery in Eph 6:14-17, applying God's own armor to the Christian's spiritual warfare. The zeal-cloak echoes the zeal of 9:7 and 37:32 — the same divine passion that preserved the remnant and overthrew Sennacherib now goes to battle against all injustice. Motyer: God's warfare is always morally grounded — he fights because righteousness requires it, not because he is aggressive by temperament.

verseByVerse.quote: So they shall fear the name of the LORD from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun; for he will come like a rushing stream, which the wind of the LORD drives. And a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression, declares the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The divine warrior's advance produces universal fear-reverence: east and west, from the rising to the setting of the sun. The rushing stream driven by God's wind is irresistible — nature's most powerful forces under divine direction. Then: a Redeemer will come to Zion. Paul quotes this in Romans 11:26 to ground the promise of Israel's eschatological salvation. Young: the Redeemer comes to those who turn from transgression — grace is universal in offer but received by the repentant.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for me, this is my covenant with them, says the LORD: My Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, or from the mouth of your offspring, or from the mouth of your children's offspring, says the LORD, from this time forth and forevermore. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The new covenant promise: Spirit and word together, given to the community and to all their descendants, forever. Not a temporary loan but a permanent gift — shall not depart. This is the new covenant of Jer 31:33-34 and Ezek 36:27 fully articulated. The Spirit gives the word; the word shapes the community; the community passes both to its children. Oswalt: the Spirit and word together are the means by which God's presence is maintained in the community when God himself is not visibly present. This is the church's inheritance.

60.subtitle: Arise, Shine
60.intro: Overview. Chapter 60 is the great vision of Zion’s glory — one of the most expansive and luminous passages in the whole of Isaiah. The nations stream to Jerusalem; their wealth flows in; kings come to the brightness of her rising. The sun and moon are superseded by the glory of the LORD. The chapter is the Old Testament ground for the closing vision of Revelation 21–22, where John takes nearly every image and places it in the new Jerusalem.

sections.title: The Light Has Come
sections.commentary:
Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you. For behold, darkness covers the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise over you, and his glory will be seen upon you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

The light that draws the nations is not Israel’s own light but the glory of the LORD risen upon her. The distinction is crucial: Israel does not generate the light; she reflects it. This is the missionary theology of the Old Testament in its most developed form: the nations come not because Israel is impressive but because God is present.

v. 3 — “Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.” Revelation 21:24 applies this verse to the new Jerusalem: “the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it.” The eschatological gathering of the nations is the fulfillment of the chapter, and it runs through the whole Bible: from Abraham’s blessing for all families (Gen. 12:3) to this vision to the great multitude “from every nation” of Revelation 7.

sections.title: The New Order
sections.commentary:
Foreigners shall build your walls; their kings shall minister to you. The gates shall be open continually; they shall not be shut day or night, so that people may bring to you the wealth of the nations. The violence that was done to Israel will be reversed; the oppressors will serve. But the reversal is not merely political; it is transformational — those who oppressed will recognize that God is with his people.

The sun shall be no more your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give you light; but the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory. Revelation 21:23 quotes this directly: “the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.” The smallest of nations will become a mighty one; the LORD will hasten it in its time.

keyVerse.quote: “Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you.”
keyVerse.note: The two imperatives — arise, shine — follow the indicative: your light has come. The rising and shining are responses to what God has done, not achievements that earn his presence. Ephesians 5:14 picks up the language: “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” The light that has come is ultimately Christ himself, the glory of the LORD incarnate.

60.reflection: The nations come to Zion’s light, but the light is the LORD’s glory, not Zion’s excellence. The church’s attractiveness to the world is not its programs or excellence but the presence of God within it. What are you relying on to draw people — the light you generate, or the light God has risen upon you? And what would it mean to “arise and shine” in the specific darkness of where you live?
60.text: <sup>1</sup>Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you.<sup>2</sup>For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will be seen upon you.<sup>3</sup>And nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.<sup>4</sup>Lift up your eyes all around, and see; they all gather together, they come to you; your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall be carried on the hip.<sup>5</sup>Then you shall see and be radiant; your heart shall thrill and exult, because the abundance of the sea shall be turned to you, the wealth of the nations shall come to you.<sup>6</sup>A multitude of camels shall cover you, the young camels of Midian and Ephah; all those from Sheba shall come. They shall bring gold and frankincense, and shall bring good news, the praises of the LORD.<sup>7</sup>All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to you; they shall come up with acceptance on my altar, and I will beautify my beautiful house.<sup>8</sup>Who are these that fly like a cloud, and like doves to their windows?<sup>9</sup>For the coastlands shall hope for me, the ships of Tarshish first, to bring your children from afar, their silver and gold with them, for the name of the LORD your God, and for the Holy One of Israel, because he has made you beautiful.<sup>10</sup>Foreigners shall build up your walls, and their kings shall minister to you; for in my wrath I struck you, but in my favor I have had mercy on you.<sup>11</sup>Your gates shall be open continually; day and night they shall not be shut, that people may bring to you the wealth of the nations, with their kings led in procession.<sup>12</sup>For the nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish; those nations shall be utterly laid waste.<sup>13</sup>The glory of Lebanon shall come to you, the cypress, the plane, and the pine, to beautify the place of my sanctuary, and I will make the place of my feet glorious.<sup>14</sup>The sons of those who afflicted you shall come bending low to you, and all who despised you shall bow down at your feet; they shall call you the City of the LORD, the Zion of the Holy One of Israel.<sup>15</sup>Whereas you have been forsaken and hated, with no one passing through, I will make you majestic forever, a joy from age to age.<sup>16</sup>You shall suck the milk of nations; you shall nurse at the breast of kings; and you shall know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.<sup>17</sup>Instead of bronze I will bring gold, and instead of iron I will bring silver; instead of wood, bronze, instead of stones, iron. I will make your overseers peace and your taskmasters righteousness.<sup>18</sup>Violence shall no more be heard in your land, devastation or destruction within your borders; you shall call your walls Salvation, and your gates Praise.<sup>19</sup>The sun shall be no more your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give you light; but the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory.<sup>20</sup>Your sun shall no more go down, nor your moon withdraw itself; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning shall be ended.<sup>21</sup>Your people shall all be righteous; they shall possess the land forever, the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I might be glorified.<sup>22</sup>The least one shall become a clan, and the smallest one a mighty nation; I am the LORD; in its time I will hasten it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem is commanded to arise and shine because the glory of the LORD has risen upon her while darkness covers the earth. Nations and kings will come to her light. Caravans from afar bring gold, frankincense, and the wealth of nations. Former oppressors will serve her. The sun and moon will no longer be needed — the LORD himself will be everlasting light. The least shall become a clan; the smallest a mighty nation.
verseByVerse.theology: New Jerusalem: Isaiah 60 is the Old Testament source for Revelation 21's vision of the New Jerusalem. The nations walking by its light (v.3; Rev 21:24), the gates never shut (v.11; Rev 21:25), no sun needed (v.19-20; Rev 21:23), the city named Salvation and its walls named Praise (v.18; Rev 21:12) — all these flow directly into John's vision. The chapter is the fullest OT description of the consummated kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer calls ch60 the sunrise chapter — Jerusalem, like a city on a hill, catches the first light of God's dawn and reflects it to a world in darkness. This is the evangelistic logic of the church: we shine not with our own light but with the reflected glory of God who has risen upon us.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you. For behold, darkness covers the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise over you, and his glory will be seen upon you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Arise, shine — the command follows the Redeemer's arrival (59:20). The light is not generated by Jerusalem but received — your light has come, the glory of the LORD has risen upon you. The darkness covering earth and thick darkness covering peoples is the spiritual condition of the nations. But the LORD rises over the city with glory that becomes visible. Jesus applies this logic in Matthew 5:14-16: you are the light of the world. Motyer: the church's mission is not to generate light but to receive and reflect the glory of the LORD. Only in his light do we give light.

verseByVerse.quote: And nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising. Lift up your eyes all around, and see; they all gather together, they come to you; your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall be carried on the hip. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Nations and kings attracted to the light — the centripetal vision of Isaiah (2:2-4; 56:7; 66:18-21). The light of the risen LORD on his people draws the watching world.
