when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."<sup>13</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame;<sup>14</sup>behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit.<sup>15</sup>You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by another name,<sup>16</sup>so that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes.<sup>17</sup>"For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind.<sup>18</sup>But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness.<sup>19</sup>I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress.<sup>20</sup>No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed.<sup>21</sup>They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit.<sup>22</sup>They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for like the days of a tree shall the days of my people be, and my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands.<sup>23</sup>They shall not labor in vain or bear children for calamity, for they shall be the offspring of the blessed of the LORD, and their descendants with them.<sup>24</sup>Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear.<sup>25</sup>The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain," says the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Hands Spread Out All Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the prayer of chapters 63 and 64, and begins by describing himself as available to people who were not looking for him. Verse 1 has him saying 'Here I am, here I am' to a nation that never called on his name; verse 2 has his hands spread out all day to a people walking their own way. Verses 3 to 5 catalogue what they were doing instead — sacrificing in gardens, offering on bricks, sitting in tombs, eating what the law forbade — and end on the most startling line in the passage: keep your distance, I am too holy for you. Verses 6 and 7 answer that there is a written record, and it will be paid.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul quotes both of the first two verses in a single breath, applying verse 1 to Gentiles who found God without seeking him and verse 2 to an Israel to whom God held out his hands all day long (Rom. 10:20-21). The doctrine underneath is that God's initiative precedes every human search: nobody in this chapter starts looking before God starts calling.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 describes a spiritual condition more dangerous than open rebellion — religious superiority worn by people whose actual practice is listed in the two verses above it. The claim to holiness is being used to keep others at a distance, which is the exact inversion of what holiness does in this book, where it drives a man to confess unclean lips.

verseByVerse.quote: I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, "Here I am, here I am," to a nation that was not called by my name. I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name."

Two chapters of desperate prayer have just ended with God apparently silent. This is his answer, and it does not begin where anyone expects. It begins with God describing himself as findable — and findable by people who were not even looking.

Then listen to what he says twice over: Here I am, here I am.

Those are the words a servant says when his master calls. They are what Isaiah himself said in chapter 6, when he heard the voice asking whom to send and answered Here I am, send me. Now it is God saying them, and he is saying them first, and he is saying them to a nation that has not called his name at all. The master is answering a summons nobody issued.

"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices."

The posture in verse 2 is the posture of appeal — arms open, held out, the gesture of someone asking another to come. And the phrase that carries the weight is all the day. Not once. Not at the crisis. For the whole length of the day, held out, to people who were walking the other way while he did it.

Paul takes these two verses and splits them. Verse 1, he says, is about the Gentiles — "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." Verse 2 is about Israel — "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people" (Rom. 10:20-21). One verse describes people who never looked and found him; the next describes people who were looked for and would not come. The difference between them is not effort.

Which settles something about how anyone comes to God. Nobody in this chapter starts the search. The hands were already out, all day, before the first person turned round — and they were still out at the end of the day, after nobody had.

verseByVerse.quote: a people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens and making offerings on bricks; who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat pig's flesh, and broth of tainted meat is in their vessels; who say, "Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you." These are a smoke in my nostrils, a fire that burns all the day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens and making offerings on bricks; who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat pig's flesh, and broth of tainted meat is in their vessels."

The catalogue is specific, and every item is a religious act. That is what makes it damning. These are not people who had abandoned worship; these are people worshipping energetically in every direction at once.

Sacrificing in gardens — the Canaanite grove shrines, with their fertility rites. Making offerings on bricks — an altar of the wrong construction, when the law was explicit about how an altar was to be made. Sitting in tombs and spending the night in secret places — consulting the dead, seeking information from the one place God had forbidden anyone to look for it (8:19). Eating pig's flesh and tainted broth — the food laws broken deliberately, as part of a rite.

Then verse 5, which is the sentence to stop at.

"Who say, 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you.'"

These same people — the tomb-sitters, the garden-worshippers — say this. To others. It is a claim to superior sanctity, used as a reason to keep other people at a distance, and it is made by the most religiously compromised individuals in the book.

Notice what holiness does everywhere else in Isaiah. When it came near a man in chapter 6 he said Woe is me, I am lost, I am a man of unclean lips. Real proximity to God produces a confession. What we have in verse 5 is the exact opposite — holiness as a boundary marker, a way of establishing that one is not like the others, and the entirely reliable sign that a person has not been anywhere near it.

"These are a smoke in my nostrils, a fire that burns all the day." The image is not anger so much as irritation that will not clear — smoke in the face, all day, from a fire somebody else lit. The same phrase as verse 2: all the day. He held out his hands all day, and all day this is what came back.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, it is written before me: "I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will indeed repay into their lap both your iniquities and your fathers' iniquities together, says the LORD; because they made offerings on the mountains and insulted me on the hills, I will measure into their lap payment for their former deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, it is written before me: 'I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will indeed repay into their lap.'"

Something has been written down, and it is lying in front of God. The picture is a ledger — an account kept, entry by entry, over years — and the reason it is mentioned is that the people in question had concluded from the silence that nothing was being recorded.

That is the ordinary inference and it is always wrong. Silence gets read as absence, or as indifference, or as tacit permission. God's answer here is that the silence was not the absence of a response; it was the postponement of one, and meanwhile the writing was going on.

Into their lap. The lap is the fold of a robe gathered up at the waist, which is what a man in that world used as a pocket — you carried grain in it, or coins, or whatever a merchant had just measured out for you. The image is deliberately commercial: this is a quantity measured and poured into the fold of the buyer's own garment. Nothing arbitrary, nothing approximate. He gets exactly what he came away with.

"Both your iniquities and your fathers' iniquities together." That is a hard clause and it should not be softened into unfairness. Isaiah is not saying children are punished for what parents did; he is describing a generation that continued its fathers' practices and so joined itself to the account. The offerings on the mountains had gone on for centuries.

The chapter has, so far, an outstretched hand in verse 2 and an open ledger in verse 6, and both belong to the same God. Neither one cancels the other, and anyone who has to choose between them has not read to verse 8.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — Two Kinds of People, and a Blessing in the Cluster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter divides. Verse 8 gives the reason it does not end in wholesale destruction: as a picker holds up a poor bunch of grapes and says do not throw it away, there is juice in it, so God will not destroy them all. Verses 9 and 10 give the servants a landscape, including a valley named after the nation's worst disgrace. Verses 11 and 12 address those who set tables for the gods of luck. Verses 13 and 14 set the two futures side by side four times over — eat and hunger, drink and thirst, rejoice and be ashamed, sing and wail. Verses 15 and 16 give the servants a new name and declare the former troubles forgotten.
verseByVerse.theology: The division running through these verses is not between Israel and the nations but inside the covenant community itself, and it is drawn by response rather than descent. Verse 12 states the ground plainly: when I called you did not answer, when I spoke you did not listen. And verse 16 twice calls God the God of truth — in Hebrew, the God of Amen, the only place in the Old Testament where that title appears.
verseByVerse.examples: The cluster in verse 8 is the remnant doctrine in a picture anyone can hold. What spares the bunch is not that it is a good bunch; it is that there is something in it worth keeping, and the picker can see it. And Achor in verse 10 is the valley where Achan was stoned (Josh. 7) — the place named Trouble becomes a field where cattle lie down, which is what Hosea meant by a door of hope (Hos. 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "As the new wine is found in the cluster, and they say, 'Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,' so I will do for my servants' sake, and not destroy them all. I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah possessors of my mountains; my chosen shall possess it, and my servants shall dwell there. Sharon shall become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As the new wine is found in the cluster, and they say, 'Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,' so I will do for my servants' sake, and not destroy them all."

Here is the reason the chapter does not end at verse 7, and it is a scene from a vineyard at harvest.

A picker lifts a bunch that is mostly ruined — shrivelled, spoilt, not worth the basket space — and is about to throw it on the ground. Then he sees juice in it. And he says the sentence that saves it: do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it. Something in this bunch will make wine.

That is the doctrine of the remnant in a picture anybody can hold. What spares the cluster is not that it is a good cluster. It plainly is not. It is that there is something in it worth having, and the man holding it can see what nobody standing further off could see.

"I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah possessors of my mountains; my chosen shall possess it, and my servants shall dwell there. Sharon shall become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me."

Two place names, and the second one is doing real work. Sharon is the fertile coastal plain, and there is no surprise in cattle there. Achor is different. Achor means trouble, and it is the valley where Achan was taken out and stoned after he stole from the spoil at Jericho — the site of the nation's first and most humiliating covenant failure in the land (Josh. 7:24-26). It was named after the disaster and it kept the name.

God says herds will lie down there. Not that the valley will be avoided, or renamed, or quietly forgotten, but that the place called Trouble will become the place where animals lie down in the afternoon because there is nothing to be afraid of. Hosea says the same thing in three words: the Valley of Achor as a door of hope (Hos. 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: But you who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny, I will destine you to the sword, and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter, because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But you who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny."

Two more gods appear, and in the Hebrew they have names: Gad and Meni, Fortune and Destiny. They were deities of luck, and the worship described is a meal — a table laid, cups filled with spiced wine, an offering set out to persuade fate to be favourable.

It is the most understandable idolatry in the chapter. Nobody sets a table for Fortune out of conviction; they do it because the future is unknown and terrifying and they want some purchase on it. Every generation has its own version of the meal, and most of them are respectable.

"I will destine you to the sword, and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter."

And there is a pun in the Hebrew that the English cannot carry. The word for I will destine is maniti — the same root as Meni, the god of destiny they have been feeding. They set a table for Destiny; God says, very well, I will destine you.

The point is not wordplay for its own sake. It is that fate was never a free-standing force to be negotiated with. There is one God who appoints outcomes, and the people laying a table for a rival have not escaped his appointment; they have simply chosen a worse one.

"Because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen." The charge is not idolatry as such. It is the failure to answer — and it lands with particular weight in a chapter that opened with God himself calling out Here I am, here I am. He answered before he was asked. They would not answer when they were.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit."

Four times behold, and four contrasts, and the effect of the hammering is that nobody can pretend the two outcomes have been blurred. Eat and hunger. Drink and thirst. Rejoice and be shamed. Sing and wail.

These are the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28 arriving at their final form, and the shape is deliberately covenantal — the same table, the same land, the same God, and two entirely different futures for people who have been living side by side.

The division here is not between Israel and the nations. Both groups in these verses are inside the covenant community. They share ancestry, worship in the same city and read the same law, and the line runs straight between them, drawn by what they did when God called. That has always been the more uncomfortable division and it is the one this book keeps insisting on.

And the terms are physical rather than abstract. Not my servants shall be blessed but my servants shall eat. The vocabulary is bread, water, singing, the noise a person makes when their heart breaks. Isaiah does not deal in general conditions; he deals in what will actually be happening at a table.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by another name, so that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by another name."

One group leaves a name behind as a byword, an example used when people want to say how badly a thing can go. The other group is given a new name altogether — which in Scripture is never a relabelling but a re-founding. Abram became Abraham; Jacob became Israel; and to the one who conquers, Revelation says, God will give a white stone with a new name written on it that no one knows except the one who receives it (Rev. 2:17).

"So that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth."

Twice in one verse God is called the God of truth, and the Hebrew is more striking than the English. It is elohei amen — the God of Amen. It is the only place in the Old Testament where God is given that title, and amen is the word a congregation says when it wants to put its weight on something: let it be so, this is reliable, I stake myself on it.

So God is here named after the word people use to agree with him. He is the God who is the Amen — the one in whom what is said and what is true have never once come apart. And at the other end of the Bible a letter opens with a greeting from "the Amen, the faithful and true witness" (Rev. 3:14), which is a title being worn by a person.

"Because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes." The last clause is the extraordinary one. Not merely forgiven, and not merely put behind the people. Hidden from God's eyes — the wound no longer visible to the one who healed it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–25 — New Heavens and a New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fullest description of the new creation in the Old Testament. Verses 17 and 18 announce new heavens and a new earth and a Jerusalem created to be a joy. Verse 19 removes the sound of weeping. Verse 20 removes infant death and premature age. Verses 21 to 23 reverse the covenant curses one by one — they will build and live in what they build, plant and eat what they plant, and not labour for nothing or bear children into calamity. Verse 24 closes the distance between prayer and answer to nothing. Verse 25 puts the wolf and the lamb at the same grass.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the goal of redemptive history, and it is emphatically physical: houses, vineyards, work, children, animals, soil. The hope held out is not escape from the material world but its repair, which is why Christian faith has always insisted on a bodily resurrection rather than a released soul. Revelation 21:1 takes verse 17 almost word for word, and Revelation 21:4 takes verse 19.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 24 is the direct answer to chapter 64, which ended with a community shouting questions at a silent sky. In the world this chapter describes, the answer arrives before the sentence is finished. And verse 25 is careful about what it does not reverse: dust is still the serpent's food, which is the one sentence of Genesis 3 left standing when everything else has been undone.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind."

The verb is bara, the word used in the first sentence of the Bible and used in Hebrew only of God. Nothing else in the language does this. And what he makes is not a tidier version of the present arrangement but new heavens and a new earth — the whole frame of things, top and bottom, sky and ground.

John saw it and reported it in almost these words: "Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away" (Rev. 21:1). Peter uses the same phrase and adds what will be living there: new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Pet. 3:13).

"The former things shall not be remembered or come into mind." That clause troubles people, and it should be read carefully. It does not promise amnesia, and it is not saying that what happened to you did not happen or did not matter — the God speaking is the one who keeps a ledger in verse 6 and counts every tear elsewhere in Scripture. What it promises is eclipse. The former things will not come into mind because there will be something in front of them large enough that the mind does not go back.

"But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness."

And then a sentence that repays a second look: God creates joy. Gladness is not described here as a mood the redeemed will manage to work up once the conditions are right. It is listed among the things he makes, with the same verb as the heavens and the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress."

The first half of the verse is easy to read past and should not be. I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people. God is the one enjoying himself here. The gladness of the new creation begins with his, and ours is downstream of it.

Then the second half, and Isaiah does something very precise. He does not say there will be no more sorrow, in the abstract. He says a sound will no longer be heard.

Anybody who has been in a hospital at night, or a house after a death, or a corridor outside a room where bad news is being given, knows that sound. It is the most recognisable noise human beings make, and it is entirely distinct from any other kind of crying. Isaiah promises a city in which it is never heard again — not because people have learned to bear it quietly, but because there is nothing left to make it.

John reaches for the same picture and makes it more intimate still: he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore (Rev. 21:4). The tears are not merely stopped. They are wiped off a face, by a hand, one person at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed."

This is the hardest verse in the chapter, and honesty requires saying why. Everything around it describes a world without weeping — and this verse still has people dying in it.

Godly readers take it two ways and neither should be dismissed. Some understand the chapter as describing a long intermediate age before the final state, in which death is drastically reduced but not abolished. Others read the whole passage as poetry that describes an unimaginable condition in the strongest terms an ancient reader had available — for whom the most extravagant possible picture of flourishing was a world where nobody buries a baby and the old die full of years. On that reading the numbers are not a ceiling but a way of saying that the ceiling is gone. The New Testament finally says it without figures: death shall be no more.

Stay with what the verse names, whichever way it is read, because the two griefs it removes are the ones that break people. An infant who lives but a few days. An old man who does not fill out his days — the life cut off with things unfinished, the plans that never got made.

Isaiah does not comfort the exiles by telling them these losses are small. He tells them the losses are going to stop. For anyone who has stood at the wrong kind of graveside that is the promise being made here, and it is made in the specific terms of the loss rather than in general assurances about eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for like the days of a tree shall the days of my people be, and my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat."

Read those two verses against Deuteronomy 28, and they turn out to be a curse being undone clause by clause. Among the covenant curses Moses set out was this: "You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it. You shall plant a vineyard, but you shall not enjoy its fruit" (Deut. 28:30). Isaiah takes that sentence and reverses it, keeping the same two examples in the same order.

It is the specific misery of a conquered people, and it is not archaic. To build something and have somebody else live in it. To plant and have somebody else pick. To do the work and watch the benefit walk away — which happens in occupied countries, and in bad companies, and in families, and to anyone who has poured years into something that was taken over by someone who did not build it.

"For like the days of a tree shall the days of my people be, and my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands."

And then the measure, which is a tree. Not a human lifespan — the life of an olive or a cedar, which stands through the lifetimes of the people who planted it and the people who buried them. The point is not merely length. It is that the days of God's people are being measured on a scale where the things they make outlast the anxiety that made them.

Long enjoy the work of their hands. Not just possess it. Enjoy it, at length. Work in the new creation is not abolished and it is not endless drudgery. It is finally worth doing, and the person who did it is still there to sit under it.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not labor in vain or bear children for calamity, for they shall be the offspring of the blessed of the LORD, and their descendants with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They shall not labor in vain or bear children for calamity, for they shall be the offspring of the blessed of the LORD, and their descendants with them."

Two futilities, and between them they cover most of what a person spends a life on.

Labour in vain. The effort that goes nowhere — the project cancelled after four years, the business that never came right, the years given to something that quietly came to nothing. Anyone who has worked hard at a thing that failed knows the specific flatness of it, which is not grief exactly but the sense of having spent something irrecoverable.

Bear children for calamity. This is the heavier of the two, and Isaiah puts it in the bluntest possible terms. It is what a mother in a besieged city thinks about: that the child in her arms is being raised for a disaster she can already see coming. It is also what any parent feels in a smaller register when they look at the world their children will have to live in and wonder what they have done in bringing them into it.

Both are cancelled in one sentence, and the ground given is not improved circumstances but lineage: they shall be the offspring of the blessed of the LORD. The reason the work will not be wasted and the children will not be born into catastrophe is that these people belong to God, and what belongs to him does not come to nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear."

To feel the weight of this, remember what has just happened in the book. Chapter 63 ended with a community asking God why he was holding back. Chapter 64 ended with three open questions and no reply — "Will you restrain yourself at these things, O LORD? Will you keep silent, and afflict us so terribly?" The prayer stopped and nothing came back.

This verse is the answer, and it does not merely promise that prayers will be heard. It removes the gap entirely. Before they call I will answer. The response is underway before the request has been made, which means the delay that shaped the whole experience of chapters 63 and 64 will not exist.

"While they are yet speaking I will hear." Anyone who prays knows the second half of that sentence from the inside — the sense of talking into a room, the pause after the amen, the wondering whether the thing was heard at all. Isaiah promises a world in which the hearing has already happened by the middle of the sentence.

And this is plainly a promise about the age to come, not a description of the present one. God does not always answer now before we call; the whole of chapter 64 exists because he did not. What this verse gives is the direction of travel. The silence is a feature of the interval, not of God, and it has a stated end.

verseByVerse.quote: The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain, says the LORD."

The peaceable kingdom of chapter 11 comes back, and it comes back as a permanent condition rather than a vision. The wolf is not restrained from eating the lamb; the wolf is grazing. The lion is not fed elsewhere to keep it off the cattle; it eats straw, like an ox, which is a change in what the lion is.

That is the difference between a truce and a new creation. Nothing here is being held apart by force. The violence built into the present order — the fact that most living things stay alive by killing other living things — is not being policed. It is being removed.

And then, in the middle of that sentence, one thing is left exactly as it was: dust shall be the serpent's food.

Go back to Genesis 3, where the serpent was told: "on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life" (Gen. 3:14). Every other curse in the chapter has been lifted. The ground, the labour, the childbearing, the dying, the predation — all of it undone. The sentence passed on the serpent stands.

Isaiah is not making a point about snakes. He is saying that in the world to come the evil that started all of this will not have been rehabilitated, negotiated with, or given a second hearing. It will be defeated, permanently and visibly, in a world where everything else has been healed.

"They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain." That is the last word of the chapter and it is the whole ambition of God for his world in six syllables. No hurting. No destroying. Anywhere on the mountain. He said he would create it, and he does not lay out what he cannot build.

66.subtitle: This Is the One to Whom I Will Look
66.intro:
Overview. Isaiah’s last chapter opens by demolishing the idea that God can be housed: heaven is his throne and the earth his footstool, so what building could anyone offer him? And then, in the next breath, the most surprising sentence in the last third of the book — this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word. Worship offered by people who have chosen their own way is put beside four atrocities and called the same thing, because the question was never the ritual.

Then a nation is born in a day, before the labour even starts; God asks whether he would bring a birth to the point of delivery and stop; and the great word of chapter 40 finally lands in its most personal form — as one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you. The book closes on a scale nothing prepares the reader for: fire and judgment with all flesh, all nations and tongues gathered to see God’s glory, survivors sent to countries that have never heard of him, foreigners taken for priests and Levites, and unending worship from Sabbath to Sabbath. The final verse is about the dead, and Isaiah leaves the two destinations standing side by side without resolving them.

keyVerse.quote: “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.”
keyVerse.note: The cosmic God — whose throne is heaven and footstool the earth — focuses his gaze on one kind of person. Not the magnificent, not the impressive, not the doctrinally complete: the humble and trembling. This is the first beatitude in Old Testament form. It is also the conclusion Isaiah has been building toward: after 66 chapters about the incomparable God, the question is not what house will satisfy him but what heart — and the answer is the broken, attentive one.

66.theology:
Condescension. Verses 1 and 2 make the argument by scale: the wider God is, the more startling his attention. He whom heaven cannot house fixes his gaze on one afflicted, broken person who shakes at his word — and nothing on that list is an achievement. Two of the three are damage. This is the first beatitude in Old Testament clothing, and Stephen quoted it to the Sanhedrin against an idolatry of the temple itself (Acts 7:49-50).

Worship, and the self-will underneath it. The four shocking equivalences of verse 3 are not an attack on sacrifice, which God commanded. The explanation is in the same verse: these have chosen their own ways. An offering made in self-will has not become a lesser offering; it has changed category. Chapter 1 said this on the book’s first page, which is how the two ends of Isaiah answer each other.

Two destinations, unresolved. Verse 23 has all flesh worshipping from one Sabbath to the next; verse 24 has the worshippers going out to look at the dead, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. Jesus quoted that verse three times in one conversation (Mark 9:44-48), which makes it harder to soften rather than easier. Isaiah offers no resolution and no reassurance — both are real, both permanent — and the only response the chapter has ever asked for is the one in verse 2.
66.reflection: Isaiah ends not with a resolution but with two destinations placed before the reader. The worm and fire of verse 24 are visible from the place of endless worship in verse 23 — the redeemed will forever know what they were saved from. After 66 chapters of the incomparable God — his holiness, his judgment, his grace, his suffering Servant, his new creation — what is your response? Is it trembling at his word? Humble faith? The book leaves the question with you, as every prophet must.
66.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me, and what is the place of my rest?<sup>2</sup>All these things my hand has made, and so all these things came to be, declares the LORD. But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.<sup>3</sup>"He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood; he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol. These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations;<sup>4</sup>I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight."<sup>5</sup>Hear the word of the LORD, you who tremble at his word: "Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake have said, 'Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy'; but it is they who shall be put to shame.<sup>6</sup>"The sound of an uproar from the city! A sound from the temple! The sound of the LORD, rendering recompense to his enemies!<sup>7</sup>"Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son.<sup>8</sup>Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children.<sup>9</sup>Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth?" says the LORD; "shall I, who cause to bring forth, shut the womb?" says your God.<sup>10</sup>"Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her;<sup>11</sup>that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance."<sup>12</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the nations like an overflowing stream; and you shall nurse, you shall be carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees.<sup>13</sup>As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass; and the hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies.<sup>15</sup>"For behold, the LORD will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire.<sup>16</sup>For by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many.<sup>17</sup>"Those who sanctify and purify themselves to go into the gardens, following one in the midst, eating pig's flesh and the abomination and mice, shall come to an end together, declares the LORD.<sup>18</sup>"For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory,<sup>19</sup>and I will set a sign among them. And from them I will send survivors to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the coastlands far away, that have not heard my fame or seen my glory. And they shall declare my glory among the nations.<sup>20</sup>And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and on dromedaries, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the LORD, just as the Israelites bring their grain offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>And some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites, says the LORD.<sup>22</sup>"For as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me, says the LORD, so shall your offspring and your name remain.<sup>23</sup>From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD.<sup>24</sup>"And they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The One to Whom I Will Look
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last chapter opens by demolishing the idea that God can be housed. Verse 1 asks what building could hold someone whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth. Verse 2 makes the whole cosmos his handiwork and then narrows to a single person he attends to: the humble and contrite who trembles at his word. Verses 3 and 4 put four acts of worship beside four atrocities and call them equivalent, because of who is offering them. Verse 5 speaks to people thrown out by their own brothers, and verse 6 has a noise coming from the temple that is God settling accounts.
verseByVerse.theology: The movement of verses 1 and 2 is the whole doctrine of God's condescension in two sentences: the wider the scale, the more startling the attention. He who fills heaven and earth looks at one small trembling person, and the looking is not pity but regard. And verses 3 and 4 give the reason worship can be worthless — not because the ritual is wrong but because these have chosen their own ways. An offering made in self-will is not a lesser offering; it is a different act altogether.
verseByVerse.examples: Stephen quoted verses 1 and 2 to the Sanhedrin minutes before they killed him (Acts 7:49-50), using them against an idolatry of the temple itself. And verse 2 is the Old Testament form of the first beatitude — blessed are the poor in spirit — and of the tax collector who would not lift his eyes (Luke 18:13). The whole book has been about an incomparable God; it turns out the question was never what house would suit him but what heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me, and what is the place of my rest? All these things my hand has made, and so all these things came to be, declares the LORD. But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD: 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me, and what is the place of my rest?'"

Picture the proportions. If heaven is the chair and the whole earth is the low stool the feet rest on, then the being described is not large — he is off the scale entirely, and the planet is a piece of furniture he is not using for much. Against that, the question about a house answers itself. Any building anyone could put up is a box on the footstool.

This is aimed at people who had a temple project and a good deal of confidence in it. Isaiah is not against the temple; God commanded it. He is against the assumption underneath it — that God can be sited, and that having sited him you have him.

"All these things my hand has made, and so all these things came to be, declares the LORD. But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word."

And there is the turn, and it is the most surprising sentence in the last third of the book. From the whole created order in one clause, to one person in the next.

To this one I will look. The verb is a deliberate gaze — to fix attention on something, to regard it. The God who cannot be housed by the cosmos looks steadily at a particular person, and Isaiah tells us how to find him. He is humble, which here means afflicted, brought low, not necessarily by choice. He is contrite in spirit — literally struck, broken. And he trembles at God's word: when Scripture says something, it registers in his body.

Nothing in the list is an achievement. Not learning, not office, not a record of service, not the ability to build anything. Two of the three describe damage. This is the first beatitude in Old Testament clothing — blessed are the poor in spirit — and it is the tax collector at the back of the temple who would not lift his eyes (Luke 18:13).

Stephen quoted these two verses to the Sanhedrin, in the last speech of his life, minutes before they picked up stones (Acts 7:49-50). He used them exactly as Isaiah did: against people who had made the building the point.

Sixty-six chapters have gone into establishing that this God is beyond comparison — the throne, the seraphim, the oceans in his palm, the nations as dust. And what he looks at is a broken person who shakes when he reads. The distance between those two facts is the distance grace has to travel, and he crosses it without apparent effort, every time.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood; he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol. These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations; I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood; he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol."

Four pairings, and each sets a prescribed act of worship beside something revolting. The ox and the murder. The lamb and the dog with its neck broken — a dog being an unclean scavenger, and the killing of one a worthless, contemptible act. The grain offering and pig's blood, which combines the forbidden animal with the forbidden substance. The frankincense and the blessing of an idol.

These are not attacks on the sacrificial system. God designed it. Every one of the four first items was commanded, and a person doing them was doing what he had been told.

The explanation comes in the second half of the verse: these have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations. The offering is identical; the man behind it is not. And Isaiah's claim is not that such worship counts for less. It is that it has changed category altogether — that an offering made by someone who has settled on his own path, and who privately enjoys what God hates, is not a weak sacrifice but a different act wearing a sacrifice's clothes.

That is a hard thing to read for anyone who attends church regularly. It means the question at a service is never whether the right things are being done. Chapter 1 said the same thing on the first page of the book — incense that is an abomination, festivals God's soul hates, hands spread out in prayer that he will not look at because they are full of blood. The book ends where it started, and the charge has not changed in sixty-five chapters.

"Because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen." There is the root of it, in the same words as 65:12. The worship failed at the point where the listening failed. A man who will not hear God on Tuesday is not able to worship him on Sunday, whatever he brings.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, you who tremble at his word: "Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake have said, 'Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy'; but it is they who shall be put to shame. "The sound of an uproar from the city! A sound from the temple! The sound of the LORD, rendering recompense to his enemies!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hear the word of the LORD, you who tremble at his word: 'Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake have said, "Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy"; but it is they who shall be put to shame.'"

Now the people of verse 2 turn up in a situation, and it repays a close look. See exactly what it is. They are being hated and expelled — and not by pagans. By your brothers. The people doing the throwing out are inside the covenant community, and they are doing it for my name's sake: this is religious persecution of the devout by the religious.

And the mockery quoted is unnervingly modern. Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy. It is said in pious language, with the right vocabulary, and it means: go on then, let's see this God of yours do something. It is a sneer built entirely out of orthodox words.

Jesus warned his disciples about precisely this arrangement — they will put you out of the synagogues, and the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God (John 16:2). The pattern in verse 5 did not stop with Isaiah's generation.

God's answer is four words: it is they who shall be put to shame. Not an argument, not a defence of the outcast, not an explanation of the delay. A statement about how the thing will end.

"The sound of an uproar from the city! A sound from the temple! The sound of the LORD, rendering recompense to his enemies!"

Three exclamations, and Isaiah writes them as a man hearing something before he can see it. Noise from the city. Noise from the temple. And then the identification — that is the LORD, paying people back. The vindication the mockers demanded arrives, and it does not arrive as a demonstration for their benefit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Born in a Day, and Comforted Like a Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A woman gives birth before the labour starts. Verses 7 and 8 press how impossible that is — shall a land be born in one day, shall a nation be brought forth in a moment? — and answer that Zion did exactly that. Verse 9 has God refusing to bring a birth to the point of delivery and then stop. Verses 10 and 11 call everyone who loves Jerusalem, and everyone who has mourned over her, to feed at her and be satisfied. Verses 12 and 13 extend peace like a river and then give the tenderest comparison in the book: as one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you. Verse 14 has bones flourishing like grass.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is the argument from divine consistency that grounds Christian assurance: God does not begin what he abandons. Paul says the same thing to the Philippians about the work begun in them. And the maternal imagery running through verses 11 to 13 is not decoration — it is how this book finally cashes the word it opened with at 40:1. Comfort my people was the commission; as one whom his mother comforts is what it turns out to mean.
verseByVerse.examples: The suddenness of verses 7 and 8 is the shape of Pentecost, where three thousand were added in a single day and a community that had not existed that morning existed by the evening. Nothing gradual, nothing accumulated. And verse 5 has already named the people this comfort is for: those cast out by their own brothers for God's name's sake.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children. Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth?" says the LORD; "shall I, who cause to bring forth, shut the womb?" says your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son."

Something impossible is being described, and Isaiah reports it flatly before drawing attention to it. A child arrives with no labour at all — no build-up, no hours, no warning.

"Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children."

Then four questions in a row, and their function is to stop the reader treating this as a figure of speech. Isaiah is insisting on how absurd the claim is. Nations are not born in a day. They accumulate — generations, wars, migrations, slow settlement — and there is no instance anywhere of one simply existing by evening that did not exist that morning.

That is exactly what he says will happen.

Read Acts 2 with this in mind. In the morning there is a room with about a hundred and twenty people in it. By the evening three thousand have been added, from fifteen named regions, speaking a dozen languages, and the church exists. No gestation. Peter preaches one sermon and a nation is brought forth in a moment, which is the only category Isaiah's question leaves available.

"Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth?" says the LORD; "shall I, who cause to bring forth, shut the womb?" says your God.

And here is the argument the whole passage rests on, put as a question no one can answer yes to. God does not take a thing to the edge of delivery and then abandon it. The one who starts a birth finishes it, because stopping there would be a kind of cruelty he is not capable of.

Paul says the same thing in one sentence to people worried about their own perseverance: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Phil. 1:6). The confidence is not in the strength of the thing being born. It is in the character of the one delivering it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her; that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her."

Notice who is invited. Two groups, and the second one is the surprise: those who love her, and those who mourn over her. The people who have spent years grieving about the state of the city are specifically named and told to celebrate.

That is a particular kindness. It is the people who cared enough to be heartbroken who are called first to the party — and it means the mourning was never wasted. Somebody who has wept for years over a church, or a family, or a country, is on the guest list precisely because of the weeping.

"That you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance."

The image is startling and is meant to be. Jerusalem is a nursing mother, and the mourners are infants at the breast — which is to say, entirely dependent, taking in what they did nothing to produce, and being satisfied, a word that means fed to the point where nothing more is wanted.

Isaiah could have described the restored city in any number of ways: a fortress, a throne, a court, a harvest. What he chooses is the most intimate physical relationship human beings have, in which one person is kept alive by another's body without ever asking for it. And drink deeply with delight — the verb suggests draining something to the bottom.

The city that was a ruin two chapters ago is now feeding people. Restoration in this book is never merely the end of trouble; it is the beginning of somebody else's nourishment.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the nations like an overflowing stream; and you shall nurse, you shall be carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees. As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the nations like an overflowing stream; and you shall nurse, you shall be carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees."

Peace like a river is a phrase worn smooth by use, and the picture underneath it is specific. A river is not a rainfall; it does not arrive in bursts and stop. It runs, at volume, past the same bank, in the dry season as well as the wet. What is promised is not a period of calm but a supply.

And then three things done to a small child by an adult, listed in order: fed, carried on the hip, bounced on the knees. The last one is not about need at all. Nobody bounces a baby to keep it alive. It is done for delight, because the adult is enjoying the child, and Isaiah puts it at the end of the sentence as the point the others were leading to.

"As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem."

Go back to 40:1, where this whole half of the book began: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. That was the commission, and for twenty-six chapters the question of what it would actually mean has been left open. Here is the answer, in the last chapter, and it could not be more personal.

God takes the plainest experience of comfort anyone has — a child who has come off worst somewhere and is being held by his mother, saying nothing useful, not fixing anything, just holding him until it stops — and says: like that. Not I will send you comfort. I will comfort you, myself, in that manner.

He is not embarrassed by the comparison and does not qualify it. The God whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, who measures the sea in the hollow of his hand and calls the stars out by name, describes himself as a mother with a crying child on her shoulder — and that is how the book's great word finally lands.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass; and the hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass; and the hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies."

"Your bones shall flourish like the grass." It is an odd image until you have felt the opposite. Bones in Hebrew stand for the deepest physical self, the part of you that aches when everything is wrong; the psalms speak of bones wasting away, bones out of joint, bones burning. What Isaiah promises is greenness in that place — the spring flush after rain, happening at the level of the skeleton.

It is a promise of recovery in the part of a person that recovers last. Anyone who has come out of a long grief knows that the mind agrees things are better some time before the body does. Here the body agrees.

Then the second half of the verse, and it holds two things together without apology: the hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies. One hand, two effects. The same intervention that greens the bones of the servants is the one his enemies meet, and Isaiah will not separate them into two different Gods for the comfort of the reader.

These closing chapters keep doing this, and it is deliberate. The kindness in verse 13 is not a softer God than the fire in verse 15. It is the same God, and what he is like depends entirely on which side of his hand you are standing on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — Fire, the Nations Gathered, and Two Endings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book closes on a scale nothing has prepared the reader for. Verses 15 and 16 bring the LORD in fire and whirlwind to judge all flesh. Verse 17 ends the garden-worshippers of chapter 65. Verses 18 to 20 gather all nations and tongues, send survivors to countries that have never heard God's fame, and have them bring the scattered home as an offering. Verse 21 takes some of those foreigners and makes them priests and Levites. Verses 22 and 23 promise that the new heavens and new earth will outlast everything, with all flesh coming to worship from one Sabbath to the next. Verse 24 is the last sentence, and it is about the dead.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 21 is the most radical inclusion in the Old Testament: offices restricted to one tribe of one nation are handed to men from Tarshish and Javan. It is Exodus 19:6 reaching further than anyone expected, and Peter applies the same words to a church drawn from everywhere (1 Pet. 2:9). Then verses 23 and 24 place two destinations side by side and leave them there. Isaiah does not resolve them, and neither did Jesus, who quoted verse 24 three times in a single conversation (Mark 9:44-48).
verseByVerse.examples: The missionary structure of verses 19 and 20 is the shape of the church: those who have seen the glory are sent to those who have not, so that they can come and see it too. And the book's final image refuses to send the reader away comfortable. Everlasting worship and everlasting loss are both real, both permanent, and the only response the chapter has asked for is the one in verse 2 — to tremble at his word.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, the LORD will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For behold, the LORD will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many."

Two verses after a mother comforting a child, this. Isaiah puts them next to each other without a transition, and the absence of a transition is the argument.

The imagery is military and it is at full stretch — fire, chariots moving like a whirlwind, fury, flames, a sword. And the scope is total: with all flesh. Not with Babylon, not with the nations, not with the rebels inside Israel. Everyone alive is inside the sentence.

"Those slain by the LORD shall be many." Isaiah writes it plainly, and it should be read plainly. There is a strand of Christian thinking that treats the wrath of God as an Old Testament embarrassment outgrown by the New; the difficulty with that is Jesus, who spoke about judgment more than anyone else in Scripture and who quotes the last verse of this very chapter three times in one conversation.

What holds the chapter together is that both of its halves are true of one God. The tenderness of verse 13 is not a mood he was in before the fire arrived. A love that is genuinely committed to what it loves must be against what destroys it, and a God who could look at the wreckage of his world and feel nothing in particular would not be worth worshipping. The fire in verse 15 is what the comfort in verse 13 costs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who sanctify and purify themselves to go into the gardens, following one in the midst, eating pig's flesh and the abomination and mice, shall come to an end together, declares the LORD. "For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Those who sanctify and purify themselves to go into the gardens, following one in the midst, eating pig's flesh and the abomination and mice, shall come to an end together, declares the LORD."

The garden cults of chapter 65 come back for their verdict, and the detail Isaiah keeps is the one that matters: these people sanctify and purify themselves before going in. There is a ritual. There are preparations. They are scrupulous about it.

That is the sting. The scrupulousness is real and it is pointed in the wrong direction — careful, costly religious effort, expended on rites God never asked for. The chapter has already said in verse 3 that this is the problem: the acts look devout and the choosing behind them is self-will.

"For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory."

And now the book opens out, in a single sentence, further than it ever has. From a handful of syncretists in a grove to all nations and tongues — every people group and every language on earth — gathered to see the glory of God.

Notice that the judgment and the ingathering are the same event. Verse 17 ends one group; verse 18 gathers the world. They are not alternatives and they are not separated by centuries in the text. The fire that consumes what will not stand and the light that draws the nations are one blaze, seen from two positions.

They shall come and shall see my glory. Everything the book has been about is in those six words. Not hear about it, not be told of it. See it.

verseByVerse.quote: and I will set a sign among them. And from them I will send survivors to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the coastlands far away, that have not heard my fame or seen my glory. And they shall declare my glory among the nations. And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and on dromedaries, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the LORD, just as the Israelites bring their grain offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And I will set a sign among them. And from them I will send survivors to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the coastlands far away, that have not heard my fame or seen my glory. And they shall declare my glory among the nations."

Read the names, because they are not decoration. Tarshish is the far west, most likely Spain — the end of the Mediterranean and the edge of the map. Pul and Lud are in Africa. Tubal is away to the north, in Asia Minor. Javan is Greece. And then the coastlands far away, which is Isaiah's phrase for everywhere he has not got a name for.

And the qualification attached to them: places that have not heard my fame or seen my glory. The mission is aimed by ignorance. The people who get sent are sent precisely where nothing is known.

Who does the sending? Survivors. The men and women who came through the fire of verse 16 are the messengers — people whose entire qualification is that they were spared and know it. There is no other credential mentioned.

"And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD ... to my holy mountain Jerusalem, just as the Israelites bring their grain offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD."

Then the traffic reverses. The nations who received the message come back carrying people — the scattered brought home on horses, in chariots, in litters, on mules and camels, the way a family conveys someone who cannot travel alone.

And the word for what they are carrying is offering. The nations arrive at the temple with a gift, and the gift is people. Paul, whose whole life was verse 19, describes his ministry the same way: he is a priest, and the offering he presents is the Gentiles themselves (Rom. 15:16).

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites, says the LORD. "For as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me, says the LORD, so shall your offspring and your name remain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites, says the LORD."

Ten words, and in their original setting they are almost unthinkable.

The priesthood was not open. It was not a matter of calling, or piety, or gifting: you were a priest if you were descended from Aaron, and a Levite if you came from Levi, and no amount of devotion could make a man from another tribe eligible. King Uzziah tried, in the first chapter of this rebuild, and came out of the temple a leper.

Some of them. The pronoun points back to verse 20 — the nations. Men from Tarshish and Javan, from the coastlands, with no ancestry in Israel at all, will be taken by God for priests and Levites. Not admitted to the courtyard. Not permitted to worship at a distance. Taken for the office itself.

At Sinai God had said Israel would be to him a kingdom of priests (Exod. 19:6), and the book has spent sixty-five chapters showing how that went. Here the promise is kept, and kept wider than the people it was made to. Peter takes those same words and hands them to congregations in five Roman provinces: you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation (1 Pet. 2:9).

"For as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me, says the LORD, so shall your offspring and your name remain."

And the guarantee on all of it is the durability of the new creation itself. The permanence of God's people is measured against the permanence of the remade universe — the two are given the same lifetime, which is to say no lifetime at all, because neither of them ends.

verseByVerse.quote: From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD."

The two phrases mark out the rhythm of Israel's calendar — the month and the week, the cycles by which time itself was measured and by which worship was scheduled. Isaiah takes them and stretches them over the new creation: from one to the next, and then the next, without end.

And the congregation is all flesh. The book has used that phrase before, and never comfortably — all flesh is grass (40:6); by fire will the LORD enter into judgment with all flesh (66:16). Here it is used for the last time, and it means everybody who is left, from every nation named in verse 19, worshipping.

What the verse describes is not an event but a permanent condition. Not a great day of worship at the end of history, but worship as the ordinary content of unending time — the thing that is simply happening, week after week, world without end.

That is a strange prospect to a modern reader, who tends to find an hour of it long enough. The strangeness is a measure of how little we have seen. In this chapter the worshippers have seen his glory (v. 18) — and once anyone has, the difficulty is not sustaining worship but stopping it.

This is where the book has been going since a young man in chapter 6 watched creatures with six wings cover their faces and heard them call to one another, holy, holy, holy. The song they were singing over one throne, in one room, in one year that a king died, turns out to be the sound of the whole world.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh."

This is the last sentence of the book, and Isaiah does not end where a writer wanting to be liked would end. One verse ago the whole world was worshipping. Now the worshippers walk out and look at the dead.

The picture is drawn from the valley outside Jerusalem where refuse was burned and the bodies of criminals were thrown — the fire never entirely out, the maggots always working. It was a real place, visible from the city wall, and its name was Gehenna. Jesus used that name for hell, and he quoted this verse — their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched — three times in a single conversation with his disciples (Mark 9:44-48).

Two things must be said plainly, without softening either.

The first is that the language is permanent. The worm does not die and the fire is not quenched; these are not temporary measures, and nothing in the verse suggests the condition comes to an end. Universalism has to get past this sentence, and Jesus, who quoted it, made it harder rather than easier.

The second is that this verse is set immediately beside the worship of verse 23, and both are held open at once. Isaiah offers no resolution. He does not tell the reader how to feel about it, does not moralise, and does not close the book on a note of reassurance. Two destinations, both real, both final, and the reader standing in front of them.

So what is the response the book asks for? It asked for it in the second verse of this chapter and has not changed the answer since: this is the one to whom I will look, he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.

Not the man who builds God a house. Not the one who is scrupulous about his rituals in the garden. Not the brother who casts others out for the name's sake. The one who is broken, who has stopped defending himself, and who shakes when God speaks — because he has understood who is speaking. That was the answer in chapter 6 when a prophet said I am undone and a coal was brought from the altar, and it is the answer on the last page.

The book began with a God whose people did not know him as well as an ox knows its owner, and it ends with all flesh before his face. Between those two sentences stands a servant who was despised and rejected, who was pierced for our transgressions, and on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all. He is the reason anyone is in verse 23 rather than verse 24, and there is no other reason. Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.

0.subtitle: Introduction
0.intro:
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem through the reigns of four kings — Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah — from around 740 to 700 BC. His call came in the year that King Uzziah died (chapter 6): a vision of the Lord high and lifted up, the seraphim crying Holy, holy, holy, and the commission to speak a word that most would refuse to hear. From that moment Isaiah became the greatest of the writing prophets — and this book became what Luther called “the fifth Gospel.”

The book divides naturally into two great halves. Chapters 1–39 address the Assyrian crisis: God’s judgment on Israel and Judah, the fate of the surrounding nations, and the demand for faith in the Holy One rather than military alliance. Chapters 40–66 address a people in Babylonian exile, not yet experienced but anticipated by prophetic foresight: comfort, homecoming, and the glorious emergence of the Servant who bears the sin of the world. The two halves share the same vocabulary, the same theology, and the same God — against all critical attempts to divide them.

The name of God that defines the book is the Holy One of Israel. It appears twenty-six times in Isaiah and only six times in the rest of the Old Testament. Holiness is not merely moral purity; it is the utter otherness of God, his transcendent glory that both terrifies and draws. Everything in Isaiah — judgment and comfort, wrath and mercy — flows from who this God is. The prophet’s task is to make the Holy One of Israel known.

The four Servant Songs (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12) form the theological heartbeat of the second half. They move from the Servant’s gentle justice to his voluntary suffering — despised, crushed, pierced for our transgressions — and his ultimate vindication. The New Testament quotes or alludes to Isaiah more than any other Old Testament book. Jesus opened his ministry with Isaiah 61. Philip expounded Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian on the road. John saw Isaiah 6 as a vision of Christ’s glory.

To preach Isaiah is to preach the whole gospel in its Old Testament register: the holiness that makes sin impossible to ignore, the grace that makes forgiveness inconceivably costly, and the glory of a God who will not rest until his purposes fill the earth as the waters cover the sea. Sproul said that no book of Scripture humbled him more. No book of Scripture delighted him more either. Both responses flow from the same source: the Holy One of Israel, sovereign, saving, and surpassingly glorious.
